💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1687, Sir Isaac Newton released his magnum opus, PhilosophiÃ¦ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), in which he described his theories of motion and gravity.
  • According to recent reports, according to a recent study from the Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories.
  • Industry observers note that the study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1687, Sir Isaac Newton released his magnum opus, PhilosophiÃ¦ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), in which he described his theories of motion and gravity. His theory of the latter accurately described the motion of the Earth's tides, something that scientists had been wrestling with for centuries. For over three hundred years, Newton's work remained scientific canon and the last word on gravity, until Albert Einstein introduced his Theory of General Relativity.

According to recent reports, according to a recent study from the Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories. While the pull of the Sun and Moon and their influence on the tides can be predicted very accurately using Newtonian gravity, GR offers a fuller description that includes gravitational waves (GWs). The upcoming study merges these two theories into a single model that could offer a new way to test our understanding of gravity.

Industry observers note that the study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB. His work extends the classical model of lunar tides to include the cross polarization of gravitational waves, one of the key ways GWs can deform spacetime as they pass through. As he explained in a FUB press release:.

Sources indicate that isaac Newton explains the tides extremely well. Albert Einstein reveals us that gravity is also dynamic and that changes in spacetime can propagate as waves. Our work brings both perspectives together and asks what traces of this might be found in high-precision measurements.

GWs were originally predicted by Einstein's Theory of General Relativity and refer to ripples in spacetime caused by the merger of massive objects. To date, thousands of GW events have been detected, the majority of which were caused by the merger of black holes or neutron stars. However, GWs can also result from smaller gravitational interactions, such as those produced by the interactions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.

Recent findings suggest that one issue addressed by Eser's study is the difficulty of distinguishing possible additional signals from measurement errors, the choice of reference frame, and uncertainties in calculating the positions of the Sun and Moon. By identifying which influences must be accounted for, Eser shows how a signal could be isolated and the possible physical effects identified. The study therefore presents a quantitative basis for future studies of tidal patterns that deviate from what Newtonian Gravity predicts. Noted Eser:.

It has been revealed that we are not claiming to have discovered a upcoming gravitational effect. What we show is how one could look for it in a targeted way. The EarthâMoon system is particularly interesting for this because we can already describe and measure its tidal effects very precisely.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The body’s inner heater weakens with age, but experiments in older mice suggest it can be turned back up.
  • As we age, staying warm can become more difficult, but the reason may go beyond changes in circulation or muscle mass.
  • Recent findings suggest that now, researchers at City of Hope have uncovered a biological mechanism that helps explain why this natural heating system slows with age.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The body’s inner heater weakens with age, but experiments in older mice suggest it can be turned back up.

As we age, staying warm can become more difficult, but the reason may go beyond changes in circulation or muscle mass. Deep inside the body, a specialized type of fat acts like a built-in heater, burning calories to produce warmth when temperatures drop. Over time, however, this system becomes less responsive, potentially affecting not only how the body handles cold but also how it uses energy.

Recent findings suggest that now, researchers at City of Hope have uncovered a biological mechanism that helps explain why this natural heating system slows with age. Their study, published in Nature, reveals how communication between nerves, immune cells, and heat-producing fat changes over time.

“Learning how the body controls this process may offer insights into obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other metabolic disorders,” stated Qiong “Annabel” Wang, Ph.D., the study’s corresponding author and an associate professor at City of Hope’s Arthur Riggs Diabetes & Metabolism Research Institute.

The body’s heat-producing fat contains cells with different levels of activity. Previous City of Hope research found that some have abundant UCP1, a protein that generates heat, while others contain less and produce less warmth. The new study identified a similar mixture in human thermogenic fat samples, although most experiments were conducted in mice.

According to recent reports, that mixture appears to give the body a reserve of heating capacity. When temperatures fall, nerve and immune signals encourage less active cells to increase their heat output. When the demand for warmth eases, the system can reduce that activity again.

According to recent reports, in older mice, this adjustment became sluggish. Their thermogenic fat retained the ability to produce more heat but took longer to respond, making it harder for the animals to maintain their body temperature during cold exposure.

The researchers then tested whether they could interrupt the pathway behind that delayed response. Using the drug mifepristone to block one part of the pathway restored some heat production in older mice. The animals generated more warmth and burned more energy. The finding suggests that at least some of the decline in thermogenic fat function may be reversible.

According to recent reports, “That possibility matters for more than staying warm,” Wang stated. “Thermogenic fat also burns glucose and fat, and its activity tends to decline with age. If scientists can find a safe, precise way to restore that activity, this foundational research could eventually deepen our understanding of age-related metabolic problems, including obesity and type 2 diabetes.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis” by Anying Song, Yifan Wang, Guan Wang, Marie Bae, Zhichao Wang, Guoming Gao, Zhuyin Wu, Geming Lu, Jieyi Meng, Jiayu Yu, Soojin Park, Adolfo Garcia-Ocaña, Patrick T. Fueger, Loredana Rao, Andrea Frontini, Yong Liu, Lei Jiang, Yi Zhu and Qiong A. Wang, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11308-7.

This study was funded by NIH/National Institutes of Health, the Caltech-City of Hope Biomedical Research Initiative Grant, the City of Hope startup, and salary-saving funds.

Sources indicate that these aren’t your slow-braised, leisurely Sunday-sauce meatballs. They’re let’s-get-this-crew-fed-at-the-end-of-a-busy-workday meatballs. The large amount of breadcrumbs isn’t just a filler; combined with the water, they make the meatballs impossibly tender and springy. You can use any ground meat you’d like; pork, lamb, turkey, or chicken (only dark meat for the poultry, though) all work well. Roasting the meatballs in the oven instead of frying them on the stovetop reduces the active cook time and makes cleanup simple.

More crowd-pleasing meatballs recipes here.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 425°. Using a sturdy wooden spoon, vigorously mix 2 large eggs, zest of 1 lemon, 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, 1 cup panko, ½ cup finely chopped dill and/or parsley, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 2 tsp. dried oregano, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, 1 tsp. ground cumin, and ½ cup water in a large bowl until nearly a smooth paste. Add 1 lb. ground beef and mix vigorously until well combined and mixture is slightly tacky. Oil your hands; divide mixture into 16 portions and roll into balls. Arrange on a large rimmed baking sheet.

It has been revealed that toss 1 large red onion, cut through root end into 2"-thick wedges, 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, a large pinch of salt, and a large pinch of pepper in a small bowl. Arrange in a single layer around meatballs. Bake meatballs and onions until meatballs are deeply browned underneath and an instant-read thermometer inserted into centers registers 160°, 25–30 minutes. Let cool slightly.

To serve, generously top with sliced cucumbers, crumbled feta, and more dill and/or parsley if desired. Serve with country-style bread and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.

The 171-foot-tall (52-meter) space vehicle, known as Ship 42, settled between a giant pair of mechanical arms extended from the South Texas launch tower where its journey began 22.5 hours earlier. The arm-capture system, nicknamed "Mechazilla," had been used three times previously to capture Starship Super Heavy boosters during suborbital flight tests, but this was the first time for a second stage coming in hot from orbit.

"Mechazilla has caught the Starship â we've been waiting to hear that for a long time," SpaceX launch commentator Dan Huot stated.

In addition to the first orbital catch, this week's test marked the longest Starship flight to date, besting a three-hour orbital flight in September.

Industry observers note that years of development â including 15 full-scale flight tests since 2023 â led up to today's orbital catch, which Huot called "the Holy Grail of spaceflight." The achievement took the sting out of the previous day's aborted effort to catch the rocket's booster using the same system, minutes after liftoff. SpaceX stated the booster was diverted when its onboard system detected a fuel-system alarm. The root cause of the alarm is under investigation.

SpaceX intends to use the launch-pad arms to recover Starship's boosters and second stages on a routine basis, achieving company founder Elon Musk's goal of creating a fully reusable, orbital-class launch system.

Sources indicate that this 15th flight test proceeded almost in textbook fashion, aside from the boosterâs offshore splashdown on launch day. During the first hours of its 14-orbit flight, Starship deployed 26 more next-generation satellites for SpaceXâs Starlink broadband internet network. All of the satellites were in good health and beginning to raise their orbits to operational altitude, the manufacturer noted.

At the end of the trip, the second stage fired a single engine for roughly 10 seconds to start its descent through the atmosphere. As the temperatures rose, a brlght glow surrounded Ship 42âs leading edges. The craft executed a bellyflop maneuver to maximize its deceleration. Then it righted itself, and fired its engines a final time to sink into Mechazillaâs arms.

SpaceX employees around the country and hundreds of onlookers near the Texas launch site cheered, while âBaby, Come Backâ played on the soundtrack for the webcast. âBaby, sheâs back,â Huot joked.

Bringing Starship into full operation is expected to speed up deployment of Starlink satellites. More importantly, Starship is slated to serve as a landing system for NASA's crewed moon missions starting as early as 2028. Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system are scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA's Artemis III mission.

In a recent development, in a post to X, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated Musk and the SpaceX team on today's successful catch. "It was almost magic ... Making more believers by the day," he wrote. Using emojis, Isaacman mentioned the achievement brought the United States "one step closer" to putting an American flag once more on the moon.

It has been revealed that spaceX's team will analyze the data gathered about Starship's performance, including the ability of Ship 42's heat shield to stand up to the rigors of atmospheric re-entry. The company is gearing up to expand Starship operations to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and yet another Starship launch site is in the works for Louisiana.

In a recent development, in the long term, Musk envisions creating a fleet of Starships that could offer point-to-point rocket travel on Earth, as well as mass transit to Mars and other off-Earth destinations. Cryptocurrency investor Chun Wang has already announced his intention to take Starship trips around the moon and Mars.

It has been revealed that "I donât think you guys understand," a software engineer named Will DePue wrote in a post to X. "You will get the chance to go to space in your lifetime. New era.".

  • Recent findings suggest that understanding what makes one pancreatic tumor different from another could help doctors tailor treatment to each patient.
  • The study, recently published in Cancer Research, was led by Nina Steele, PhD, an assistant professor in UC’s College of Medicine and a Cancer Center member, in collaboration with Howard Crawford, PhD, scientific director of the Henry Ford + Michigan State University Pancreatic Cancer Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Immune cells may help pancreatic tumors hide from the body’s defenses, with differences between patient groups offering clues that could eventually guide more personalized treatment.

Recent findings suggest that understanding what makes one pancreatic tumor different from another could help doctors tailor treatment to each patient. Researchers at the University of Cincinnati Cancer Center have found newly introduced clues in both cancer cells and the immune cells around them.

The study, recently published in Cancer Research, was led by Nina Steele, PhD, an assistant professor in UC’s College of Medicine and a Cancer Center member, in collaboration with Howard Crawford, PhD, scientific director of the Henry Ford + Michigan State University Pancreatic Cancer Center.

Steele began the project at Henry Ford Health. Working with colleagues there and at UC, she mapped genomic information from a representative sample of Americans diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. The team used a multiomic approach, examining multiple layers of biological information.

It has been revealed that “We didn’t have an accurate reflection of all of the patients impacted by the disease reflected in the data,” Steele said. “There had never been a large-scale multiomic effort looking at tens of thousands of biological markers across a diverse cohort of pancreatic cancer patients.”.

Pancreatic cancer incidence and survival vary across American populations, with Black African Americans 20% more likely to develop the disease. Comparing their tumor samples with those from non-African American patients, the researchers found differences in B cells, a type of immune cell. In Black patients’ samples, these cells were more abundant and more immunosuppressive, dampening the body’s natural immune response against cancer.

“This may mean the B cells are helping the cancer cells hide in this patient population,” Steele said. “This could help explain why this population is more likely to get the cancer, and why it’s worse when they get it, but more work is needed on pancreas tissues from individuals that do not have cancer.”.

The cancer cells themselves also revealed distinct molecular signatures between the two groups.

In a recent development, “The cancer cells make unique RNAs and proteins, so that could be relevant to how individual patients from different groups could respond to targeted therapies like RAS inhibitors,” Steele stated. “The markers upregulated in Black patients likely represent a type of cells typically associated with drug resistance, so this biological difference could play a role in outcomes.”.

In a recent development, RAS inhibitors target proteins involved in cell growth. Further research is needed to understand the mechanisms behind the observed differences and their effects on outcomes. The findings could eventually help researchers identify upcoming pancreatic cancer subtypes, as has happened in breast and prostate cancer, and develop more personalized treatment approaches.

“The Cancer Center is here to serve everybody, and to find the answers that help all patients,” Steele said. “The hope is to know more about the characteristics of the cancer cells earlier on, so that we have a blueprint of attack for what therapies come after current standards of care in a very rational way. We’re headed toward forecasting, the ability to better predict what will happen to every patient in their journey before it happens.”.

In a recent development, reference: “Spatial Transcriptomics on a Diverse Pancreatic Cancer Cohort Reveals Race-Related Differences in Tumor Subtypes and Immune Microenvironments” by Yuesong Wu, Daniel James Sålas-Escabillas, Aoqi Xie, Ian M Loveless, Yasmine Baca, Kailee Hartway, Rama Shankar, Samuel D Zwernik, Logan Schneider, Ashley George, Madison George, Allison Wombwell, Julie M Clark, David S Kwon, Bin Chen, Benjamin H Hinrichs, Ralph Francescone, Débora Barbosa Vendramini-Costa, Kerem Ozcan, Zhengfan Xu, Ling Huang, Brian K Theisen, Yuehua Cui, Howard C Crawford and Nina G Steele, 19 October 2026, Cancer research. DOI: 10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-25-2748.

This study was funded by grants from the Lustgarten Foundation and the Sky Foundation and National Cancer Institute grant No. R00CA263154 awarded to Steele.

According to recent reports, san Francisco diners became acquainted with powerhouse couple Laura and Sayat Ozyilmaz through their championing of Eastern Mediterranean cuisine at Dalida. That restaurant told the story of Sayat’s upbringing and influences in Istanbul, Turkey, opening in 2023 inside a historic building within the lush environs of the Presidio and earning critical acclaim for the duo’s cooking.

In the years since, diners came to know Laura outside of Dalida. She completed an impressive run on Top Chef in 2024, where viewers saw her deftly plant one foot in Mediterranean food and another in Mexican cuisine, showcasing her skill in both fields throughout the season. With the 2026 debut of the Ozyilmazes’ restaurant Maria Isabel, the food feels like an even fuller expression of Laura’s heritage and personal history.

Named after Laura’s sister (Maria) and her mother (Isabel), the restaurant steeps in Mexican matriarchy, highlighting female winemakers, ceramics made by Mexican producers, and indigenous Mexican ingredients. The menu channels Laura’s upbringing in Guerrero and her family’s Sinaloan roots, as recounted through mariscos and maiz, moles and salsa macha. The ceviche Acapulqueño reimagines the Fanta- and ketchup-laden version instead with marigold flowers and preserved Seville oranges dressing tender shrimp and raw scallop; petals — and three fried shrimp heads — adorn the top. Duck enmoladas showcase the power of mole negro against a seasonal mole (sometimes a peach manchamanteles, other times a rhubarb rendition, but always compelling). Chochoyotes, a lesser-seen dish in San Francisco, demonstrates the restaurant’s ability to apply masa in different ways — in this case, dumplings — while harnessing the earthy flavor of huitlacoche. Maria Isabel is both a conduit for diners to connect with complex Mexican flavors and a view into Laura’s vision of the Mexico of her past and future. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF.

A rare few get to sample the restaurant’s elaborate tasting menu full of ingredients like high-end uni and dry-aged fish; reservations for the 15-course feast are nearly impossible to get.

In a recent development, the ambitious chef, at 36, isn’t afraid to stretch in many directions. That is until he opened Roya, his most personal restaurant and a project that has been in the works for more than eight years. Here, he manifests the depth and diversity of Persian cuisine, a bold feat for the middle of Texas. The space, designed with his brother Ali Hajimaleki, feels transportive with intricate tile mosaics, burnished gold and dark blue hues, and delicate chandeliers.

There’s been an electric energy to the Philly restaurant scene in recent years. The city, ever the underdog, has long punched above its weight; now, the rest of the world has come to the same realization. Amid this buzz, two newer restaurants have outrun the shadow cast by the city’s substantial names: Cambodian noodle house Mawn, which opened in 2023, and Southeast Asian oyster house and raw bar Sao, which opened last September.

At their helm is the slick, stylish Phila Lorn. The restaurants he runs with his wife Rachel feel singular, blending the influences of his Philadelphia upbringing with his Cambodian background in food that feels playfully free and emboldened by a lack of boundaries between cuisines. At Mawn, funnel cake meets coconut macaroons, and vinegar peppers enhance scallops in red curry. At Sao, the crispy rice in the nam khao salad, which features Italian sausage, feels analogous to arancini. Tuna carpaccio is served with crispy shallots and jalapeños, then cured in lime until it picks up the aura of the bowls of beef pho on Washington Avenue.

In a recent development, hear Lorn talk, with his South Philly-bred bravado (and requisite uses of “jawn”) giving him a commanding presence, and it’s clear that the city’s culinary community is listening, rallying, and getting stoked to eat more of his food. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tucson-based chef Aaron Lopez had a vision that started in his small California city of El Centro, an agricultural city near the U.S.-Mexico border. There, he hatched a plan to create a menu imbued with the techniques and flavors of the Sonoran Desert that spans northern Mexico, Arizona, and southeastern California. Trained at top kitchens in Los Angeles and beyond, Lopez researched by going deep into the desert, armed with a camera and his wits. A year later, he and his wife June Chee carried the project to Tucson, a larger venue still deeply embedded in the desert, but with a new audience.

Inside the high-ceilinged, brick-walled downtown space, Ursa serves as a hushed gallery for Lopez and his team’s $150 tasting menu, which merges Indigenous cooking techniques with foraged and locally farmed ingredients. Barrel fruit (a yellow cactus) topped with the tang of pickled chiltepin leaves is the first bite, a luscious treat you may never see on a European plate. Quail breast arrives on a metal skewer dressed in pickled yucca, hovering over a jujube broth like a quiet offering. Goat roasted in agave, pit barbacoa-style, is unveiled tableside and served over softened tepary beans.

It has been revealed that at every turn, with no extraneous adornments, the kitchen lets the produce and meats boast their innate nature. Lopez eschews conventional comfort, reimagining a meal of cactus, corn, sunflower tea, and beans as true luxuries, and the results are evocative and powerful. His message — seeing the value and beauty of this landscape, its people, its ingredients, and the way it all comes through the cooking — is the luscious pith of the cactus you find beneath the surface of the American Southwest. — Matthew Kang, correspondent.

The First Foreign Astronaut Will Visit China's Tiangong Space Station in Two Weeks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 25th, 2026, China's Shenzhou 24 mission will launch for the Tiangong space station atop a Long March 2F rocket.
  • The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) nominated Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud from Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO (The Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission).
  • It has been revealed that the process officially began in February 2025, when China and Pakistan signed an agreement in which Pakistani astronauts would be trained and selected to participate in missions to Tiangong.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On November 25th, 2026, China's Shenzhou 24 mission will launch for the Tiangong space station atop a Long March 2F rocket. It will be the country's 18th crewed spaceflight and will see three taikonauts rendezvous with the Tianhe core module. Similar to previous Chinese crewed missions, the names of the crew are not expected to be announced until the day before the flight - except for one. On this particular flight, a Pakistani astronaut will accompany the pilot and commander, becoming the first foreigner to travel to Tiangong.

The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) nominated Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud from Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO (The Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission). One of these astronauts will accompany the two Chinese taikonauts as a payload specialist, marking the first joint spaceflight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's space program. After spending a week aboard the station, the Ali or Daud will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

It has been revealed that the process officially began in February 2025, when China and Pakistan signed an agreement in which Pakistani astronauts would be trained and selected to participate in missions to Tiangong. The two candidates were chosen after a rigorous selection process consisting of preliminary screenings, secondary evaluations, and final selection, which concluded in April 2026. Once Ali and Daud complete training in China, one will be selected for the mission while the other will serve as the backup astronaut.

Industry observers note that this agreement represents an historic expansion of China's ambition in space and a major shift in the strategic partnership between the two nations. Previously, the two cooperated on the development of terrestrial infrastructure, and are now focused on collaborative deep-space exploration. For Pakistan, this represents an opportunity to send its first astronaut to space, edging out India by close to a year. Per India's Gaganyaan program, India's first crewed mission is expected to launch no sooner than Q2 2027.

For China, this is an important step toward the kind of international cooperation typical of NASA and the European Space Agency. It also aligns with their lunar ambitions, which will culminate in the creation of the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS). China's growth as a major space power continues and is now taking on partners!

#19466. A 120-Year-Old Gap in Einstein’s Physics May Hold the Key to the Universe’s Earliest Matter

A 120-Year-Old Gap in Einstein’s Physics May Hold the Key to the Universe’s Earliest Matter

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A missing piece in Einstein’s century-old theory could help scientists understand how matter behaved in the universe’s earliest moments, revealing more about a time we can barely recreate.
  • In particle accelerators, scientists smashed ions together at nearly the speed of light to recreate the fluid that existed just after the Big Bang.
  • That fluid, called quark-gluon plasma, offered a glimpse of the universe’s earliest matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A missing piece in Einstein’s century-old theory could help scientists understand how matter behaved in the universe’s earliest moments, revealing more about a time we can barely recreate.

In particle accelerators, scientists smashed ions together at nearly the speed of light to recreate the fluid that existed just after the Big Bang. The resulting droplets were roughly the size of an atomic nucleus and survived for only tens of septillionths of a second. One way to investigate their interior was to track heavy quarks, particles that traveled through the droplets without being part of the surrounding fluid.

That fluid, called quark-gluon plasma, offered a glimpse of the universe’s earliest matter. In the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang, matter existed as a trillion-degree mixture of quarks and gluons, subatomic particles moving at close to the speed of light. This state lasted just a few microseconds before the particles came together to form more stable protons and neutrons.

According to recent reports, reading the clues carried by heavy quarks required an accurate description of how the fluid pushed and pulled them. Albert Einstein established a relationship between a particle’s motion and a fluid’s microscopic structure in 1905. At speeds approaching that of light, however, the familiar description missed some of the interactions that shaped a particle’s journey.

Sources indicate that jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT’s Center for Theoretical Physics, a Leinweber Institute, and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) developed a theory to address that gap. It predicted how a particle moving at relativistic speeds, meaning close to the speed of light, was likely to be pushed and pulled as it passed through a fluid. They reported their findings in Physical Review Letters.

It has been revealed that the researchers began with a relativistic heavy quark traveling through a gas of weakly interacting quarks and gluons. Those weak interactions made the calculations manageable. They calculated the forces acting on the heavy quark through the strong nuclear force, the fundamental force that held quarks and gluons together, to determine how its momentum was likely to change.

Sources indicate that their calculation produced a probability distribution, a curve showing how likely different changes in momentum were. It also described the likelihood of kicks of different strengths, since stronger kicks produced larger changes in momentum.

“Our result reveals a new source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion,” Du Plessis said. “How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside.”.

The idea of learning about a fluid by watching particles move through it had roots in a much more familiar setting. In 1827, botanist Robert Brown observed grains of pollen jiggling and swirling in seemingly still water. That erratic movement became known as Brownian motion and later inspired Einstein’s work.

It has been revealed that einstein’s 1905 theory explained how invisible activity within a fluid could keep a larger particle moving. Atoms and molecules in the fluid exerted random forces that combined to kick and jostle the particle, while drag from the fluid slowed it down. The relationship between these random kicks and drag determined how the particle eventually reached the same temperature as its surroundings.

According to recent reports, scientists subsequently used Einstein’s explanation to study many fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. They assumed that a particle passing through the plasma would experience a balance of microscopic kicks similar to that experienced by pollen in water. In this familiar picture, the kicks followed a bell-shaped probability distribution. Typical kicks clustered around the peak, while extreme kicks occupied the tails and were equally unlikely in opposite directions.

Recent findings suggest that “Einstein showed that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings,” Du Plessis explained. “For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we’ve known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did.”.

The upcoming calculation resembled Einstein’s bell-shaped curve only for small kicks.

According to recent reports, “The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare,” Du Plessis stated. “For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected.”.

According to recent reports, when the researchers repeated their calculations for plasmas made up of different particles, they found the same tilted pattern, with uneven tails at either end of the distribution. They also recognized the same structure in an earlier calculation for a strongly coupled plasma, where particles interacted strongly, despite the differences in the underlying microscopic physics.

Industry observers note that “This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized,” Du Plessis said. “This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks.”.

The researchers envisioned applying the theory to predict how heavy quarks moved through quark-gluon plasma, then comparing those predictions with experiments. That comparison could help characterize the plasma’s microscopic structure and establish what kind of fluid existed in the universe’s first moments.

Industry observers note that du Plessis said the primordial plasma was likely “more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It’s more like a liquid and less like a gas.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Heavy Quark Transport Is Non-Gaussian beyond Leading Logarithm” by Jean F. Du Plessis and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld, 5 November 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/7fd5-1kq5.

Sources indicate that research supported in part by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Office of Nuclear Physics under grant Contract No. DE-SC0011090, by Grant No. NSF PHY-2309135 to the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics (KITP), and by Grant No. 994312 from the Simons Foundation. This research has benefited from the Mitchel Postdoctoral Scholar Career Development Fund at KITP.

The 2026 Restaurant Dishes of the Year

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From an earthy curry crab callaloo dip to a plate of pickled walleye cheeks, these were editors’ most memorable bites.
  • Our editors ate in hundreds of restaurants across the country this year, but certain dishes left a lasting impression, and we’re recognizing them in this new national Eater Award category.
  • According to recent reports, from a textbook execution of the ubiquitous 2026 entree — roast chicken — to an innovative fish preparation offering Midwestern diners a new way to experience a familiar ingredient, these dishes are all worth celebrating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From an earthy curry crab callaloo dip to a plate of pickled walleye cheeks, these were editors’ most memorable bites.

Our editors ate in hundreds of restaurants across the country this year, but certain dishes left a lasting impression, and we’re recognizing them in this new national Eater Award category.

According to recent reports, from a textbook execution of the ubiquitous 2026 entree — roast chicken — to an innovative fish preparation offering Midwestern diners a new way to experience a familiar ingredient, these dishes are all worth celebrating. — Missy Frederick, editorial director.

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

When experiencing a five-course tasting menu ($145), I wasn’t expecting toast to be a main attraction. But even with competition from luxurious courses featuring everything from a complex Hokkaido scallop to an assertive charred rib-eye with peaches, All Well’s puffed grain toast left a lasting impression.

After three years at two-Michelin-starred Oriole, Larry Feldmeier partnered with Noah Sandoval, fellow Oriole alum and James Beard winner for Best Chef: Great Lakes, to open the ambitious West Loop restaurant All Well, which offers both a la carte bar options and the aforementioned tasting; the toast is only available as part of the latter experience.

Sources indicate that the dish arrives to the table amplified with nutty buckwheat butter sweetened with honey, the backdrop for a pasta stuffed with triple-cream Délice de Bourgogne and a cauldron of salty chicken brodo. You’ll dive into the pasta, of course, using the bread to sop up the rich beurre blanc. Like a performer waiting in the wings for their monologue, the puffed grain toast takes center stage. The toast effectively offsets the creaminess and saltiness of the rest of the dish, but can stand on its own even without the accompanying pasta. Its subtle sweetness almost acts as a mid-meal dessert, a distinctive break in a seamless dinner you don’t quite want to end. — Isaiah Reynolds, audience editor.

The only thing about Oklahoma City that feels even vaguely reminiscent of the Caribbean is the sheet-pan-flat horizon. And yet inside a gaping industrial dining room downtown, there’s Dougla Kitchen, where diners sip fruity rum drinks out of plastic bags and acclaimed chef Andrew Black digs deep in his past to bring OKC locals a taste of his Indo-Jamaican upbringing. I fully admit this Midwestern-born, California-raised girl doesn’t encounter ruddy callaloo greens as often as she’d like (my hunch is neither do most Oklahomans). No matter. What Black manages to do with this deceiving pile of greenish-brown mush, dank with hand-picked crab and sparkling with curry spices, translates the soul of Caribbean home cooking in a single scoop. I didn’t know it was possible to be overwhelmed by a sense memory from a life that’s not your own, but this heady appetizer does that, served with a side of crisp taro chips and worth lingering over all afternoon with a couple of Red Stripes. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

In a recent development, to understand California cuisine in 2026, look no further than Henrietta, a neighborhood bistro that has struck a just-right balance of precision and ingenuity while imbuing a feeling of nostalgia that begs locals and travelers alike to return. The restaurant’s intentions come across most clearly in its roast chicken, served as a just-salty-enough half chicken hunked into handheld pieces with deep, smoky char marks. The prize chicken pile gets tucked onto a plate alongside a scorched lemon half and a heaping, chicory-heavy Caesar panzanella blanketed under a layer of Parmesan that could be a snowcap on a stretch of the San Gabriel Mountains. With the chicken, Henrietta nods to forebears (namely San Francisco’s Zuni), while making the dish its own with a Baja-born Caesar salad that feels distinctly Los Angeles, dotted with torn fistfuls of bread from the neighboring local Clark Street Bakery. Of course, 2026 continues to be the year of the Great Chickening, where roast chicken has become many a restaurant’s calling card — and an easy way into the cultural cache. In Los Angeles alone, Sqirl (with its upcoming dinner menu) and Pasjoli have both put out progressive, near-intoxicating spins on the dish, but Henrietta’s has lodged itself into the collective imagination with its brazen simplicity. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest.

The striking cantaloupe and verjus terrine at Nashville’s Junior offers a glimpse into the minds of chef Philip Krajeck and chef de cuisine Brian Mejia, the duo behind the high-technique kitchen. A “terrine” slice arrives with pieces of cantaloupe suspended in a clear gelatin made with verjus, the pressed juice of unripened grapes. One corner is covered in tiny, diced cubes of cantaloupe dressed in citrus-forward turmeric oil; another gets draped in chamomile-steeped cream. The mix of textures and flavors comes together in a dynamic symphony: the bright, acidic cubes of summer-ripened fruit against the calming mellowness of chamomile and gelatin layers that meld cantaloupe juice sweetness with crisp verjus.

In a recent development, the dessert’s structural elegance, which highlights a French variety of melon grown by a local farmer, may not immediately reveal its full complexity: Clear gelatin features a layer of clarified cantaloupe juice with encased melon slices, stacked between two layers of verjus gelatin. The melon gets compressed to intensify its flavors. Somehow, Junior managed to make Jell-O cool again — and dare I say, even sophisticated? — an example of Junior’s steady confidence that makes the restaurant an irresistible experience. — Dianne de Guzman, lead editor, Eater SF.

According to recent reports, though people outside the Midwest may not be familiar with freshwater whitefish walleye, there it’s a classic comfort food, a staple of Lenten fish fries, state fair booths, and Lake Erie fishermen’s freezer stashes. At Rosy, chef Vinnie Cimino leans on that familiarity to help convince his customers to experience a beloved ingredient in an entirely new way. Pickled walleye cheeks ($17) have been a recurring staple — if a fleeting one — on Rosy’s Eastern European-leaning menu since the restaurant opened in February 2026. Kate’s Fish in Cleveland’s historic West Side Market provides walleye filets for sister restaurant Cordelia; when breaking down and fileting each fish, the fishmongers save the cheeks until they have a formidable stash. About every three weeks, Rosy can offer pickled walleye cheeks for around four days at a time. It’s a thoughtful move for sustainability, but also for succulence, as fish cheeks are a prized cut for their luscious texture.

Cimino conceived the dish as a nod to Jewish fish-pickling practices (for me, the results also brought to mind a tender ceviche). Seasonal vegetables are pickled with lemon — an earlier version invoked German-style potato salad, spring brought asparagus, and, when I went in June, bell pepper, carrot, and dill were in the mix. They’re then combined with the cheeks, which get a separate hot-pickling treatment involving red wine vinegar, salt, sugar, bay leaf, peppercorns, and coriander. “People really gravitate toward it,” Cimino claims. “We’ve built up a great trust with our diners.” While the dish won’t be replacing fried walleye at area fish fries anytime soon, Cimino feels proud that when at Rosy, diners have been more than willing to go along with him for the ride. — MF.

Industry News: Navigating Lunar Orbit Using Nothing But Shadows And A Power Meter

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Humanity is promptly starting to saturate our ability to track all of the satellites we have in deep space.
  • Solar panel output is something every spacecraft already tracks, typically in the form of Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT), which is an algorithm designed to point a craftâs solar sails at the Sun to maximize the amount of incoming solar radiation it receives.
  • Engineers usually spend a lot of time intentionally avoiding eclipses, because they can be really hard on the spacecraft itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Humanity is promptly starting to saturate our ability to track all of the satellites we have in deep space. NASAâs Deep Space Network (DSN) has been the workhorse for tracking such things for decades, but is quickly being overwhelmed by the number of requests it receives. Which in turn makes it harder to track some of the missions that have been introduced recently. A fresh paper, available in pre-print on arXiv, from Ian Down, James McElreath, and Manoranjan Majji, of Advanced Space, Space Exploration Engineering, and Texas A&M respectively, offer a no-cost solution to that tracking problem - use solar array data from a spacecraftâs eclipse to determine where it is.

Solar panel output is something every spacecraft already tracks, typically in the form of Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT), which is an algorithm designed to point a craftâs solar sails at the Sun to maximize the amount of incoming solar radiation it receives. But eclipses, where a spacecraft positions itself so that a body its orbiting is between it and the Sun, is also something every spacecraft experiences, at least for a little while.

Engineers usually spend a lot of time intentionally avoiding eclipses, because they can be really hard on the spacecraft itself. The solar arrays stop generating electricity, draining the battery, and everything on the craft gets much, much colder. However, the precise timing of how those blackouts travel across the solar panels of a spacecraft holds valuable information.

It has been revealed that fraser interviews astrodynamacist Dr. Aaron Rosengren, talking about the three-body problem of lunar orbits.

Astronomers know the exact positions of the Sun, Earth, and the Moon years in advance using advanced planetary maps. Given how much data weâve collected on those three bodies, we also know the precise shape and locations of the shadows those three bodies cast into space. Each shadow comes with two nested cones - the penumbra, where the Sun is partially blocked, and the umbra, where it is completely cut off.

When a spacecraft crosses into one of those cones, the amount of solar radiation hitting its solar panels drops precipitously, but its electronics continue to operate due to the on-board battery engineers placed there precisely to deal with these eclipses. By recording the precise timestamp where the voltage starts to drop, and when it starts to pick back up again after the spacecraft leaves the shadow, a navigation algorithm can determine its three dimensional location in space without needing any cameras, star trackers, or radio signals.

According to recent reports, that sounds simple in theory, but in practice getting that precise measurement correct is difficult. The Moon has no atmosphere, so its shadow is very jagged and tracks the mountains and craters dotting its surface. Each of those features can change the eclipsesâ timing by a few seconds. Earth, on the other hand, is a whole other ball of wax - or ball of gas and rock as the case may be. Itâs squished slightly at the poles, and its atmosphere can blur the Sun, as well as enlarging its shadow, making it difficult to differentiate precisely what part of the planet the spacecraft is passing over at any given time.

Fraser talks about different techniques to find your way in the cosmos.

To solve this problem, the researchers turned to a dataset of over 22,000 historical observations of lunar craters being covered by Earthâs shadow, which was collected by astronomers between 1842 and 2011. Using this data, the algorithm was able to map certain parts of the Earthâs shadow to specific ground features, allowing a more granular idea of where the specific spacecraft is passing over during its eclipse.

Recent findings suggest that to prove the system works, the researchers used another interesting data set - the actual flight telemetry from CAPSTONE, a CubeSat mission operated by Advanced Space, where Mr. Down, the lead author, works. CAPSTONE, which was intended to test the orbit for NASAâs now discontinued Lunar Gateway, recently completed its mission in July 2026. But on January 11th 2026, it traveled through the Moonâs shadow, with its solar panel voltage dropping from 23V to near zero, then picking back up to 31V when the panels hit sunlight again.

It has been revealed that using that data, the researchers timed the spacecraftâs entry and exit to the Moon shadow to within 15 seconds of the CAPSTONE's actual path. In addition to running the algorithm on real-life data, they also simulated a scenario where a spacecraft missed a check-in with ground stations and had its position uncertainty drift by several kilometers. Processing the eclipse data without any further information cut that uncertainty by more than 60 %.

Sources indicate that perhaps the most crucial feature of this whole system is that it's essentially free. It doesnât require any additional hardware, or is âzero-Size Weight and Powerâ (zero-SWaP) in spacecraft jargon. To be clear, it doesnât entirely replace ground-based radio tracking. But it does provide a safety net. And as more and more spacecraft start venturing beyond low Earth orbit, and continue to overwhelm our active tracking systems, that zero-cost safety net could prove very valuable indeed.

I.M. Down, J. McElreath, & M. Majji - Eclipse Observables for Navigation in Cislunar Space.

Scientists Unlock a Upcoming Way To Photograph Events That Vanish in Trillionths of a Second

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eleven carefully timed images can connect the early and later stages of an ultrafast event, offering scientists a way to investigate fleeting processes that are difficult to repeat.
  • A limited set of images can leave gaps in a laser pulse or shock wave’s story.
  • According to recent reports, conventional imaging methods operate on microsecond, or millionth-of-a-second, and millisecond, or thousandth-of-a-second, timescales, usually capturing images at evenly or nearly evenly spaced intervals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eleven carefully timed images can connect the early and later stages of an ultrafast event, offering scientists a way to investigate fleeting processes that are difficult to repeat.

A limited set of images can leave gaps in a laser pulse or shock wave’s story. Its first moments and later development may unfold on very different timescales, so taking snapshots at regular intervals can miss changes that connect one stage to the next.

According to recent reports, conventional imaging methods operate on microsecond, or millionth-of-a-second, and millisecond, or thousandth-of-a-second, timescales, usually capturing images at evenly or nearly evenly spaced intervals. Single-shot ultrafast imaging typically uses a uniform interval within a selected time window. With only a finite number of frames available, that choice can favor a detailed view of one brief stage over a record of the broader process.

A team led by Keiichi Nakagawa, an associate professor in the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Tokyo, developed an approach that gives researchers more control over where those frames fall. Called logarithmic ultrafast photography, it distributes a fixed number of images across time, concentrating them around moments when characteristic changes occur.

“We wanted to find a way to connect these very different timescales in a single measurement. In other words, we wanted to see both the first instance and what follows, without having to choose one or the other,” said Keitaro Shimada, a postdoctoral researcher in the Nakagawa Group and lead author of the study.

Sources indicate that the team implemented the approach in sequentially timed all-optical mapping photography, or STAMP, a technique that combines ultrafast imaging with high image quality. To adjust the timing, they used band-resolved individual delay generation, or BRIDGE. It extracts wavelength bands, which are portions of the light spectrum, in sequence and allows their timing to be adjusted independently. Each band remains linked to a specific instant in the process being recorded.

According to recent reports, that control lets researchers place frames at selected moments on timescales ranging from femtoseconds, or quadrillionths of a second, to nanoseconds, or billionths of a second. Instead of maintaining a regular interval, they can customize the gaps between images to resolve rapid changes and follow subsequent stages within the same recording.

The technique can capture key moments with 11 frames spanning five orders of magnitude in time, a 100,000-fold range. The report also describes this as equivalent to an approximately 260-frames-per-second exposure, although it does not explain the basis for that comparison.

Sources indicate that “We are particularly interested in phenomena that are difficult to reproduce exactly. In those cases, recording the early and later stages of the same event can reveal relationships that might be lost when a sequence is reconstructed from separate experiments,” stated Nakagawa, a co-author and principal investigator of the study.

In a recent development, the researchers’ targets include short-lived phenomena whose peaks are difficult to catch and connections between phases of a physical process that have remained unseen because they occur on different timescales. They propose using the technique in laser processing, material dynamics, plasma and shock-wave research, and biomedical applications.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Logarithmic ultrafast photography with band-resolved individual delay generation” by 19 October 2026, Optica. DOI: 10.1364/OPTICA.610944.

Funding: Japan Science and Technology Agency (JPMJAX22K8); Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (JPMXS0118067246).

What Are Thanksgiving Sides That Don't Need to Go in the Oven?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, on Thanksgiving the oven is always precious real estate for the quintessential spread—stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potatoes, and, of course, the turkey.
  • It has been revealed that if there was a proverbial dartboard of Thanksgiving problems, you have just hit the bull’s-eye.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook. Tell us about it! Dear Bon Appétit is an advice column where we answer your culinary conundrums with handpicked recipes and well-seasoned advice. Submit a question here.

In a recent development, on Thanksgiving the oven is always precious real estate for the quintessential spread—stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potatoes, and, of course, the turkey. In years past, the stress of getting everything in and out of the oven with the right amount of time has been a nuisance that I’d like to avoid this year. Are there any Thanksgiving sides that feel classic but don’t need the oven? —Oven-whelmed.

It has been revealed that if there was a proverbial dartboard of Thanksgiving problems, you have just hit the bull’s-eye. (And as someone who has never hit a real bull’s-eye in her life, I mean this as quite the compliment!) Even if you place oven racks strategically—even if you have one of those fancy double ovens—there’s always a bottleneck of dishes that need to be roasted and baked.

The solution is not to plot out an overwrought schedule of when things go in and out, and in and out, but to ruthlessly reduce the number of recipes that require the oven in the first place.

With that in mind, I would like to point out that turkey can thrive in other settings. And no, I’m not talking about deep-frying it in your yard, which we all know is a rowdy and risky idea, as proven in Gilmore Girls season three, episode nine. You could grill it. You could smoke it. Both delightful.

Recent findings suggest that but you asked about sides specifically, so sides are what we will tackle today. Beyond the classics like mashed potatoes, boxed stuffing, and cranberry sauce, here are 10 recipes that do not need an oven at all—and brazenly, boldly get away with it.

According to recent reports, green Beans and Mushrooms With Crispy Shallots. The same cozy flavors as a classic green bean casserole—earthy mushrooms, frizzled shallots—but it comes together entirely on the stovetop. Now is the time to branch beyond white button or baby bella; opt for shiitake or oyster, the wonkier the shape the better.

Green Beans With Tahini Sbagliato. For something less traditional, from Samin Nosrat’s recent cookbook, this recipe is make-ahead-friendly on multiple fronts. You can blanch the green beans a day ahead and whip up the tahini-miso sauce up to four days ahead. All that’s left on Turkey Day is assembly.

Recent findings suggest that brussels Sprouts Stir-Fry With Cheddar and Golden Raisins. Thinly sliced and swiftly sautéed, brussels sprouts take on a savory char. The cheddar could be swapped out for Gouda, or any aged cheese you love. Likewise, the golden raisins could be replaced with dried cranberries or chopped dates. It’s flexible!

Recent findings suggest that air Fryer Crispy Brussels Sprouts With Honey Butter. Or free up the stove and turn to your trusty air fryer instead. In the concentrated and circulating heat, the sprouts’ outer leaves become crackly like potato chips, craveable enough to go back for thirds.

Sweet Potatoes With Tahini Butter. Most sweet potatoes in our archive are roasted, so isn’t it ironic that one of our most popular recipes is steamed. Author Carla Lalli puts it perfectly: “Steaming offers extreme speed and high hydration, which means that whatever you cook will be done rapidly and always moist. Sweet potatoes in particular benefit from this treatment, which makes their flesh pudding-like and fluffy.”.

Recent findings suggest that glazed Carrots. Li’l retro! These saucy carrots are sweet but not too sweet thanks to a floral mixture of orange juice and honey, plus a welcome zing from fresh ginger. I could see parsnips swapping in happily here.

Parsnip Purée. Speaking of parsnips, from the Barefoot Contessa herself, this is a cousin to mashed potatoes that, in my humble opinion, is a whole lot better. Parsnips have a je ne sais quois, needing no more than butter, salt, and pepper, to shine bright.

Adult Mac and Cheese. Despite its title, this dish will be a hit with grown-ups and kids alike. It comes together on the stove with just six ingredients (and that’s including salt!). A few of its rave reviews: “Staple now in my house,” “Super easy and always delicious!” and “Lovelovelove. I’ve made this so many times.” Medium shells catch the sauce like little canoes; or could be a fun moment for radiatori.

It has been revealed that kale Salad With Pecan Vinaigrette. Pecans are good for more than pie. Here they turn into a nutty dressing for ruffled kale and perky radishes. Though salad is not the first (or even second) thing one might think of for Thanksgiving, it has become an absolute must on my family’s table. A refreshing reprieve to all the richness. We have more great options here.

Instant Pot Collard Greens. On a holiday table, when there’s so much going on, sometimes a simple dish is just the thing. Bacon, greens, onion, chile, done. An Instant Pot is like a Thanksgiving cheat code, freeing up the oven and the stove too.

According to recent reports, readers, what sides are you making this year for Thanksgiving? Share menu inspiration in the comments!

According to recent reports, if one newly introduced place in Chicago needs no further hype, it is Bad Butter. You’ll know you’re there when you spot the line cascading out of the whitewashed storefront along West Cortland Street, a queue that doesn’t let up until the pastry case is empty. Formerly a head baker at Soho House Chicago, Dan Koester was stuck at home like the rest of us in 2020, handing off excess home-baked sourdough loaves to friends and family and making some available for free pickup. After he was officially laid off that summer, he debuted his own online bakery business, earning a massive following along the way.

It has been revealed that one residency at the Emily Hotel later, Koester debuted his Bucktown bakery, demonstrating the full range of his skill. Still warm, charred, and dimpled flats of focaccia showered with scallion furikake rest on its shelves. Impossibly crisp and exquisitely laminated twice-baked almond croissants burst with subtle, aromatic almond paste. A spicy harissa monkey bread with a cloudlike texture is cooled by a pool of creamy labneh drizzled with silky olive oil.

The bakery’s menu has breadth and also manages to arc with the season. Customers snake along the floor waiting their turn to claim a towering cruffin, dusted in fine grains of sugar and piped full of ginger plum jam, or a seasonal tart piled with plump, lacquered blueberries. A pastry box filled with these confections is well worth the wait. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager.

In a recent development, born as an underground dinner party operated out of Karla Subero Pittol’s Echo Park garage, Chainsaw finally got its own digs in November 2025 in the form of a lively cafe in Melrose Hill, an unquestionably gentrifying neighborhood that has become home to some of Los Angeles’s best independent restaurants. At the cafe, Subero Pittol channels her Venezuelan heritage through a menu of arepas plump with beans, limey guasacaca, and cheese; a Venezuelan hot dog (“perro caliente”) buoyed by an acidic slaw; and her bracingly tart passionfruit-lime icebox pie, which commands a cult following all its own.

Stepping into Chainsaw feels like you could be in Subero Pittol’s own kitchen as she greets regulars and newcomers as if they are old friends. Customers study a handwritten menu that changes daily — it doesn’t help to come in too attached to any one dish (save the ever-present icebox pie) when you may get tempted by another. The cafe’s impact on Los Angeles feels clear in the near-constant crowds that hover outside, reading their newspapers over an espresso or tucking into the latest of Subero Pittol’s ideas, such as a full English breakfast served for a single day. In a city lacking in untamed Venezuelan cooking, Chainsaw offers a home for Subero Pittol to celebrate the cuisine in a way that feels distinctly Los Angeles. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest.

Industry observers note that with both Afghan and Latin American influences, Diljān gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights.

Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an important Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned by toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater Upcoming York.

It has been revealed that san Francisco’s pastry game is stronger and more competitive than ever before, and Parachute Bakery steps to the forefront of a crowded field with a mix of patisserie standards and seasonal standouts. At his Ferry Building bakery, pastry chef Nasir Armar marries his fine dining training, honed at Michelin-starred Sorrel and Saison, with flavors that make everyone sit up and take notice (and snap a food photo or two for their socials).

Vegetables and savory complements are given their own footing on the menu. Stalks of grilled asparagus shine in a baton-shaped croissant shell, with fennel jam, sheep’s milk ricotta, and ramp pesto alongside them; one brief, bordering-on-gimmicky croissant got piped with clam chowder, a reference to the soup in a bread bowl famously served on the city’s wharf. Even potato-laden samosas and bright tomato shakshuka get interpreted into pastry form. Parachute succeeds with its experimental vision, a hype well-earned that leaves fans clamoring for what they’ll come up with next. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF.

#19459. This Rare Binary Star Emits Radio Pulses Every Few Minutes. Will It Eventually Explode?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1394 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

This Rare Binary Star Emits Radio Pulses Every Few Minutes. Will It Eventually Explode?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1394 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unusual electromagnetic signals permeate the cosmos, and they range from powerful and deadly gamma-rays down to generally harmless radio waves.
  • Radio waves are widespread throughout the cosmos because they come from objects with a wide variety of temperatures.
  • One of these phenomenon are called long-period radio transients (LPTs), and their periodic radio pulses range from a few minutes to several hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unusual electromagnetic signals permeate the cosmos, and they range from powerful and deadly gamma-rays down to generally harmless radio waves. The sources of many of these signals are well-understood, and in some cases, special spacecraft have been launched to monitor them. But some remain unexplained.

Radio waves are widespread throughout the cosmos because they come from objects with a wide variety of temperatures. Radio astronomy has been around for decades, so many of these are well-understood. But not all of them. Some of them have only been discovered more recently and are awaiting an explanation.

One of these phenomenon are called long-period radio transients (LPTs), and their periodic radio pulses range from a few minutes to several hours. That's key because it differentiates them from pulsars and their extremely short radio periods. Astronomers have only detected about 15 LPTs in total, and they've had difficulty explaining exactly what they are and how they generate their radio pulses.

There are different hypotheses invoked to explain them. They could be magnetars, which are neutron stars with extremely powerful magnetic fields that rotate very slowly. Or they could be something exotic and speculative, like strange dwarf pulsars.

But at least some of them have been confirmed to be White Dwarf-Main Sequence (WDMS) binaries, a binary star containing a white dwarf (WD) and another main sequence star. Astronomers have only been able to confirm the white dwarf's companion in a handful of cases, and in those, the companion is a red dwarf.

Now astronomers have identified for the first time a LPT that consists of a white dwarf with a Sun-like, G-type star as its companion. Their results are published in Nature Astronomy in a paper titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion." The lead author is Dr. Sam McSweeney, who made this discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR.

At the time of this research, there were only 12 detected LPTs, and the ones with identified components favoured WD and red dwarf pairs. "An optical follow-up confirmed that at least 4 (ouf of 12) long-period transients are binary systems comprising a white dwarf and an M dwarf," the authors write. But this newly-detected LPT, named GPM J071507â114153, bucks that trend. "It is a binary system comprising a low-mass white dwarf and a G-type star identified via optical spectroscopy.".

Industry observers note that âWe detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,â said co-author Natasha Hurley-Walker, Associate Professor at the Curtin Institute of Radio Astronomy.

The MWA detected 214 separate pulses, and the MeerKAT pinpointed its location based on 33 detected pulses. 26 of MeerKAT's pulses were co-detected by the MWA.

Recent findings suggest that the new LPT has a period of only 7.9âminutes, which is almost certainly from its rotation. The properties of its radio pulses, like its polarization, are modulated by a longer period of about 1.3âdays, which the researchers say is the binary system's orbital period.

Industry observers note that follow-up optical observations and spectrometry came from the Keck Telescopes. "The optical counterpart of J0715-1141 was observed with the low-resolution imaging spectrometer on the Keck 1 telescope on Mauna Kea, Hawaii," the authors write. Those observations were a pair of 1,200 second exposures. They let the researchers determine the nature of the WD's partner star.

According to recent reports, this figure from the research shows the optical spectrum of the new LPT, J0715-1141, compared to model spectra from F-type, G-type, and K-type stars. The spectrum most closely matches that of a G-type, Sun-like star. "As a comparison, hotter F-type and cooler K-type stars show distinct spectral features not present in the data," the authors write. The three panels on the right highlight this in three different elements. Image Credit: McSweeney, S.J., Hurley-Walker, N., Bahramian, A. et al. A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion. Nat Astron (2026).

According to recent reports, in this case, the WD's binary partner is a star like our Sun, which is far more massive and luminous than the M dwarfs (red dwarfs) found in other LPTs. So this rules out the idea that only WD-red dwarf pairs can generate LPTs.

Astronomers and astrophysicists want to know exactly how these radio pulses are generated. Can any of their observations help researchers determine the exact source of the radio pulses? Not exactly, but the clarity of the pulses helps narrow it down.

âThis is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,â said lead author McSweeney.

"We conclude that in long-period transients powered by white dwarf binaries, the coherent radio pulsed emission crucially depends on its interaction with the companion star, which we show can be G-type stars in day-long orbits," the researchers write.

There's another suprise in these findings. The pulses from the WD let the researchers detect stellar flares from the Sun-like star as it passed in front of the WD.

According to recent reports, âAs a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a âstellar prominenceâ, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a starâs surface,â Hurley-Walker remarked. âItâs amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.â.

This image highlights a solar prominence from the Sun in 2010, with Earth shown for scale. The researchers were able to detect one of these coming from the main sequence star in the pair, as the white dwarf moved behind it. That's pretty impressive for a star that's 5,000 light years away. Image Credit: NASA/SDO.

Sources indicate that one questions astronomers ask is how these types of binaries form, and the researchers have a hypothesis for that. They say the system could've formed through binary evolution. "One possibility is that the present configuration of the system arises through post-common-envelope (CE) binary evolution," they write. The progenitor of the system most likely had an intermediate-mass primary with a lower-mass companion on a wider orbit. "As the primary evolved off the main sequence and expanded into a giant, unstable mass transfer initiated a CE phase, during which orbital energy and angular momentum were transferred to the envelope, leading to its ejection and substantial orbital shrinkage.".

The primary star was left as an exposed stellar core, and evolved to become a WD, creating the situation the astronomers see today: a WD star with a G-type partner, that are still in a binary relationship, but detached from the common envelope they once shared.

As for the system's future, it could hold a cataclysmic explosion.

Binaries like this that have left their common envelopes, and that consist of a WD and a massive main-sequence star, are potential breeding grounds for eventual Type Ia supernovae. This can happen as their orbit decays and the WD accretes material from its companion. Once enough material builds up on the accreting WD, it explodes and destroys the WD. Or they could created a double degenerate WD-WD merger, if the main sequence companion collapses before the binary orbit decays.

Could the radio signals from LPTs be used to find the progenitors of these supernovae explosions?

"Radio detections of LPTs may offer a route to finding cooler WDs around hotter stars at greater distances than traditional ultraviolet and optical surveys," the authors write.

The upcoming Square Kilometre Array could be the key to this.

"In an era of larger and more sensitive radio surveys, such as those to be conducted by the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, this may form a newly introduced pathway for investigating the progenitors of type Ia supernovae," the authors write.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fabric woven at the molecular level could help factories separate chemicals with less energy, opening a new path toward more sustainable manufacturing.

Reducing the environmental impact of manufacturing requires more than finding cleaner materials. It also means finding ways to make industrial processes use less energy and produce fewer hazardous byproducts. One promising approach comes from an unexpected place: the ancient craft of weaving.

In a recent development, researchers from the University of Texas at Austin and Zhejiang University have developed a molecularly woven fabric that can separate benzene from cyclohexane, two chemicals that are notoriously difficult to separate using conventional methods. The material could offer a more energy-efficient way to handle chemical separation, potentially reducing the energy demands of industries that manufacture nylon, paint, polyurethane, furniture foams, and detergents. The research was published in Nature.

Cyclohexane is an important industrial chemical used to manufacture a range of everyday products. It is commonly produced from benzene, a known carcinogen, which can also remain as an unwanted byproduct. Removing the benzene is essential, yet the two chemicals have nearly identical boiling points, making conventional separation difficult.

Chemical plants typically rely on distillation, a process that heats mixtures to separate substances according to their boiling points. Chemicals with sufficiently different boiling points can vaporize at different temperatures, allowing one to be collected separately. Benzene and cyclohexane, however, vaporize at nearly the same temperature and tend to separate poorly. The process often requires additional additives and considerable energy.

“Unbelievable amounts of energy go into chemical separation. It’s one of the top energy sinks in the modern world,” remarked UT chemist Jonathan Sessler, one of the corresponding authors of the study. “In a sense, we are addressing the challenge of improving efficiency using one of humanity’s oldest technologies: weaving. It’s remarkable that the same principle of interlacing works at the molecular level.”.

The researchers developed a material made from four molecular networks that weave over and under one another, forming an interconnected structure. Each layer can take one of two mirror-image arrangements. In one, the networks cross in a clockwise spiral, while the other follows a counterclockwise spiral. This property, known as chirality or handedness, allows the researchers to alternate between the two arrangements as they stack the layers.

The resulting material forms a springy, thick fabric that can capture benzene from a mixture. Its interlocking, multi-thread structure also makes it stronger than conventional fabrics made by weaving individual threads in a single layer.

According to recent reports, watch a video showing how these layers self-assemble and stack. Credit: University of Texas at Austin.

Unlike materials that require complicated manufacturing processes, this molecular fabric is self-assembling. Its chemical structure naturally guides the networks into their woven arrangement.

“The whole thing converges by itself based on the underlying chemistry, which is especially cool because it allows the creation of these upcoming materials in a facile way,” Sessler noted.

The fabric can also be reused. After absorbing benzene from a chemical mixture, researchers heat the material to vaporize the captured benzene, preparing it for another round of separation.

Sessler and the Zhejiang University team, led by professors Feihe Huang and Guangfeng Li, tested the material using a mixture containing equal amounts of benzene and cyclohexane. A single application absorbed 97.9% of the benzene. Multiple passes could provide additional separation for processes requiring greater purity.

The researchers also demonstrated that the material could separate several other compounds of commercial interest, suggesting that its potential applications extend beyond benzene and cyclohexane.

At Zhejiang University, the team has demonstrated how the fabric could be used on a larger, industrial scale. However, an economic analysis has not yet been completed, so its eventual cost and commercial practicality remain uncertain.

If the technology proves viable, it could offer manufacturers a way to reduce the energy required for separating industrial chemicals. Improving these processes could help limit the environmental footprint of manufacturing, particularly across industries that depend on cyclohexane and other commercially important compounds.

According to recent reports, reference: “A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric” by Mengbin Wang, Shuai Fang, Xuedong Xiao, Zhewen Guo, Tianyu Shan, Han Han, Chun Tang, Ding Xiao, Guangguo Wang, Zhongwen Liu, Bohan Zhao, Shang Li, Ming Liu, Yan-Fang Wang, Jinbo Li, Ming Li, Liya Chen, Zhenglin Du, Chong Yao, Yizhao Du, Jiyong Liu, J. Fraser Stoddart, Jonathan L. Sessler, Guangfeng Li and Feihe Huang, 4 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11218-8.

In a recent development, the work at UT was supported by the Robert A. Welch Foundation and the work abroad was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Zhejiang Provincial Natural Science Foundation of China, the ‘Pioneer’ and ‘Leading Goose’ R&D Program of Zhejiang, the Ministry of Education of China and the China Postdoctoral Science Foundation.

The Best Fresh Restaurants in America in 2026
