#19447. China Signals Its Intention to Land on Jupiter's Moon Callisto

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1383 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

China Signals Its Intention to Land on Jupiter's Moon Callisto

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The China National Space Administration (CNSA) has been talking about a mission to the Jovian system since 2018.
  • Tianwen-4 obviously isn't a sample return mission.
  • The CNSA declared a latest opportunity for payloads for its Tianwen-4 mission to Jupiter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The China National Space Administration (CNSA) has been talking about a mission to the Jovian system since 2018. It's named Tianwen-4, and it will build on the success of other recent missions like Chang'e 6, which collected the first sample from the lunar far side in 2024.

Tianwen-4 obviously isn't a sample return mission. But according to recent developments, it will attempt another extremely challenging mission profile: a landing on Callisto.

The CNSA declared a latest opportunity for payloads for its Tianwen-4 mission to Jupiter.

"The primary objectives of the Tianwen-4 mission are to achieve Jovian orbiting, as well as orbiting and landing exploration of Callisto, and to advance scientific research on the Jovian system," the announcement reads. To improve the mission's performance and success, the CNSA is asking for instrument proposals from within China and from outside partners.

According to recent reports, the orbiter itself will carry 10 instruments, and the payload will include multiple cameras, imagers, and spectrometers, as well as a particle detector and a magnetometer. But the announcement also addresses the needs of a Callisto Lander.

"The lander is planned to carry 2 scientific payloads: Callisto Surface Composition Analyzer and Callisto Lander Magnetometer," it reads.

The surface composition analyzer will be a Raman spectrometer. Raman spectrometers can analyze the composition of rocks with the light from a laser, and are becoming a standard part of planetary missions. NASA's Perseverance rover uses an ultraviolet Raman spectrometer to measure fine-scale mineralogy and to detect organic matter. The ESA's upcoming Rosalind Franklin rover will have one, and JAXA's Martian Moons Explorer carries one in its IDEFIX rover.

Callisto's surface is heterogenous on a small scale. There are small bright patches that seem to be pure water ice and there are other patches that appear to be a mixture of rock and ice. These are intermixed with larger, darker areas that are not ice. But spectral identification is uncertain. The Tianwen-4 lander and its Raman spectrometer should be able to determine the compositions of these components. There's also lots of carbon on the surface, and the instrument should be able to tell if its primordial carbon or altered carbon.

In a recent development, this mosaic of Callisto images from the Voyager 1 mission shows a large-scale feature named Valhalla. It's an old impact crater with concentric rings expanding outward. They extend outward for about 1,500 km, and a bright central point, probably the original impact basin, is about 600 km across. Image Credit: NASA/JPL.

While Jupiter's other moons like Ganymede, and especially Europa, have strong evidence for subsurface oceans, Callisto's composition and structure is less certain. It appears to be partially differentiated, and magnetometer readings are ambiguous regarding an ocean. But if the Tianwen-4 lander's Raman spectrometer can determine if some of its surface composition is aqueously altered, that would be evidence in favour of an ocean.

The lander's other instrument will be a surface magnetometer. By combining its data with the data from the orbiter's magnetometer, ionospheric signals and signals from the moon's surface can be separated. That will reveal more about its interior, especially regarding its potential subsurface ocean.

It has been revealed that it would be nice to have a better understanding of Callisto, since it and the other Galilean moons are expected to have formed in-situ, unlike some other Solar System moons. Some of those appear to be captured objects. So understanding Callisto is an avenue to understanding Jupiter itself, the dominant planet in our system.

It has been revealed that callisto's internal structure is uncertain, but it seems to be differentiated, with multiple ice layers and a rock and metal core. It may also have a saltwater ocean, but is far from certain. Image Credit: By Kelvinsong - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/31643955.

According to recent reports, landing on any of the Galilean moons is challenging, but Callisto might be the least challenging. It's probably not the best scientific destination among them, but it is the most accessible. For one thing, it's outside Jupiter's extremely powerful radiation belts, where radiation is strong enough to degrade sensitive instruments after short exposure times. Think of NASA's Juno spacecraft and its wide orbit. It only makes short dives into the radiation belts. Even then, Juno protects its most sensitive parts inside a titanium vault.

Callisto is furthest from Jupiter compared to the other three Galilean moons, so its gravity well is shallower. Less precious propellant is required to land there. Tianwen-4 can also use gravity assists at Callisto to prepare for orbital insertion.

Callisto is further away from Jupiter than the other Galilean moons. The other three are deeper inside its magnetic fields and powerful radiation belts, which makes visiting them much more hazardous. The radiation dose on Callisto's surface is weaker and won't take such a heavy toll on sensitive electronics. Image Credit: By B. Smithin Szalay, J. R., Smith, H. T., Zirnstein, E. J., McComas, D. J., Begley, L. J., Bagenal, F., et al. (2022). Water-group pickup ions from Europa-genic neutrals orbiting Jupiter. Geophysical Research Letters, 49, e2022GL098111.

It has been revealed that another reason Callisto is the preferred moon for a surface mssion is the its surface. Callisto's surface is ancient, cratered, and stable. It's a geologically quiet place compared to Io, for instance. It doesn't suffer from the same tidal heating and constant volcanic upheaval that Io suffers from. There are no mountains or volcanoes, only ancient crater on top of ancient crater. This makes hazard avoidance easier, since orbital images are unlikely to have changed from the time they were captured to the time the lander arrives there.

According to recent reports, but Callisto is still challenging. It's an airless moon, and that creates its own difficulties. Atmospheric breaking isn't an option. The time delay also ranges from about 35 to 50 minutes, so round-trip communication is double that. That means the landing must be autonomous.

The best surface images come from the Galileo mission, and that spacecraft imaged most of Callisto at poor resolution. Only some small areas are imaged at higher resolutions of tens of meters per pixel.

According to recent reports, this image of Callisto is made from data from Galileo and Voyager 1 and 2. It emphasizes how heavily cratered the moon's ancient surface is, and how uniform it is. There are a few smooth areas, and no mountains of volcanoes. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/DLR.

Industry observers note that but the mission plan calls for Tianwen-4 to orbit Callisto at an altitude of 300 km. Galileo got to within 138 km of the moon, but that was 25 years ago. Camera technology has advanced since then, and Tianwen-4 will carry a pair of visible light imaging cameras. One of them, the wide-angle camera (JWAC), is dedicated to mapping Callisto's surface and topography. Tianwen-4's proposed mapping orbit is 300 km in altitude. From that height, the JWAC operates at about 90 meters per pixel.

According to recent reports, in 2020, the CNSA outlined a timeline for the Tianwen-4 mission that would see it launch in September of 2029. To preserve precious propellant, the spacecraft will perform a slingshot flyby of Venus in April 2030, then a pair of slingshots with Earth in 2031 and 2033.

In 2035 it will reach Jupiter and enter an orbit around the gas giant, also making flybys of irregular moons. That's phase one. Phase two starts with two gravity assists with Callisto, then in February 2038, it will enter an orbit around the moon. At some point after that, the Callisto lander will be released.

This plan was first outlined in 2020, so it will likely be changed. The instrumentation on the orbiter could be changed, too, and that includes its mapping camera and its resolution. But with their call for instrument proposals, the CNSA is making one thing clear: they intend to land on Callisto.

How a New Restaurant Injected Retro “Latin Soul” Into a New-Build Space

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bar Nuestro on private dining nooks, vintage sourcing, and more﻿.
  • It has been revealed that opened at the end of October, Bar Nuestro is Washington, D.C.’s newest bistro serving European- and Latin-inspired dishes and drinks.
  • Pre Shift: Tell me about the design concept for Bar Nuestro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bar Nuestro on private dining nooks, vintage sourcing, and more﻿.

It has been revealed that opened at the end of October, Bar Nuestro is Washington, D.C.’s newest bistro serving European- and Latin-inspired dishes and drinks. Founder Daniella Senior and designer Shawn Hausman (whose firm worked on iconic spaces like the Chateau Marmont and the ’80s club Area) collaborated on the project, ensuring that the space captured the same retro vibe as the menu. I especially hope their mini-private-dining room concept catches on.

Pre Shift: Tell me about the design concept for Bar Nuestro.

It has been revealed that daniella Senior: We wanted the space to really feel—even though it’s a new buildout—that it’s been there a long time. I’m kind of tired of the same aesthetic going around, one that’s almost too clean, too new, too matchy-matchy. I think that doesn’t, at times, help you communicate what the food is trying to communicate. For us, the food and the space work together. We wanted it to feel very Old World. We took a lot of inspiration from Vienna’s old corner cafes, which have been institutions for a while. We wanted a “We’ve been here a minute” type of feel.

Sources indicate that from our furniture to our tiles, [the Bar Nuestro team and designer Shawn Hausman] sourced a lot of vintage pieces, about 25 percent of the furniture. We have chairs that came from Austria and Italy in the ’30s and fabric with vintage patterns. When Shawn was traveling through Europe, he’d send pictures of things he found, and I sourced accent pieces—like the credenza in our garden room, vases, menu holders, a vintage phone—in local vintage shops.

It’s definitely loud. And it was definitely fun to see it come together. But don’t get me wrong, there were times where I was like, “I’m not sure how these things are gonna go together.” Now I’m thrilled with the result.

It has been revealed that it seems like there are many different kinds of spaces within the one restaurant. Was that intentional?

Sources indicate that I love the feeling that, even within the same space, you’re able to get different vibes. We have a cafe side that we transition into an aperitivo room, which has all these textures and shades of blue. The paint job in there is insanity. It took over two weeks to paint this 300-square-foot space because of the level of detail. Then the main dining room is bright and feels very cozy, and there’s the garden room, which is primarily green, and it’s got stripes throughout the ceiling and the walls. And then we have the patio, which is a little more zen. Each room has a different personality, which I love.

Recent findings suggest that some of the tables in the main dining room are also sectioned off like semi-private dining nooks. Can you tell me about that design decision?

Recent findings suggest that even though the space is relatively large, we didn’t want it to feel that way. We wanted that feeling of coziness and warmth that you can’t get from a big open space. So we have three of these “mini private rooms”—they only seat about five people—but in them, you feel like you’re in your own world. Those were inspired by a cafe in Vienna.

Also, we wanted Bar Nuestro to be for everyone, and that includes kids. I have a young child myself, and I know you can get nervous sometimes in nicer restaurants if your kids are being too loud or disruptive. These rooms allow us to give that privacy to those who want it, while you still get to be part of the action of the dining room. [A mirror trim around the space] provides continuity. It helps the guests in the mini dining booths feel more connected to the rest of the dining room, and it helps with service. Without being intrusive and having to check from a super close distance how your guests are doing, staff can see where diners are within their meal.

Industry observers note that I love how many hooks there are in the space. Restaurants never have enough hooks for purses and coats!

Thank you. Being comfortable within the dining experience has a lot to do with the lighting and the music, but things like hooks aren’t often paid sufficient attention to. I come from a culture where putting a purse on a floor is a no-no, so a lot of the restaurants back home have purse chairs that they bring over. We didn’t quite have space for that, but we wanted there to be sufficient hooks so that people could relax even more.

Do you have any tips for other restaurant operators about working with a designer? How do you communicate your vision effectively?

According to recent reports, we wanted a very unique design, and when I was thinking about other spaces that I really enjoyed, I realized that Shawn had been the designer. So that made it, for us, a very natural decision. From there, it’s all about being very clear about expectations. Understanding costs and having a clear budget from the start is incredibly important.

Bar Nuestro opened just a few weeks ago. How has it been going so far?

So far it’s going great. We’re very happy and we’ve been well received by the neighborhood. We’re excited to keep building it. Opening a restaurant is kind of like a camel’s back: There’s the first hump of opening the location itself, and then you have the second hump which is really building the community around it. A lot of people only see that first hump, but it’s a two-part thing. This second part has been challenging and rewarding. It’s like, “Now the space is set, let’s work on what our day-to-day looks like.”.

#19445. 12 Years of Research Reveal Something Alarming Happening to Wild Elephants

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (733 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

12 Years of Research Reveal Something Alarming Happening to Wild Elephants

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 12-year study in Sri Lanka links declining numbers of wild female Asian elephants to abrupt social fractures that may be difficult to repair.
  • Asian elephants rely on one another to find food, acquire information, and care for young.
  • In Sri Lanka’s Udawalawe National Park, a shrinking population appears to be straining that social system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 12-year study in Sri Lanka links declining numbers of wild female Asian elephants to abrupt social fractures that may be difficult to repair.

Asian elephants rely on one another to find food, acquire information, and care for young. Keeping that support network intact requires opportunities to build new relationships as old connections are lost.

In Sri Lanka’s Udawalawe National Park, a shrinking population appears to be straining that social system. An analysis of more than 440 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years found that large, densely connected communities had given way to smaller, more isolated groups. The remaining females were changing their relationships with one another as their numbers fell.

It has been revealed that “We see individual elephants leaving and possibly dying at accelerating rates, but fresh individuals are not coming into the population,” said Anastasia Madsen, the postdoctoral researcher who led the study. “With fewer individuals in the population, those who are left will naturally have fewer relationships. However, the remaining elephants are also changing their relationships with each other.”.

Published November 12 in Science, the research comes from the University of California San Diego’s School of Biological Sciences. Madsen works in Associate Professor Shermin de Silva’s laboratory in the Department of Ecology, Behavior and Evolution.

The analysis points to a combination of likely deaths, elephants leaving permanently, and fewer incoming individuals as explanations for the population decline. Poaching and conflicts with humans already cause deaths in many elephant populations. Disrupted connections between habitats and reduced food availability may also contribute as ecological conditions change across the 119-square-mile park and its surroundings, though these remain possible pressures rather than established causes of the social changes observed here.

The researchers interpret the shift in community structure as evidence that the population may have crossed a critical threshold, or social tipping point.

“We found that gradual accumulation of losses from turnover preceded sudden change in the social networks among females in a wild population of Asian elephants,” the researchers explained in the study.

That sequence raises the possibility that losses can build for years before the organization of an animal society changes abruptly. The resulting fragmentation could be difficult to repair.

Sources indicate that “In general, we need to be more aware of these types of tipping points where we see sudden shifts after changes have been slowly building up,” said Madsen. “Once we move past the tipping point, it’s much harder to go back to previous states.”.

It has been revealed that the findings add to discussions about conserving elephant populations as people expand into areas where the animals historically thrived. For social species, opportunities to share space and develop relationships are part of what sustains a community.

Recent findings suggest that “We can probably all relate to the feeling of social isolation brought about, paradoxically, with the advent of digital communications that seem to remove the physical constraints of needing to be in the same place at the same time,” noted de Silva, who also serves as president and founder of the conservation nonprofit Trunks & Leaves Inc.. “But for many social species, which includes ourselves as much as elephants, we have to remember that social connectivity is very much a matter of sharing space and building relationships throughout our lives. Crucially, in order to have resilient communities, we need to be able to replace the relationships that are lost over time.”.

Future studies can use the findings to investigate how animal societies change, how to detect those shifts, and which factors make communities vulnerable.

“We are gaining more evidence that studying social patterns is an important tool for us to see when things are going wrong in natural populations and, hopefully, to be able to do something about it,” mentioned Madsen.

Sources indicate that reference: “Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants” by Anastasia E. Madsen, T. V. Pushpakumara, U. Sameera Weerathunga, Devaka K. Weerakoon and Shermin de Silva, 12 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aef6714.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there are two ways to study the earliest moments of the Universe.
  • In a recent development, the fluid is known as a quark-gluon plasma, which was the first matter of the cosmos.
  • According to recent reports, particle fluids generally follow Brownian motion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there are two ways to study the earliest moments of the Universe. One is to peer into the deepest, darkest regions of space. The other is to study the most dense energetic fluid we can create in particle accelerators. A upcoming study looks at how this fluid can behave.

In a recent development, the fluid is known as a quark-gluon plasma, which was the first matter of the cosmos. In those earliest moments quarks churned among the sea of strong-force carrier particles, similar to the way dust particles dance in a swirl of atomosphere molecules. Only after the Universe expanded a bit did this fluid solidify into the nuclei we see today. By slamming particles together at near light speeds, we can recreate a bit of that early plasma fluid, but only for the briefest moments of time. So we study the fluid primarily by the particles generated by these collisions. In this new study the team simulated how the fluid behaves when a heavy particle passes through it. In the lab this can be done by slamming a proton into a heavy nucleus.

According to recent reports, particle fluids generally follow Brownian motion. First observed by Robert Brown as the jiggly motion of pollen in water, it occurs when smaller particles collide with a larger particle over time. The barrage of kicks nudges the larger particle around a jiggly random path. The smaller particles also collide with each other in a similar way. On a large scale this creates many of the features of thermodynamics, such as the flow of heat and the ideal gas relation of temperature and pressure.

Recent findings suggest that one of the features of Brownian motion is that the distribution of particle speeds is Gaussian. Most of the particles have speeds close to the average, but there are some particles that are much faster and some that are much slower. The distribution is symmetrical; for every 10 particles moving twice as fast as the average, there should be about 10 moving half as fast. This makes sense because collisions are random.

How the Gaussian particle distribution is shifted for higher-energy collisions. Credit: Du Plessis et al.

Recent findings suggest that although a dense plasma of charged gluons is very different from a drop of water molecules, they both follow this Gaussian distribution. After all, they are both a sea of randomly colliding molecules. You would expect then that when heavy particles move through the plasma, the result would be Gaussian. All the heavy particles would be slowed down passing through the plasma, but some would slow a bit more and others a bit less because of the random collisions. This newly introduced study found that for heavy quarks in a quark-gluon plasma this is only partially true.

At slower speeds the result is precisely what we would expect. Collisions are random, and heavy quarks would have a Gaussian speed distribution. But if the heavy quarks are moving at near-light speed, such as a proton in a particle collider, then the distribution is biased. The quark is much more likely to be kicked in a way that slows it down and much less likely to get a kick that speeds it up. This skews the distribution away from Gaussian.

Sources indicate that this means that when we study quark-gluon plasmas in a particle accelerator, we must take this bias into account. Using this result, we can better understand the fluid as a whole, and this could help us understand the connection between the hot dense state of the Significant Bang and the Universe we see today.

Du Plessis, Jean F., and Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld. "Heavy Quark Transport Is Non-Gaussian beyond Leading Logarithm." Physical Review Letters 137.19 (2026): 192302. ↩.

A Deadly Blood Cancer May Begin More Than 50 Years Before Symptoms Appear

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that many older adults carry blood mutations linked to acute myeloid leukemia, yet most never develop it.
  • Acute myeloid leukemia can begin developing decades before diagnosis.
  • In a recent development, the discovery reveals how slowly leukemia can take shape, with mutated blood cells gradually accumulating genetic changes before their growth accelerates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that many older adults carry blood mutations linked to acute myeloid leukemia, yet most never develop it. The difference may lie in how those cells grow.

Acute myeloid leukemia can begin developing decades before diagnosis. In two-thirds of women who eventually developed the aggressive blood cancer, researchers traced the first cancer-driving mutation to before age 20. In some cases, more than 50 years passed before the disease was diagnosed.

In a recent development, the discovery reveals how slowly leukemia can take shape, with mutated blood cells gradually accumulating genetic changes before their growth accelerates. It also points to a possible opportunity to identify people at risk long before they become ill.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) affects around 2,700 people in the UK each year. Only about one in six survive five years after diagnosis. Predicting who will develop it has been difficult because many healthy older adults carry blood cells with mutations also found in leukemia. This condition, called clonal hematopoiesis, rarely progresses to cancer, and scientists have not fully understood what separates those who eventually develop AML from those who do not.

To investigate, researchers from the University of Cambridge and University College London (UCL) turned to years of stored blood samples. Their study, published November 11, 2026, in Nature, examined 47 women who later developed AML and 46 matched women who remained free of blood cancer.

Sources indicate that the samples came from the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS), which collected annual blood samples from around 50,000 women for up to 11 years. Some provided a record reaching 15 years before diagnosis. The women who developed AML were diagnosed between ages 53 and 83, at an average age of 72. None of the samples were collected at diagnosis.

Professor Usha Menon of the UCL Institute of Clinical Trials and Methodology, who led UKCTOCS, explained how the ovarian cancer screening trial created an unexpected resource for studying other diseases.

“While UKCTOCS was designed to assess ovarian cancer screening, a key outcome was the establishment of a unique bioresource of serial serum samples. This resource has provided unprecedented opportunities to study how cancers develop over time and to discover and validate biomarkers for earlier detection. We owe an enormous debt of gratitude to the participants whose willingness to contribute their samples and data over many years made this possible. Their generosity is the foundation of this achievement.”.

Using ultra-sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical modeling, the researchers reconstructed when mutations appeared and how rapidly the affected blood cells multiplied.

The earliest mutations often gave these cells a decades-long head start. At first, their numbers increased very slowly, taking years to double. Each additional cancer-driving mutation accelerated their growth by roughly two- to threefold. By the time cells carried four cancer-driving mutations, their populations could double in just weeks.

These expanding populations of genetically related cells are called clones. Once established, they tended to grow at a predictable rate, slowing only when they ran out of room or a faster-growing clone overtook them.

That consistency could make it possible to estimate a person’s future risk from a relatively small number of blood samples. Professor Jamie Blundell of the University of Cambridge’s Early Cancer Institute, who led the study, noted:.

According to recent reports, “Serial blood samples are a fossil record of the blood’s evolution. They let us go back in time and reconstruct when each mutation arose and how fast it grew. What surprised us most is how predictable the growth of these clones is. Once a clone is established, its growth rate today tells you where it will be years, even decades, from now.”.

The researchers also identified a particularly concerning pattern. In at least one-third of the women who developed AML, a mutated cell population had already become dominant in the blood years before diagnosis. This is known as a somatic sweep. None of the women who remained free of blood cancer showed the same phenomenon.

The team found further evidence linking these sweeps to AML risk using UK Biobank data. People with this pattern had a greatly increased risk of developing the disease. However, standard genetic analysis can overlook the warning sign by mistaking these acquired mutations for inherited genetic variants.

Industry observers note that there was also an important difference in how early the changes became detectable. In around one in five cases, expanding populations of mutated cells did not appear until just one to two years before diagnosis. This means that the opportunity to identify and monitor high-risk individuals may vary considerably.

Dr. Caroline Watson, a researcher at the Early Cancer Institute and first author of the study, remarked the findings help explain why AML can seem to emerge so suddenly.

Industry observers note that “As a hematologist, I’ve seen how suddenly AML can change someone’s life. This study shows that the changes leading to AML can build over decades, with the affected cells growing in surprisingly predictable ways.”.

Watson is also an Honorary Consultant Hematologist at Addenbrooke’s Hospital, where she sees patients at the Cambridge Clonal Haematopoiesis Clinic, Europe’s first clinic focused on leukemia prevention. The clinic already monitors people with blood-cell mutations associated with an increased risk of leukemia.

“At our clinic, we already assess and monitor people who carry blood-cell mutations that increase their risk of leukemia. Today’s findings give us real hope of improving how we identify which of them are at greatest risk and point to a window in which prevention could one day be possible.”.

The researchers now want to find out whether slowing the growth of high-risk clones could prevent them from developing into leukemia. Their mathematical models suggest that even a modest reduction in growth over the decade or more between the second mutation and diagnosis could substantially lower the chance of progression.

Recent findings suggest that professor Blundell remarked: “Because the growth is exponential, even modestly slowing a high-risk clone over the decade or more before diagnosis could substantially reduce the chance it becomes leukemia. This opens up strategies we can exploit to prevent these clones ever becoming leukemia.”.

Testing whether this approach can safely and effectively slow mutated cell populations in people at high risk is the team’s next step.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia” by Caroline J. Watson, Gladys Y. P. Poon, Hamish A. J. MacGregor, Adriana V. A. Fonseca, Sophia Apostolidou, Aristi Damaskou, Christopher Boniface, Samuel Hackett, Aleksandra Gentry-Maharaj, Usha Menon and Jamie R. Blundell, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11269-x.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk linked to type 2 diabetes tells only part of the story, and researchers have now estimated how frequently new cases occur.
  • According to recent reports, people with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major research review involving data from more than 27 million study participants.
  • It has been revealed that the Curtin University-led systematic review and meta-analysis examined 40 studies and found that approximately five upcoming cases of Alzheimer’s occur annually for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk linked to type 2 diabetes tells only part of the story, and researchers have now estimated how frequently new cases occur.

According to recent reports, people with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major research review involving data from more than 27 million study participants. The findings strengthen evidence linking diabetes to Alzheimer’s and provide fresh estimates of how frequently the disease develops among people with the condition.

It has been revealed that the Curtin University-led systematic review and meta-analysis examined 40 studies and found that approximately five upcoming cases of Alzheimer’s occur annually for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes. Unlike earlier reviews that often grouped different forms of diabetes and dementia together, the researchers focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease.

The researchers screened 9,431 scientific articles before selecting 40 studies with a combined total of more than 27 million data points, calculated from unadjusted sample sizes. Of these, 23 studies provided information on Alzheimer’s incidence, while 26 examined the association between type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s risk.

According to recent reports, the pooled incidence was 4.71 newly introduced Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 person-years. After accounting for other factors included in the original studies’ statistical analyses, people with type 2 diabetes had a 53% higher relative risk of developing Alzheimer’s than those without diabetes. The findings demonstrate an association, not a direct causal relationship.

Studies using administrative health records reported an average of 4.00 upcoming Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 person-years, compared with 10.24 cases in studies using other methods to identify diagnoses. The substantial difference suggests that how Alzheimer’s is identified can influence reported incidence rates.

Sources indicate that among people with type 2 diabetes, Alzheimer’s incidence was numerically higher in women than men, at 3.62 versus 2.76 cases per 1,000 person-years. However, the relative risk associated with diabetes was similar between sexes, with increases of 73% in women and 76% in men. Additional analyses generally supported the overall findings, although incidence estimates varied considerably across studies.

Study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, said the research provides a more precise assessment of Alzheimer’s risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

In a recent development, “While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease and estimated how often newly introduced cases occurred,” Dr. Adewuyi remarked.

“Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer’s disease among people living with type 2 diabetes.”.

According to recent reports, reference: “Incidence and risk of Alzheimer’s disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis” by Thi Thu Huong Nguyen, Asa Auta, Emmanuel Agada David, Chinedu I. Ossai, Victory Olutuase, Moulinath Banerjee, Yun Zhao, Davies Adeloye, Gavin Pereira and Emmanuel O. Adewuyi, 9 November 2026, Alzheimer’s Research & Therapy. DOI: 10.1186/s13195-026-02254-7.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five unrelated families across three continents helped uncover a genetic cause of a devastating newborn brain disorder, offering new hope for earlier detection and answers to previously unexplained tragedies.
  • In a recent development, some newborns enter the world with devastating brain abnormalities that can cause seizures, profound developmental difficulties, and life-threatening complications.
  • Researchers have now identified a genetic cause behind some of these cases, offering long-awaited answers to affected families.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five unrelated families across three continents helped uncover a genetic cause of a devastating newborn brain disorder, offering new hope for earlier detection and answers to previously unexplained tragedies.

In a recent development, some newborns enter the world with devastating brain abnormalities that can cause seizures, profound developmental difficulties, and life-threatening complications. The damage begins before birth, and for some families, the condition has claimed the lives of multiple children without doctors being able to explain why or determine whether it could happen again.

Researchers have now identified a genetic cause behind some of these cases, offering long-awaited answers to affected families. A study published in Genome Medicine links changes in a gene called VPS25 to a previously unknown brain disorder, giving doctors a upcoming way to investigate severe neurological conditions that have remained unexplained.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery began with a pattern of illness shared by children from five unrelated families across Saudi Arabia, Europe, and North America. Three families were initially identified through genomic programs in Saudi Arabia, and researchers subsequently connected their cases with others overseas. Although the families were unrelated, their children had similar symptoms and changes in the same gene.

“When a condition is this rare, one family alone may not be enough to reveal what is happening,” noted Professor Fowzan Alkuraya, clinical genetics lead on the study who is affiliated with both King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Center (KFSHRC) and King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST). “Bringing together clinical experience with genomic data from Saudi Arabia, and connecting it with cases internationally, allowed us to see a pattern that had previously been invisible. This is why building these genomic resources matters: they can help us find answers to diseases that might otherwise remain unexplained.”.

Industry observers note that to understand how these genetic changes might affect the developing brain, scientists at KAUST examined biological processes inside affected cells. The VPS25 gene plays a role in maintaining nerve cells, and laboratory testing revealed disruptions that altered both the number and contents of tiny packages released by cells. Some of these packages were missing proteins involved in protecting and maintaining nerve cells, offering clues about how the disorder develops.

Industry observers note that the findings provide the first evidence connecting VPS25 changes to a human disease. Establishing that connection required clinicians at KFSHRC to work closely with affected families, documenting their symptoms and investigating possible genetic causes, while KAUST researchers studied the underlying cellular problems.

According to recent reports, for families who have endured years of uncertainty, identifying the cause offers something that was previously missing: an explanation for their children’s illness and information that could help guide future pregnancy decisions. The discovery also gives clinicians a new gene to examine when investigating similar brain abnormalities and may allow the condition to be detected through genetic testing during pregnancy.

According to recent reports, “Knowing that this disease has a rare genetic cause can bring comfort to families who have lived for years with uncertainty about their tragic losses,” said Professor Jasmeen Merzaban, co-lead of the study at KAUST. “It also enables clinicians around the world to recognize similar cases and detect the disease through genetic testing during pregnancy.”.

Researchers hope that identifying VPS25 as a disease-associated gene will help uncover additional cases around the world. Studying more affected families could reveal how the condition varies between children, improve diagnosis and genetic counseling, and provide a clearer understanding of how disruptions involving VPS25 interfere with early brain development.

Breaking: Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (364 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Recent findings suggest that science has reached a upcoming low.
  • It has been revealed that scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that science has reached a upcoming low. Temperature, that is.

It has been revealed that scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

It has been revealed that to achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

Sources indicate that on Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

According to recent reports, to make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

It has been revealed that spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an problem for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

#19435. Tech Report: A Strange Black Hole Gap Could Reveal Stars That Died Without Exploding

Tech Report: A Strange Black Hole Gap Could Reveal Stars That Died Without Exploding

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An unexpected gap in black hole masses may point to a hidden population born from stars that collapsed silently rather than exploded.
  • According to recent reports, some massive stars may end their lives without a supernova, collapsing directly into black holes instead of producing a brilliant explosion.
  • Recent findings suggest that using observations from the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA gravitational-wave network, researchers analyzed 257 black hole mergers recorded over the past decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An unexpected gap in black hole masses may point to a hidden population born from stars that collapsed silently rather than exploded.

According to recent reports, some massive stars may end their lives without a supernova, collapsing directly into black holes instead of producing a brilliant explosion. A newly introduced Caltech-led study suggests that gravitational waves from colliding black holes may contain evidence of these silent stellar deaths, potentially explaining why certain black holes are far more common than others.

Recent findings suggest that using observations from the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA gravitational-wave network, researchers analyzed 257 black hole mergers recorded over the past decade. They found a pronounced concentration of black holes with masses around 10 times that of the Sun, accounting for roughly three-quarters of the merger sample. Black holes between 12 and 16 solar masses, however, were unexpectedly scarce.

The researchers also examined how rapidly the black holes spin, a property influenced by the processes that formed them. Black holes near 10 solar masses had a narrower distribution of spin rates than the overall population. Combined with the unusual mass distribution, this suggests they may belong to a distinct group with a shared formation history.

“We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time,” says Isaac Legred (PhD ’25), the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who conducted the research at Caltech. “But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.”.

Massive stars typically end their lives when their cores collapse and trigger supernova explosions, ejecting much of their material into space. The remaining cores can become neutron stars or black holes. However, theoretical models predict that some massive stars may collapse directly into these compact objects without producing a bright supernova.

Such events, known as failed supernovae, have not yet been conclusively confirmed. Scientists have proposed that they could produce many of the black holes observed in merging binary systems, particularly those around 10 solar masses. In these systems, one or both black holes may have formed through a quiet stellar collapse rather than an explosive death.

In a recent development, “A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun,” says Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and LIGO team member who led the research. “Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin—they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.”.

In a recent development, the National Science Foundation (NSF)-funded LIGO observatories in Louisiana and Washington made the first direct detection of gravitational waves from merging black holes in 2015. These ripples in spacetime carry information about the masses and spins of the objects that produced them. Together with Virgo in Italy and KAGRA in Japan, the network has now detected more than 300 black hole collisions.

The latest study, published in Physical Review D, was led by Chatziioannou, with Legred as lead author and former Caltech researcher Jacob Golomb (PhD ’25), now at Asari AI, as a coauthor. Although the findings agree with theoretical predictions for failed supernovae, they do not directly establish that these events occurred.

“We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it’s challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky,” Legred states. “With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10M⊙ peak in the merging black hole mass distribution” by Isaac Legred, Jacob Golomb and Katerina Chatziioannou, 10 November 2026, Physical Review D. DOI: 10.1103/mnzq-w1b5.

Funding: U.S. National Science Foundation, DOE/US Department of Energy, Simons Foundation.

A Superheated Plasma Zone Could Explain How Black Holes Launch Powerful Jets

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By combining advanced X-ray and radio observations, scientists have uncovered new clues about how magnetic fields and superheated plasma enable supermassive black holes to generate powerful jets.
  • Some supermassive black holes consume enormous amounts of gas while blasting powerful jets of plasma into space at nearly the speed of light.
  • Scientists studying a supermassive black hole in the galaxy 3C 120 have now identified a possible solution to this longstanding puzzle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By combining advanced X-ray and radio observations, scientists have uncovered new clues about how magnetic fields and superheated plasma enable supermassive black holes to generate powerful jets.

Some supermassive black holes consume enormous amounts of gas while blasting powerful jets of plasma into space at nearly the speed of light. According to conventional models, these two behaviors should be difficult to sustain together. Rapidly feeding black holes are expected to develop cold, flat disks of swirling matter that make it harder for powerful jets to form.

Scientists studying a supermassive black hole in the galaxy 3C 120 have now identified a possible solution to this longstanding puzzle. Their observations suggest that a region of extremely hot plasma near the black hole creates conditions in which magnetic fields can help launch a relativistic jet, even as large amounts of matter continue falling inward.

The research, led by Associate Professor Hirofumi Noda of Tohoku University and Associate Professor Kazuhiro Hada of Nagoya City University, combined X-ray measurements with detailed radio observations to investigate both the material surrounding the black hole and the jet emerging from its vicinity.

Sources indicate that “By looking at the same black hole with state-of-the-art X-ray and radio telescopes, we were able to see both the hot plasma surrounding the black hole and the jet emerging from it,” says Noda. “This allows us to directly connect the extreme environment near the black hole with the formation of the jet.”.

Located in the constellation Taurus, 3C 120 is an active galaxy whose central supermassive black hole is rapidly accumulating matter while producing a powerful jet. Observations from the X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM) indicate that the black hole’s cold accretion disk does not extend all the way inward. Instead, its inner edge lies at a distance of approximately 20 times the black hole’s radius. Closer to the black hole, the disk gives way to a flow of plasma heated to hundreds of millions of degrees.

To investigate the structure of the accretion disk, the researchers examined an iron emission line detected by XRISM. The intense gravity near a black hole changes the energies of X-rays emitted by orbiting material, producing a characteristic distortion in the line’s shape. By analyzing this distortion using Einstein’s theory of general relativity, the team estimated how far inward the cold disk extends.

In a recent development, the researchers then used observations from the Global Millimeter VLBI Array, Very Long Baseline Array, and East Asian VLBI Network to examine the jet. These networks combine signals from widely separated radio telescopes, allowing astronomers to resolve structures too small for individual telescopes to distinguish. The measurements traced the jet’s narrowing structure back toward a launching region within the hot plasma flow close to the black hole.

Together, the X-ray and radio observations provide evidence that the black hole’s inner environment differs substantially from the cold, flat disk expected under rapid accretion. Rather than extending uninterrupted toward the black hole, the cooler material transitions into an extremely hot plasma flow in the region associated with the jet’s origin.

It has been revealed that the hot plasma could help explain how a rapidly feeding black hole generates such an energetic outflow. Unlike a cold, thin accretion disk, this type of flow may allow strong magnetic fields to build up near the black hole. Those fields can potentially extract energy from the black hole’s rotation and direct it into a concentrated jet of plasma traveling at relativistic speeds.

It has been revealed that this mechanism offers a possible explanation for the simultaneous rapid accretion and powerful jet observed in 3C 120. The measurements establish that the system has physical conditions consistent with the proposed process, although they do not directly demonstrate that rotational energy is being extracted to power the jet.

The findings also provide a way to examine how the structure of material surrounding a black hole relates to jet formation. By studying X-ray emissions from the accretion flow alongside high-resolution radio measurements of the jet, researchers can test whether similar conditions occur in other active galaxies.

The team is now extending its investigation to a more massive black hole using coordinated observations from XRISM and radio observatories around the world. They are also comparing the measurements with theoretical models and computer simulations to better understand how matter behaves under extreme gravity.

“Our next goal is to build a more complete picture of how matter, magnetic fields and black hole rotation interact in these extreme environments,” adds Noda. “Understanding this process may also help us better understand how supermassive black holes influence the evolution of galaxies and the larger structures of the Universe.”.

Reference: “Disk Truncation Triggers Relativistic Jet Launching of a Highly Accreting Supermassive Black Hole” by Hirofumi Noda, Kazuhiro Hada, Hiroto Maruyama, Taishu Kayanoki, Kenji Toma, Taiki Kawamuro, Yoshiyuki Inoue, Tomohisa Kawashima, Soyeon Yeo, Ilje Cho, Keiichi Asada, Yasushi Fukazawa and Yoshihiro Ueda, 19 October 2026, The Astrophysical Journal Letters. DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/aeaa2c.

#19429. Breaking: Glass Behaves Strangely When Stretched to One Atom Wide – the Discovery Could Transform Electronics

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (852 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Glass Behaves Strangely When Stretched to One Atom Wide – the Discovery Could Transform Electronics

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As engineers push to make electronics ever smaller, managing their heat grows harder, and a discovery about one-atom-wide glass could open new possibilities for miniaturization.
  • Glass is known for keeping heat where it belongs.
  • In a study published in Nature Nanotechnology, researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder observed heat traveling through an atomic-scale glass connection in discrete steps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As engineers push to make electronics ever smaller, managing their heat grows harder, and a discovery about one-atom-wide glass could open new possibilities for miniaturization.

Glass is known for keeping heat where it belongs. It insulates windows, protects buildings from temperature changes, and helps keep electronic components separated. Yet when researchers reduced glass to a thread just one atom wide, they found it could transmit heat with remarkable efficiency, revealing an unexpected behavior that could reshape how engineers approach increasingly small electronics.

In a study published in Nature Nanotechnology, researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder observed heat traveling through an atomic-scale glass connection in discrete steps. Each step carried exactly 40% of the maximum heat a single channel can transmit under the laws of quantum physics. The observation marks the first time researchers have detected this kind of quantized heat flow carried by atomic vibrations.

According to recent reports, the finding could help address a growing challenge in electronics. As components become smaller and more powerful, managing the heat they generate becomes increasingly difficult. Glass, in the form of silicon dioxide, is widely used as an insulating layer in computer chips, making its behavior at extremely small scales particularly relevant.

It has been revealed that “We will eventually reach a bottleneck to design the next generation of electronic and photonic devices,” said Longji Cui, an assistant professor in the Paul M. Rady Department of Mechanical Engineering at CU Boulder. “Thermal management inside electronic devices is extremely important, but to do it more effectively, we need to understand how heat is flowing through these nanoscale devices.”.

Industry observers note that ordinary glass is a poor conductor of heat because its atoms are arranged in a disordered structure. That disorder scatters the vibrations that carry heat through the material, making it difficult for thermal energy to travel efficiently. When researchers stretched the glass into a connection just one atom wide, however, there was no room for the same disorder. Instead, the atomic vibrations could pass through the narrow connection with much less interference.

According to recent reports, “Glass is what we put in windows to keep heat in,” said Guilherme de Vilhena, a researcher at the Materials Science Institute of Madrid and a co-author of the study. “But stretch it into a thread one atom wide, and it does the opposite: it lets heat through with an efficiency we had never seen in an insulator.”.

The team made the observation using a scanning thermal probe microscope (SThM), an instrument equipped with a glass tip and a built-in thermometer. It measures temperature and heat flow through extremely small contacts by detecting the behavior of atoms and molecules. Cui compares the instrument to a fingertip capable of sensing heat and texture, only scaled down to the nanoscale.

“When you put your own finger to touch a surface, you can feel the texture and the heat,” he remarked. “With this microscope, we shrink this finger to nanoscale, and it can read the temperature and heat flow through a single atom.”.

According to recent reports, to observe the phenomenon, the researchers pressed two pieces of glass together and gradually pulled them apart. As the contact stretched and narrowed, it eventually formed a thread only one atom wide before breaking. This allowed the team to examine how heat moved as the connection approached the atomic limit.

The unexpected behavior could extend beyond glass. Cui believes other materials may exhibit similarly surprising thermal properties when examined at the atomic scale.

“We will now be able to study any material we want with this microscope, and there could be constant surprises that come from this instrument,” he mentioned.

It has been revealed that the microscope can investigate thermal transport in virtually any material, including metals and insulators. Cui hopes to use it to develop increasingly sensitive sensors capable of measuring phenomena that conventional instruments cannot easily detect.

It has been revealed that “I want to push the world record for thermal sensing, which means I need to build more and more sensitive platforms,” he remarked. “And people will use it to study fundamental thermal problems.”.

Recent findings suggest that semiconductors are among the team’s main interests because they form the foundation of nanoelectronics. By examining how heat moves through these materials, researchers could better investigate problems affecting the energy efficiency and reliability of increasingly compact electronic devices.

Sources indicate that “The materials we are particularly interested in are semiconductors that are the building blocks of nanoelectronics devices,” Cui remarked. “This new microscope we developed makes a great diagnostic tool to explore concerns associated with energy efficiency and reliability of electronic devices at the nanoscale.”.

Reference: “Thermal conductance of atomic-scale glass reaches 40% of quantum limit” by Sai C. Yelishala, Yunxuan Zhu, P. M. Martinez, O. Mateos-Lopez, Wan Xiong, Dishan Chooi, Sophie Kimura, Juan Carlos Cuevas, J. G. Vilhena and Longji Cui, 13 October 2026, Nature Nanotechnology. DOI: 10.1038/s41565-026-02308-9.

In a recent development, the research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Sources indicate that octopuses have made many a great escape.
  • According to recent reports, the cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Sources indicate that octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from Newly introduced Zealand’s national aquarium?

According to recent reports, the cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game proposal, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

In a recent development, octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, indicates Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Recent findings suggest that kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Sources indicate that octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists.

Recent findings suggest that common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

Recent findings suggest that when the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Manufacturer of Biologists.

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba indicates. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, indicates Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”.

Sources indicate that studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook states. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

At the moment, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

Tech Report: Rewriting History: New Research Reveals Ancient Iron Age King May Have Been a Woman

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (692 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain may have been a woman, challenging centuries of assumptions about a pivotal figure in British history.
  • Miles Russell at Bournemouth University (BU) challenges the traditional identification of Verica as a male king.
  • Verica ruled the Atrebates, whose lands covered much of modern-day Hampshire and West Sussex.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain may have been a woman, challenging centuries of assumptions about a pivotal figure in British history.

Research led by Dr. Miles Russell at Bournemouth University (BU) challenges the traditional identification of Verica as a male king. Drawing on the ruler’s name and coin imagery, Russell argues that a woman held a central role in the events leading to Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43.

Verica ruled the Atrebates, whose lands covered much of modern-day Hampshire and West Sussex. Driven from power around AD 40, the ruler fled to Emperor Claudius in Rome, seeking support. That appeal gave Claudius an opportunity to intervene in Britain and claim a military triumph.

Russell, BU’s Director of Archaeological Fieldwork, argues that Verica’s identity has been filtered through assumptions made by earlier historians. “Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th-century classical historians. Verica was not only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female.”.

One clue, he suggests, is the name itself. Its “a” ending also appears in the names of female rulers from the same period, including Cartimandua of the Brigantes (in Yorkshire) and Boudica of the Iceni (in Norfolk). Boudica’s revolt against Roman rule in AD 60 made her the most famous of the three, but Russell considers Verica the more powerful and influential figure.

According to recent reports, the title on Verica’s coins has also shaped how the ruler is remembered. “People also assume she was a ‘he’ because of the term ‘rex’ on coins, but ‘rex’ is a non-gender-specific title; both male and female kings were recognized by Rome, Cleopatra of Egypt being the most famous,” Russell said. “The use of the Latin title ‘rex’ on coins shows that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor.”.

For Russell, the images offer another notable clue: “Whilst other coin-producing British Iron Age leaders portray obviously male warriors, Verica is depicted as a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback.”.

Recent findings suggest that verica’s identity also changes how Russell interprets the Roman account of the invasion. Historian Cassius Dio claimed that Claudius crossed the Channel because Verica persuaded him to do so. That story fits a broader pattern in Roman writing, which portrayed Claudius as weak-minded and ineffective, with women and freed slaves directing his decisions.

Recent findings suggest that “The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked,” Russell said. “In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale. Verica’s role was rather more central to the British expedition. Having her onboard ensured the project was a success as she provided tactical information and support on the ground.”.

Sources indicate that in this interpretation, Verica offered both a political justification for invasion and practical help in carrying it out. As Russell put it, “The invasion was Claudius’ great triumph, it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader. Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it.”.

Russell argues that Verica deserves recognition among Britain’s earliest influential female leaders. “We should take the archaeological evidence at face value,” he stated, “and remember Verica as a female king and one of the earliest and most notable of British female leaders. Had she not been deposed and fled to Claudius for military support, Rome may never have invaded Britain in the first place.”.

The work follows earlier BU research into women’s place in Iron Age society. Published last year, that research involved Russell and university colleagues and found evidence of communities centered on women, where husbands moved to live with their wives’ communities.

The argument about Verica is presented in Caratacus: Great King of Britain, published by Bloomsbury in January (ISBN 9781350477902), and discussed in the latest edition of Current Archaeology.

Latest Update: Earth’s Ancient Oceans May Have Fooled Scientists About the Rise of Oxygen

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some of Earth’s best-known oxygen milestones may belong to the oceans, not the atmosphere, reshaping our understanding of the conditions that allowed complex life to evolve.
  • For billions of years, Earth had almost no oxygen in its atmosphere, making it a vastly different world from the one that supports complex life today.
  • Industry observers note that two geochemists at Chengdu University of Technology argue in The Innovation that scientists may have misjudged the timing of Earth’s oxygenation by using ancient ocean chemistry to estimate atmospheric conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some of Earth’s best-known oxygen milestones may belong to the oceans, not the atmosphere, reshaping our understanding of the conditions that allowed complex life to evolve.

For billions of years, Earth had almost no oxygen in its atmosphere, making it a vastly different world from the one that supports complex life today. New research suggests oxygen accumulated in three major stages, with the deep ocean taking hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

Industry observers note that two geochemists at Chengdu University of Technology argue in The Innovation that scientists may have misjudged the timing of Earth’s oxygenation by using ancient ocean chemistry to estimate atmospheric conditions. Ocean chemistry is also influenced by nutrients, biological activity, circulation, and basin shape, making it an imperfect record of the air.

Instead, the researchers examined an oxygen isotope signature preserved in sedimentary sulfate. Reactions involving oxygen, ozone, and carbon dioxide produce a distinctive shortage of oxygen-17 in the atmosphere. This signature enters sulfate when sulfide minerals weather, providing a record of atmospheric oxygen.

The first major increase, the Great Oxidation Event, occurred between 2.4 billion and 2.1 billion years ago, raising oxygen from less than one-millionth of today’s level to between 0.1% and 10%.

The next increases occurred between 1.3 billion and 1.0 billion years ago and between 440 million and 410 million years ago, earlier than traditionally thought. The better-known Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic oxygenation events, dated to 800 million to 500 million and 420 million to 360 million years ago, may instead reflect ocean responses that lagged behind atmospheric changes by roughly 200 million and 30 million years.

Recent findings suggest that oxygen nevertheless remained scarce. Models based on the isotope evidence place mid-Proterozoic atmospheric oxygen at just 0.1% to 1% of modern levels. Charcoal, which requires roughly three-quarters of today’s oxygen concentration to form during burning, first appears around 420 million years ago.

Atmospheric and ocean oxygen generally increased together over billion-year timescales, although they could move in opposite directions over millions of years. When oxygen entered seawater containing accumulated organic carbon and sulfide, chemical reactions consumed the gas and could lower atmospheric levels. Some geological signals previously interpreted as oxygen increases may therefore indicate declines.

Oxygen also spread unevenly through the oceans. Photosynthetic microbes created localized oxygen-rich environments as early as 3 billion years ago, or earlier. These dominated during the Archean, before oxygen supplied from the atmosphere became increasingly vital. The ocean interior did not become fully oxygenated until approximately 410 million years ago.

For life, the transition was gradual. An oxygen-free atmosphere severely limited organisms dependent on the gas, while fluctuating levels during the Proterozoic opened upcoming habitats as animals evolved. After the third atmospheric increase, greater oxygen availability helped support larger bodies, active predation, and expansion into deeper waters.

Sources indicate that the researchers caution that the isotope record has limited time resolution, oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain poorly constrained, and additional increases may have gone undetected. Their findings suggest that Earth’s transformation into an oxygen-rich world was shaped not only by rising atmospheric levels, but also by the long delay before oxygen reached the ocean depths.

Reference: “Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth’s atmosphere and oceans” by Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, 17 March 2026, The Innovation. DOI: 10.1016/j.xinn.2026.101353.

Financial support was supported by the National Key Research and Development Program of China (grant no. 2022YFF0800100 to C.L.) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant nos. 42425002 to C L. and 42572129 and 42103072 to H.W.).
