Tech Report: This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Recent findings suggest that most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater.
  • Industry observers note that scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Industry observers note that scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani indicates. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani states.

Industry observers note that for amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

In a recent development, scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani indicates.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these complications. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

In a recent development, G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart claims. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#19414. Arctic Bacteria May Be Using Sunlight and CO2 in a Way Scientists Never Expected

Arctic Bacteria May Be Using Sunlight and CO2 in a Way Scientists Never Expected

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An Arctic bacterium’s genes hint at an unexpected way of using carbon dioxide, raising the possibility that similar survival strategies exist in oceans far beyond the polar regions.
  • Industry observers note that in the Arctic Ocean, where nutrients and usable organic matter can be scarce, a tiny bacterium may have found a remarkable way to survive.
  • The bacterium, known as Porticoccus arcticus, lives in the frigid waters of the Beaufort Sea, north of the Yukon in the Arctic Ocean’s Canada Basin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Arctic bacterium’s genes hint at an unexpected way of using carbon dioxide, raising the possibility that similar survival strategies exist in oceans far beyond the polar regions.

Industry observers note that in the Arctic Ocean, where nutrients and usable organic matter can be scarce, a tiny bacterium may have found a remarkable way to survive. Think of it as having a built-in solar charger and an unusual food supply. By capturing energy from sunlight and using a chemical called acetone, it may be able to turn carbon dioxide into some of the building blocks it needs to grow.

The bacterium, known as Porticoccus arcticus, lives in the frigid waters of the Beaufort Sea, north of the Yukon in the Arctic Ocean’s Canada Basin. At some locations, it accounted for up to 9 percent of detected bacteria, suggesting it is an important member of the region’s microbial community. In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers at Concordia University uncovered genetic evidence of an unusual metabolism that could help explain how these organisms survive in such a challenging environment.

Sources indicate that one of the keys appears to be acetone, a chemical produced naturally by marine organisms, including microscopic algae, and through reactions between sunlight and dissolved organic matter. Scientists already knew that some marine bacteria could consume acetone, but P. arcticus appears to have a different way of putting it to use.

It has been revealed that its genes point to a process called acetone carboxylation, which combines acetone with carbon dioxide to produce compounds that can enter the cell’s central metabolic pathways. These chemical pathways allow cells to process carbon and make the materials they need to function and grow.

The researchers found the complete set of genes required for acetone carboxylation within the bacterium’s relatively small genome. They also identified multiple genes for proteorhodopsins, light-sensitive proteins that help cells capture energy from sunlight. Genes involved in both acetone processing and light capture were among the organism’s most active, suggesting that it may be able to use sunlight for energy while supplementing its carbon supply through acetone metabolism and carbon dioxide assimilation.

What makes this combination especially intriguing is that the researchers had not set out to look for bacteria with these abilities.

“The genomic composition of these organisms led us to reconstruct the different types of energy and carbon metabolisms that exist,” mentioned David Walsh, a professor in Concordia’s Department of Biology and the study’s corresponding author. “That is how we found this very specific set of genes associated with the use of acetone, which was unexpected. We discovered that the organism’s genes were telling us about something we did not suspect was happening in an ecosystem. This was a surprise, as we were not actively looking for acetone-degrading bacteria that can use light.”.

Walsh explained that the findings point to two distinct metabolic abilities, including a way of obtaining energy that researchers call photoheterotrophy.

It has been revealed that “This study introduces two newly introduced discoveries,” he said. “The first is a group of organisms, P. arcticus, that has a unique metabolism that uses organic carbon while at the same time has the capacity to use light as an energy source. We call this process photoheterotrophy.

“The second discovery is the way the organism consumes acetone to also consume carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere. This acetone-mediated inorganic carbon assimilation combines what animals do — eating food, in this case, acetone — with what plants do: fixing CO2.”.

It has been revealed that the genetic evidence suggests that P. arcticus has developed a way to take advantage of several resources available near the ocean surface. However, the findings describe its potential metabolic capabilities rather than directly measuring how much carbon dioxide the bacteria take up.

Whether these abilities will help the bacterium cope with a warming Arctic Ocean remains uncertain. Walsh does not yet know how changing conditions will affect P. arcticus, although shifts in sea ice could alter the availability of sunlight and acetone, potentially changing where the organism can thrive.

The researchers also initiative to investigate whether bacteria in other oceans and freshwater environments possess similar capabilities. Such investigations could help determine whether this unusual combination of sunlight capture and carbon assimilation is a specialized Arctic adaptation or a more widespread microbial survival strategy.

Reference: “Evidence of an acetone carboxylation pathway in photoheterotrophic bacteria from the Arctic Ocean” by Susan McLatchie, Sara Palestini, Asher Woodhead, Tony Gutierrez and David A. Walsh, 26 September 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78082-y.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team states these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, notes paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

It has been revealed that the bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0).

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Sources indicate that taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

According to recent reports, blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Industry observers note that distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

Recent findings suggest that in a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

In a recent development, those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

It has been revealed that grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she notes. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”.

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, claims she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she states.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer states. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”.

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”.

According to recent reports, as for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice notes. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”.

Breaking: Not All Physical Activity Protects Your Brain, Scientists Warn

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Across 30 countries, researchers found that exercising during free time was linked to lower dementia risk, while physically demanding work was linked to higher risk.
  • After spending an entire day on your feet, going for a walk or bike ride might seem unnecessary.
  • A major analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that those who were most physically active during their leisure time had a 24% lower risk of dementia compared with those who were least active.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across 30 countries, researchers found that exercising during free time was linked to lower dementia risk, while physically demanding work was linked to higher risk.

After spending an entire day on your feet, going for a walk or bike ride might seem unnecessary. Yet new research suggests that being physically active at work may not provide the same protection against dementia as exercising in your free time.

A major analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that those who were most physically active during their leisure time had a 24% lower risk of dementia compared with those who were least active. In contrast, physical activity performed on the job was associated with a 20% higher risk.

The findings, published in The Lancet Public Health, raise an important question about the familiar advice to move more. If physical activity is good for the brain, why might its benefits depend on where and how it takes place?

Industry observers note that researchers at the University of Southern California (USC) examined this question by combining evidence from 74 cohort and case-control studies conducted across 30 countries. The participants ranged in age from 45 to 93 and were followed for a median of 10 years. During that time, researchers tracked diagnoses of dementia from all causes, including Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia.

According to recent reports, the analysis was led by David Raichlen, a professor of biological sciences and anthropology at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences. It is the first systematic investigation of whether the “physical activity paradox,” previously documented in cardiovascular research, also applies to dementia. The paradox describes how physically demanding occupations may fail to provide the same health benefits as recreational exercise and may even be associated with greater disease risk.

“The findings challenge the long-held assumption that ‘every move counts’ for brain health,” noted Natan Feter, the study’s first author, a postdoctoral fellow in Raichlen’s Evolutionary Biology of Physical Activity Lab at USC and a researcher in the Graduate Program of Epidemiology at Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.

One possible explanation lies in what happens around the physical activity itself. Walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports during leisure time are generally activities people can choose and adjust to their comfort level. They may also provide opportunities to socialize, relax, and reduce stress.

Sources indicate that A physically demanding job often presents very different circumstances. Workers may spend hours standing, repeatedly lifting heavy objects, or completing strenuous tasks with little opportunity for recovery. Unlike a recreational workout, these activities may occur alongside workplace hazards and pressures that extend well beyond the physical effort involved.

Manual occupations, for example, can expose workers to greater psychosocial stress, less control over their working conditions, and higher levels of air and noise pollution. These factors have independently been linked to dementia risk. Workers may also struggle to find time or energy for recreational exercise, particularly when access to safe places for physical activity is limited.

It has been revealed that for these reasons, the researchers believe the higher dementia risk associated with occupational activity is unlikely to result from movement itself. Instead, the working conditions and broader social environments surrounding physically demanding jobs may help explain the difference.

According to recent reports, the relationship also changed depending on how much activity people performed. Higher levels of leisure-time exercise were associated with progressively lower dementia risk, although the association eventually leveled off. Occupational activity followed the opposite pattern, with dementia risk increasing alongside greater activity before reaching a similar plateau.

Not every form of daily movement could be evaluated with the same confidence. Household physical activity appeared to be beneficial, although that finding came from just one study. Active commuting was associated with a modestly higher dementia risk, but only two studies examined this relationship. The researchers emphasized that more evidence is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn about either activity.

There are also important limits to what the larger analysis can establish.

According to recent reports, because the studies were observational, the findings cannot prove that physically demanding work causes dementia or that leisure-time exercise directly prevents it. Nearly all the studies relied on participants reporting their own physical activity, which can introduce errors in memory and reporting. Most of the evidence also came from high-income countries, despite expectations that low- and middle-income countries will experience the largest increases in dementia cases over the coming decades.

Industry observers note that even with these limitations, the contrasting associations remained after researchers accounted for factors including age, education, and chronic diseases. Multiple sensitivity analyses, which test whether findings hold under different analytical assumptions, produced consistent results. Feter said this consistency strengthens the case for taking the relationship seriously.

Sources indicate that the importance of context may extend beyond physical activity. In a related study published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia the previous month, Raichlen, Feter, and their colleagues examined how different sedentary behaviors relate to brain structure.

In a recent development, they found that mentally engaging activities performed while sitting, such as working at a desk, were associated with greater volume in regions of the brain’s cortex compared with more passive activities, such as watching television. These regions included areas involved in executive function, which supports abilities such as planning and decision-making. Like the findings on physical activity, these associations do not establish cause and effect.

Industry observers note that the researchers stress that their findings should not discourage people from working physically demanding jobs. Instead, they suggest that dementia prevention strategies need to account for the conditions under which people are active, including the opportunities they have to exercise for enjoyment outside work.

“In other words, when it comes to protecting the brain, the context of physical activity may matter just as much as movement itself,” Raichlen mentioned. “Improving access to safe parks, walking trails and recreational facilities, ensuring people have adequate leisure time for exercise, and reducing harmful workplace exposures may ultimately prove as important as promoting physical activity itself.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Domain-specific physical activity levels and risk of dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis” by Natan Feter, Paula Iso-Markku, Tiladia Markarian, Dylan M Luong, Jack Gunnink, Natália Schröder, Eduardo Lucia Caputo, Jayne Feter, Anamika Nanda, Sarah Hourihan, Gustavo S da Silva, Ashley Ventura, Daniela Benzano Bumaguin, Yann C Klimentidis, Gene E Alexander, Daniel Umpierre, Pedro C Hallal, Airton José Rombaldi and David A Raichlen, September 2026, The Lancet Public Health. DOI: 10.1016/S2468-2667(26)00142-8.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that for children newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, insulin is essential for controlling blood sugar, but it cannot stop the immune system from destroying the cells that produce it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For children with type 1 diabetes, managing blood sugar is a lifelong challenge, but a newly approved treatment offers hope of preserving their body’s ability to produce insulin.

Industry observers note that for children newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, insulin is essential for controlling blood sugar, but it cannot stop the immune system from destroying the cells that produce it. A newly approved treatment offers a way to slow that damage and preserve more of the body’s own insulin production. However, families have only a short window after diagnosis to consider the option.

Sources indicate that in June 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expanded its approval of teplizumab to include children and adolescents ages 8 to 17 with newly diagnosed stage 3 type 1 diabetes. This is the stage when symptoms appear and insulin treatment becomes necessary. The expansion was granted through the FDA’s accelerated approval pathway, based on evidence that the drug helps preserve insulin production. Teplizumab was already approved for people ages 1 and older with stage 2 type 1 diabetes to delay progression to stage 3.

Recent findings suggest that type 1 diabetes develops when the immune system attacks beta cells in the pancreas, which produce insulin to help the body use energy from food and regulate blood sugar. Some of these cells usually remain when symptoms first appear. Teplizumab targets the immune cells responsible for the damage, potentially extending the “honeymoon” period when patients still produce some insulin themselves.

Industry observers note that “Insulin is essential in stage 3 type 1 diabetes, but it doesn’t address the immune process that is destroying the cells that make insulin,” said Kimber Simmons, MD, MS, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine and a physician-scientist at the Barbara Davis Center for Diabetes. “Teplizumab gives us an opportunity to preserve some of the beta cells and insulin-producing capacity that a person still has. The goal is to intervene early enough to make a meaningful difference.”.

Recent findings suggest that evidence supporting the expanded approval came from the PROTECT clinical trial, which involved 328 children and adolescents. After 78 weeks, participants who received teplizumab retained significantly more insulin-producing capacity than those given a placebo. Researchers measured this using C-peptide, a marker of how much insulin the body produces naturally.

In a recent development, nearly 95% of children treated with teplizumab maintained a clinically meaningful level of their own insulin production, compared with about 79% of those receiving placebo. Separate studies involving people with type 1 diabetes have linked higher C-peptide levels with fewer episodes of severe low blood sugar, reduced insulin requirements, and a lower risk of certain complications, including diabetic eye disease.

The timing of treatment is particularly vital. Teplizumab must be started within eight weeks of diagnosis, while participants in PROTECT began treatment within six weeks. Earlier research also suggested that starting treatment sooner may produce stronger responses.

It has been revealed that treatment involves two 12-day courses of daily intravenous infusions, typically six months apart. Potential side effects include rash, headache, nausea, and temporary reductions in lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. More serious risks include cytokine release syndrome, an inflammatory reaction, infections, and viral reactivation. Experienced medical teams and careful monitoring are therefore necessary.

It has been revealed that teplizumab does not cure type 1 diabetes or eliminate the need for insulin. Instead, it introduces another way to manage the disease by addressing the underlying immune process.

According to recent reports, to help clinicians and families navigate these decisions, Simmons led a national group of clinical trial investigators and pediatric diabetes specialists in developing practical guidance published in Diabetes Care. Supported by Breakthrough T1D, the guidance combines clinical trial evidence with experience in everyday patient care. It covers patient selection, potential benefits and risks, shared decision-making, safety monitoring, and treatment planning.

Simmons, who also practices at Children’s Hospital Colorado, co-authored the published results of both PROTECT and PETITE-T1D, a study examining teplizumab in children younger than 8 with stage 2 type 1 diabetes.

“Once a treatment is approved, the question becomes: How do we actually do this in the clinic?” mentioned Simmons. “The way patients are treated in the real world doesn’t always line up perfectly with a clinical trial protocol. We wanted to give clinicians practical guidance so they can have informed conversations with families and make thoughtful, safe decisions.”.

The guidance also addresses a longstanding challenge in medicine: translating research advances into routine care.

“Research demonstrates that, on average, it takes 17 years for landmark medical breakthroughs to become widely adopted in routine clinical practice. Closing that gap is essential to getting the best science to people sooner,” remarked Breakthrough T1D Senior Vice President of Medical Affairs Anastasia Albanese-O’Neill, Ph.D., APRN, CDCES. “Breakthrough T1D is focused on efforts that will close this gap in a way that is safe and supports shared decision-making between clinicians and families. This new clinical guidance serves as an important tool that will help guide timely care for children with a new stage 3 type 1 diabetes diagnosis. We’re grateful to the leaders who provided their expertise and time to develop it.”.

The authors emphasize that teplizumab should be incorporated into existing diabetes care rather than delivered through an entirely separate treatment system.

“We don’t want to create a separate pathway that fragments care,” stated Simmons. “This is an opportunity to be thoughtful about how we use a newly introduced therapy while keeping the whole patient in view. Our specialty needs to stay focused on providing the best coordinated care we can.”.

Reference: “Clinical Guidance for Disease-Modifying Immunotherapy in Children and Adolescents With Upcoming-Onset (Stage 3) Type 1 Diabetes” by Kimber M. Sherr, Emily K. Sims, Kupper Wintergerst and Michael J. Haller, 11 November 2026, Diabetes Care. DOI: 10.2337/dci26-0061.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even prostate tumors resistant to standard treatments responded to an experimental molecule in animal studies, raising the possibility of a different approach to advanced disease.
  • Most cancer drugs work by blocking proteins or signaling pathways that help tumors grow.
  • The approach targets the androgen receptor (AR) and a helper protein called p300, which work together to activate genes that fuel prostate cancer growth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even prostate tumors resistant to standard treatments responded to an experimental molecule in animal studies, raising the possibility of a different approach to advanced disease.

Most cancer drugs work by blocking proteins or signaling pathways that help tumors grow. Researchers at the University of Michigan Health Rogel Cancer Center are testing a different approach. Instead of blocking two cancer-driving proteins separately, they have developed a molecule that locks them together, disrupting their activity and showing promising results against prostate cancer.

The approach targets the androgen receptor (AR) and a helper protein called p300, which work together to activate genes that fuel prostate cancer growth.

“Our molecule acts like a molecular brace, connecting these two cancer-driving proteins in an abnormal configuration that traps them in an inactive state,” said senior study author Arul M. Chinnaiyan, MD, PhD, director of the Michigan Center for Translational Pathology and S.P. Hicks Professor of Pathology at Michigan Medicine.

“This shuts down two oncogenic signaling pathways simultaneously, enabling highly effective killing of tumor cells while sparing normal cells. Our preclinical findings suggest that this approach could offer a more effective treatment strategy for prostate cancer,” Chinnaiyan stated.

It has been revealed that the researchers call the approach DALTAC, short for domain-alteration chimeras. It builds on a growing field known as chemically induced proximity, which uses small molecules to bring proteins together and change how they function. Related approaches include PROTACs, which trigger the breakdown of specific proteins, and transcriptional/epigenetic chemically induced proximity (TCIP), which alters gene regulation.

“Our molecules consist of two inhibitors joined by a carefully designed short linker. By gluing two cancer-driving proteins together, they alter the proteins’ natural interactions,” noted senior study author Shaomeng Wang, PhD, Warner-Lambert/Parke-Davis Professor in Medicine, professor of internal medicine, pharmacology and medicinal chemistry, and director of the Michigan Center for Therapeutic Innovation.

The team tested DALTAC molecules in prostate cancer cell lines, mouse models, and three-dimensional organoids derived from human cells. The molecules were more effective at killing tumor cells than combining separate AR and p300 inhibitors, with less toxicity to normal cells. In animal studies, they produced lasting responses and worked against tumors resistant to standard treatments.

Industry observers note that “Our optimized molecule is approximately 1,000 times more potent in tumor cells than the combination of inhibitors targeting these proteins separately, while sparing normal cells that lack these interactions. We also optimized the molecules for oral bioavailability, a key step toward developing a pill for patients,” Wang remarked.

The findings, published in Nature, resulted from a collaboration between Chinnaiyan’s laboratory, which specializes in prostate cancer biology, and Wang’s laboratory, which focuses on medicinal chemistry and drug discovery.

“These are remarkable preclinical results,” Chinnaiyan remarked. “The durable responses suggest an opportunity to develop a more effective treatment for advanced prostate cancer, including castration-resistant prostate cancer, if these findings translate to patients.”.

The research remains at the preclinical stage, and the approach has not yet been tested in humans.

“Our teams are working closely to identify a drug candidate suitable for testing in human clinical trials,” Wang said.

The researchers also believe that changing how proteins interact could offer a broader strategy for developing treatments against other cancers and protein targets beyond AR and p300.

Reference: “Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer” by Jie Luo, Jianzhang Yang, Jean Ching-Yi Tien, Mi Wang, Sumit Das, Xiaoju Wang, Eleanor Young, Jelena Tošović, Rahul Mannan, Weiguo Xiang, Xia Jiang, Jocelyn Cai, Yihan Liu, Kenneth Gu, Somnath Mahapatra, Shiting Li, Yitong Yin, Sanjana Eyunni, Abigail J. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

Recent findings suggest that researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng indicates, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

Sources indicate that we live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Industry observers note that zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he claims.

Industry observers note that the researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s vital, Zeng notes, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

According to recent reports, it’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng claims, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Scientists Discover Two Monster Black Holes at the Dawn of Time That Shouldn’t Exist

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A rare cosmic discovery offers new clues about how early galaxy interactions may have fueled the rapid growth of supermassive black holes.
  • Astronomers have discovered two enormous black holes shining as quasars just 900 million years after the Big Bang, challenging theories of how supermassive black holes formed in the early Universe.
  • Sources indicate that the system, designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, is the most distant compact quasar pair ever identified.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A rare cosmic discovery offers new clues about how early galaxy interactions may have fueled the rapid growth of supermassive black holes.

Astronomers have discovered two enormous black holes shining as quasars just 900 million years after the Big Bang, challenging theories of how supermassive black holes formed in the early Universe. One contains roughly 1.5 billion times the Sun’s mass, while its companion weighs about 400 million solar masses.

Sources indicate that the system, designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, is the most distant compact quasar pair ever identified. Its two members are separated by approximately 18,100 light-years, about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way.

Recent findings suggest that “There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two,” indicates Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab who led the international study. “We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.”.

Quasars are intensely luminous regions surrounding actively feeding supermassive black holes. As gas spirals inward, it heats up and releases tremendous amounts of radiation, sometimes outshining every star in the surrounding galaxy.

During the Universe’s first billion years, galaxies rapidly assembled within growing concentrations of dark matter. Galaxy collisions and mergers could funnel gas toward central black holes, fueling their growth. Yet the enormous masses of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua remain difficult to explain within the limited time available.

The discovery emerged from the Aether survey, a James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) program led by Emanuele Paolo Farina of NSF NOIRLab/Gemini. Researchers examined 200 early quasars, representing approximately 43% of those known from this period, using Webb’s Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit.

Recent findings suggest that while inspecting the observations, scientists noticed that quasar J1602+4228A appeared to have a faint companion. Follow-up observations with the Gemini North telescope in Hawaiʻi confirmed that the two sources could be distinguished individually, despite their exceptionally close apparent separation.

It has been revealed that “The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights,” says Onorato. Additional observations helped researchers further characterize both quasars.

Astronomers expect pairs of active black holes to form as galaxies interact and merge. However, black holes shine as quasars for relatively short periods, making it difficult to catch two neighboring objects in this luminous phase simultaneously.

Industry observers note that the challenge is even greater in the distant Universe, where faint objects separated by tiny angles are difficult to resolve. Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is only the third known quasar pair discovered during cosmic dawn, when the first generations of galaxies and black holes were taking shape.

Researchers suggest that Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua may lie in an exceptionally dense region of the early Universe, where frequent galaxy interactions supplied gas for rapid star formation and black hole growth. This remains a possible explanation rather than a confirmed account of the system’s origins.

“Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment,” says Onorato. “It’s a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.”.

The Hawaiian nickname translates to “Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.” It was created through the A Hua He Inoa program in collaboration with Hawaiian language and astronomy institutions.

Reference: “Nāpōwawā‘enakaulua: A Close Quasar Pair at Cosmic Dawn in the Aether Survey” by Silvia Onorato, Emanuele Paolo Farina, Roberto Decarli, Klaudia Protušová, Elia Pizzati, Debora Pelliccia, Devin S. #19400. Scientists have a bold newly introduced strategy to slow down human aging by changing how our cells talk to each other

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1155 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists have a bold newly introduced strategy to slow down human aging by changing how our cells talk to each other

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists propose rebalancing the GPCR receptor family, which 40 percent of drugs already target, to delay several diseases of aging at the same time.
  • Sources indicate that heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and Alzheimer’s are often associated with aging.
  • To a group of pharmacologists, that is the wrong way of thinking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists propose rebalancing the GPCR receptor family, which 40 percent of drugs already target, to delay several diseases of aging at the same time.

Sources indicate that heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and Alzheimer’s are often associated with aging. They get treated as three different problems, by three different specialists, with three different sets of pills.

To a group of pharmacologists, that is the wrong way of thinking.

The three diseases share a handful of aging processes, and those processes run through one family of receptors on the surface of cells. Nearly 40 percent of today’s drugs already act on that family.

The scientists propose treating the family as one network and nudging it back toward a younger balance, so that several diseases of aging are delayed at once.

It has been revealed that it’s a proposal rather than an experiment. The paper reviews what is known about these receptors and lays out a blueprint. No drug or combination of drugs has been tested against aging in this way.

Stuart Maudsley of the Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, Florida, is the senior author, with nine co-authors in the United States, Britain, and Canada.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview with Earth.com, he stated the case rests on practicality rather than on proof. “Our argument is not that GPCRs have already been shown to outperform every other approach,” he said.

“It is that they offer an unusually practical set of entry points into this interconnected biology, because we already know how to target many of them with medicines.”.

The receptors are called G protein-coupled receptors, or GPCRs. Each one sits in a cell’s outer membrane and passes a message from outside the cell to the machinery inside.

The message might come from a hormone, a nerve signal, or a nutrient. Humans have roughly 800 of them in five families, and about 720 belong to the largest family.

It has been revealed that many familiar medicines work on these receptors, each prescribed for one disease. Beta blockers for heart failure and blood pressure drugs that block angiotensin act on them.

So do the Parkinson’s drug istradefylline and the diabetes and weight-loss drugs semaglutide and tirzepatide.

According to recent reports, maudsley compared the body to a transport network. Repairing one road helps, he said, but it may not clear congestion caused by problems across the wider system.

In the same way, treating one disease pathway can be valuable without fixing the linked disturbances that leave a person open to several other conditions of aging.

The paper’s central observation is that the five families, which differ widely in structure, age in the same way. Cells carry fewer of the protective receptors on their surface.

The receptors end up in the wrong place inside the cell, their signaling weakens, and the subtypes that drive inflammation become more stable or more numerous.

The authors tie those changes to the standard list of aging’s hallmarks: chronic low-level inflammation, failing mitochondria, DNA damage, worn-out protein maintenance, and the exhaustion of stem cells.

The list also includes the buildup of senescent cells, which stop dividing but keep sending out inflammatory signals.

It has been revealed that in the authors’ reading, the decline of this receptor family accounts for many of those hallmarks. The evidence behind that ranges from approved drugs to animal and cell studies.

That is the part Maudsley called most interesting. Very different receptor families, he mentioned, connect to the same problems in aging, and that convergence is what makes a network therapy worth testing.

Industry observers note that the proposal is not to turn the receptors up. “Crucially, this is not about switching all GPCR activity up or down,” Maudsley said.

“Some signals may need strengthening, others restraining, and the right balance will depend on the tissue and the individual. Precision, rather than blanket stimulation, is the central idea.”.

Sources indicate that the authors describe several tools. One is a drug that triggers only part of a receptor’s response. Another binds a receptor at a second site to tune it rather than switch it.

According to recent reports, A third is a single molecule that acts on several receptors at once. A computer model of an individual patient’s biology would help choose among them.

They also propose pairing receptor drugs with other anti-aging treatments, such as drugs that clear senescent cells or improve metabolism.

The authors wrote that this could be “the greatest leap in medicine since antibiotics.” They also wrote that biology may never offer a cure for everything.

Industry observers note that asked by Earth.com what the first test would be, Maudsley described a small one. Take an aged animal model. One group gets a treatment that supports metabolic resilience, another gets a treatment that limits persistent inflammation, and a third gets both.

Then measure physical function, metabolic control, and tissue health rather than a single lab marker.

The combination would have to beat either treatment alone, and the team would also need evidence that the benefit ran through the receptor network they meant to change.

Sources indicate that if it did, he noted, the next step would be a randomized trial in a defined patient group. That trial would test whether the network can be influenced safely in people, which is not the same as claiming to have slowed human aging.

It has been revealed that maudsley told Earth.com he expects the field to deliver on its goal of more healthy years within five to ten years, given the pace of computational biology. That is his forecast; the paper sets no date.

Sources indicate that the paper names its own limits. Part of aging is the slow buildup of random copying errors in DNA, and the authors wrote that no treatment has been shown to reduce that error rate. Their strategy aims at what cells do in response to the damage, not at the damage itself.

Many GPCRs bind several different molecules and set off several signals, which makes a clean, selective drug hard to design.

Recent findings suggest that for gene-based approaches, getting the treatment into most tissues is an unsolved problem. And stimulating stem cells to repair tissue could raise the risk of cancer.

It has been revealed that two of the authors have a commercial stake. Silke Dodel co-founded AstraNexa and founded Deep Science, two companies in Boca Raton, Florida, and Roza Bejanyan works for AstraNexa.

The other authors are at Moffitt, the Department of Pharmacology at the University of Cambridge, McGill University, and Florida Atlantic University.

Whether rebalancing a receptor network delays even two of these diseases of aging at the same time in an animal is the open question. The combination experiment Maudsley laid out is where an answer would start.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Science.

#19399. The world grows more than enough food for everyone on Earth, yet hunger and food shortages increase each year

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1168 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

The world grows more than enough food for everyone on Earth, yet hunger and food shortages increase each year

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Economists argue that food shortages now come from war and climate shocks, not empty fields.
  • Recent findings suggest that we do not have a problem growing food.
  • The real problem is getting that food to the people who need it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Economists argue that food shortages now come from war and climate shocks, not empty fields.

Recent findings suggest that we do not have a problem growing food. In fact, global farms produce more calories per person every year, even as the human population grows.

The real problem is getting that food to the people who need it. Extreme hunger and local food shortages are at the moment expected to worsen in at least 13 countries.

Elizabeth Robinson, an environmental economist at the London School of Economics, argues that the planet isn’t short of food. Conflict is the main reason for those limited supplies, she wrote, and climate change is increasingly part of it.

Recent findings suggest that robinson directs the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at LSE. She made the case in an opinion article published in the BMJ‘s climate glitch. She drew on U.N. hunger reports and climate assessments. with no newly introduced data of her own.

According to recent reports, in an interview with Earth.com, she stated the trouble starts with where the food is. “There is still plenty of food, but often it is in the wrong place, and takes too long to reach people in need,” Robinson said.

The U.N.’s Food and Agriculture Organization and World Food Program identify 13 hotspots where they expect acute food shortages to increase.

Armed conflict and violence affect twelve of them, Robinson wrote, and four face a risk of famine: Sudan, South Sudan, the Gaza Strip, and Somalia.

According to recent reports, beyond the hotspots, around 60 to 70 percent of the world’s most undernourished people live in areas affected by conflict. By one estimate she cited, 85 percent of those facing hunger live in conflict-affected countries.

Fighting cuts off food at every stage. Farmland is abandoned or becomes harder to farm, and people are driven from their homes. Access to markets is restricted, and prices climb past what families can pay.

Where conflict leads to food shortages, more children grow up stunted, Robinson wrote. The U.N. Security Council formally recognized the link between hunger and conflict in a 2018 resolution, and climate change is making that link harder to break.

Hotter years and more extreme weather, including heatwaves and swings in rainfall, cost farmers their crops as well as shifting the distribution of pests and plant diseases, Robinson wrote. Food prices also become less predictable.

An estimated 123.7 million more people experienced moderate or severe food shortages in 2023 because of extra heatwave days and drought months, compared with the 1981 to 2010 average. Robinson took that figure from the 2025 Lancet Countdown report on health and climate change.

Each force makes the other worse. Reports show that food shortages trigger violence and political unrest, and conflict, in turn, deepens hunger.

Researchers broadly agree that climate change is a threat multiplier, Robinson wrote, and studies show that climate shocks worsen hunger in places that are already at war.

Asked by Earth.com what has changed since she wrote the piece, Robinson said the timing is what worries her most.

“I am really concerned that just as a particularly strong El Niño is peaking, and the number of people facing severe hunger is increasing, funding for food assistance is falling,” Robinson mentioned.

That El Niño is expected to strengthen, she said, which will be another climate shock for places where food security is already stressed.

It has been revealed that the FAO and WFP have added northeast Nigeria and Somalia to the highest-concern group in their Hunger Hotspots outlook, she noted. Haiti has now moved to the very high concern category.

According to recent reports, in her view, conflict, climate shocks, El Niño and high input costs are all happening at the same time. The effects will build, she said, because planting and fertilizer supplies are being disrupted.

Robinson isn’t not convinced that the international community is taking the situation seriously enough.

Ukraine has historically supplied a significant share of the world’s wheat, corn, barley and sunflower oil, and Russia’s invasion disrupted each of those markets, Robinson wrote.

Sources indicate that in addition, the U.S.-Iran war has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which is affecting energy and fertilizer prices. That matters for next season’s harvests in countries that depend on inputs from the region.

Supply is also concentrated. Just five breadbasket countries supply around four fifths of the corn traded internationally. Three crops, rice, wheat and corn, provide over 40 percent of the world’s food calories.

Governments can make shocks worse. After Russia invaded Ukraine, reports indicated that some countries hoarded grain while others imposed export restrictions, just as they had during the 2008 food crisis. Both moves amplify shocks, Robinson wrote.

Sources indicate that robinson’s prescription starts with emissions. Agriculture and the food system account for almost a third of global emissions, she wrote, and cutting them while feeding a growing population won’t be simple.

Shifting toward more plant-based diets in higher-income countries and cutting food loss and waste would lower emissions and leave more food available.

Countries that rely less on trade and more on storage and domestic production can dampen price spikes, she wrote. Cooperation on regional storage may be more achievable than global coordination.

According to recent reports, farmers need climate insurance, drought-resistant seeds and smart irrigation. The most vulnerable households need targeted safety nets, in cash or food, when prices rise.

According to recent reports, in the short term, Robinson told Earth.com, keeping food moving through war zones may matter most. “So right now, protecting access routes could well do the most good, but this is very much a short term measure, and not easy,” she remarked.

“Climate change, conflict, and the resulting increase in hunger that is being experienced around the world, come from choices our governments are making,” she said.

That is her judgment after decades of work on food insecurity, and the BMJ article is a commissioned opinion piece, not a peer-reviewed study.

Industry observers note that the open question is the size of the climate share. Researchers have not agreed on how much of conflict-linked hunger is driven by climate change. The 123.7 million figure counts heat and drought alone, not the wars they may feed.

In the short term, support that arrives before a crisis peaks, protecting local harvests or sending cash and food to affected households, can reduce hunger, Robinson wrote.

The lasting fix, however, is bigger: in the medium to long term, “systemic changes are needed across the full agri-food supply chain, from what we grow, and how, through to what we eat.”.

“But we need to see far more commitment from governments,” she remarked. The food exists. Whether it reaches the people who need it before the next shock is up to the governments from whom she is asking for more.

The full article was published in the journal BMJ.

#19397. Five cows abandoned on a remote island in 1871 grew into a herd of about 2,000 despite extreme inbreeding

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (898 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Five cows abandoned on a remote island in 1871 grew into a herd of about 2,000 despite extreme inbreeding

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five cattle introduced to Amsterdam Island in 1871 grew into a herd of 2,000 before being eradicated in 2010.
  • In 1871, a French farmer from La Réunion brought five cattle to Amsterdam Island, in the southern Indian Ocean, and left them there.
  • According to recent reports, their descendants peaked at about 2,000 animals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five cattle introduced to Amsterdam Island in 1871 grew into a herd of 2,000 before being eradicated in 2010.

In 1871, a French farmer from La Réunion brought five cattle to Amsterdam Island, in the southern Indian Ocean, and left them there.

According to recent reports, their descendants peaked at about 2,000 animals. A 2024 genomic study found the herd highly inbred, with average inbreeding of 33 percent.

The animals revealed no significant purging of their most harmful mutations, yet the population persisted until it was eradicated in 2010. Their genomes point to a brief founding bottleneck and an ancestry already suited to the island.

Amsterdam Island covers about 21 square miles (55 square kilometers) and lies some 2,760 miles (4,440 kilometers) southeast of Madagascar. It belongs to the French Southern and Antarctic Lands.

In a recent development, once ashore, the cattle roamed and bred freely. They “thrived within a few generations in a seemingly inhospitable environment,” the researchers wrote.

The herd reached peaks of around 2,000 animals in 1952 and again in 1988. A sharp decline in 1953 followed an outbreak of infectious disease, probably paratuberculosis.

It has been revealed that concern that the cattle threatened endemic species led to control measures from 1988, aimed at restoring the island’s terrestrial ecosystem. Culls took place in 1988 and 1993, and the herd was eradicated in 2010 following a decision by the authorities.

Recent findings suggest that the herd was controlled by shooting and fencing to protect the Amsterdam albatross, a seabird found only on the island. The fences came down once they were no longer needed, according to the Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels (ACAP).

Mathieu Gautier of the Centre for Biology and Management of Populations in Montpellier, France, led the research, published online in June 2024.

Sources indicate that laurence Flori, also in Montpellier, and Tom Druet of the University of Liège in Belgium were joint senior authors. The team genotyped 18 animals, 12 collected in 1992 and six in 2006, and sequenced the whole genomes of eight females from the 1992 group.

The herd’s ancestry mixed two cattle groups. About 73.1 percent came from European taurine cattle and about 26.9 percent from Indian Ocean zebu, with uncertainty ranges of roughly 71 to 77 percent and 23 to 29 percent.

Sources indicate that all eight sequenced animals carried the same maternal lineage, mitochondrial haplogroup T1b1. That lineage is found in most African cattle, including African zebus.

Industry observers note that the two ancestries mixed almost at the same time as the herd was founded. Assuming a six-year generation time, the estimate puts that mixing around 1860, give or take 15 years.

Industry observers note that genome-based models point to an intense but brief bottleneck in the late 19th century. Using a method called GONE, they estimate that about 20 generations ago, the effective population size fell to about 4.8.

It has been revealed that effective population size measures how many animals actually pass on their genes, not how many are alive. The same models put the herd’s later effective size at about 1,500, and they showed no sign of a decline tied to the 1950s disease outbreak.

Industry observers note that most of the inbreeding arose a few generations after the bottleneck, in ancestors living about 15 generations back. Because the population expanded quickly, little new inbreeding built up later.

The herd’s autozygosity, the stretches of DNA carried in two identical copies from a shared ancestor, was mainly related to the founder event.

Average inbreeding barely changed between the two sampling years, from 32.6 percent in 1992 to 32.9 percent in 2006. Genetic diversity fell only moderately despite the high inbreeding.

In a recent development, inbreeding can expose harmful recessive mutations, which show their effects only when an animal inherits two copies. Natural selection can then weed them out, a process called purging.

Genetic drift is the random change in gene variant frequencies from one generation to the next, and it is strongest in small populations.

On Amsterdam Island, the genomes showed high drift and slightly weaker selection against mildly harmful variants.

Unlike some populations that have stayed small for a long time, the herd indicated no significant purging of highly harmful variants.

The bottleneck also left a flatter spread of gene variant frequencies across the genome, a signature of strong genetic drift.

The authors attribute the herd’s success in a harsh environment to preadaptation inherited from its European taurine ancestors.

According to recent reports, that suggests the island posed no strong climatic challenge. It also contradicts earlier claims, based on crude physical data, that the cattle had shrunk through island dwarfism.

According to recent reports, A scan of the genomes for signs of selection pointed mostly to genes related to nervous system function. The researchers link those genes to rapid feralization, as domestic animals returned to a free-roaming life.

That shift was driven by changes in behavior and complex social restructuring, according to the study.

According to recent reports, the herd offers insight into how populations can establish themselves swiftly and adapt in challenging environments. Feral populations like this one also carry unique genetic legacies that raise ethical questions for conservation efforts.

The study was published in the journal Molecular Biology and Evolution.

Tech Report: Euclid space telescope unveils first major data release, including map of 900 million galaxies

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.
  • 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.
  • According to recent reports, "These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

According to recent reports, "These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery.".

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Sources indicate that scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Sources indicate that gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

Industry observers note that in its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, "Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here.".

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

In a recent development, the Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Industry observers note that among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope intends to survey.

Recent findings suggest that this image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

#19394. Scientists find a way to spot planets hidden in Webb’s images

Scientists find a way to spot planets hidden in Webb’s images

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New software helps Webb spot faint planets by modeling stellar glare, revealing a planetary signal missed in earlier image processing.
  • Photographing faint planets around other stars requires exceptionally stable telescope optics.
  • A shift that small changes the glare around a star enough to swamp a planet’s light.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New software helps Webb spot faint planets by modeling stellar glare, revealing a planetary signal missed in earlier image processing.

Photographing faint planets around other stars requires exceptionally stable telescope optics. Even the James Webb Space Telescope’s optical components can shift by a few nanometers during observations.

A shift that small changes the glare around a star enough to swamp a planet’s light.

A team led from Northwestern University has now reduced the effects of those shifts with software instead of hardware.

Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, a doctoral student at Northwestern University and its astrophysics center, CIERA, led the work with his adviser, Jason Wang.

The team’s program builds a working model of Webb’s own optics and tunes it until the model’s starlight matches the real glare, wobbles included.

Run on Webb images taken two years ago, it picked out the giant planet 51 Eridani b at a wavelength where standard processing had found nothing.

Across four sets of observations, it made Webb two to 15 times more sensitive to faint planets.

“That is a very tricky problem because even the tiniest changes in the telescope can affect how that glare appears,” Ferrer-Chavez remarked.

“Slight shifts or tilts – even on the scale of just a few nanometers – can change the pattern of light.”.

Young giant planets shine at about one hundred-thousandth the brightness of their stars in infrared light.

Sources indicate that A mask inside the camera, called a coronagraph, blocks most of the starlight. A halo of leftover glare remains, and a planet has to be found inside it.

For about 20 years, astronomers have handled that halo by photographing a second, planet-free star and subtracting its glare from the first image.

The method works best when the telescope’s optics remain unchanged between observations.

The optics do not remain perfectly stable.

Pointing errors and heat drifts change the optics between one picture and the next, so the two halos don’t match.

That mismatch sets the limit on how faint a planet can be.

Recent findings suggest that wang said engineers try to make telescopes extremely stable and haven’t fully succeeded. “Small thermal changes could cause a mirror to expand or contract by a picometer,” he said.

“Telescopes like JWST have cryocoolers to keep the instrument super cold. Those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate.”.

The team’s program, called FLIP, starts from the standard computer model of Webb’s optics maintained by the Space Telescope Science Institute.

It adds about a million adjustable settings for the mirrors, the position of the star behind the mask and the response of every pixel.

Then it nudges those settings until the simulated glare matches a real image.

The nudging uses the mathematical machinery that trains artificial intelligence, which can adjust millions of settings at once.

According to recent reports, “We used the same computational tools that researchers use to train AI models, but we did not actually use AI,” Wang said. “Because we already know the physics, we don’t need AI to understand what’s happening.”.

FLIP first tunes itself on a reference star, then fine-tunes on the image that might hold a planet.

To keep it from erasing a real planet along with the glare, the team plants fake planets in the image and stops the fitting when their signals stop improving.

A full run takes about 35 minutes on a single graphics card.

The team reprocessed published Webb images of three stars and compared FLIP with the standard method on each.

It has been revealed that around HIP 65426, the known planet’s signal was about 1.6 times stronger. Around 51 Eridani, the planet’s signal doubled at one wavelength.

At 4.3 micrometers, where the original analysis had found nothing, FLIP produced a detection.

The 4.3-micrometer band matters because carbon dioxide in the planet’s atmosphere absorbs light there, which is part of why the planet was so faint.

Earth’s own atmosphere blocks that light, so no telescope on the ground can make the measurement.

The third star, TYC 5899, has no known planets, and its reference images were taken four months before the science image, the kind of gap that defeats the standard method.

In a recent development, FLIP still recovered a fake planet planted in the data that the standard method missed. Close to the star, it was about 15 times more sensitive.

“We indicated that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn’t see,” Wang said. “This is real data in a real scenario.”.

In all four observations, residual glare still limited FLIP’s sensitivity, leaving room for further improvement.

The authors also wrote that their model can correct for the telescope’s small shifts but hasn’t yet been calibrated to measure them.

The detector model and the computing cost both need work, they wrote.

The team’s next step is to measure the planet’s brightness at 4.3 micrometers and test earlier hints that its atmosphere holds about five times the heavy elements of its star.

More than 100 Webb observations have been taken in surveys like the one that produced the TYC 5899 image. The team wrote that the discovery potential of reprocessing them is large.

The biggest test the authors named is NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory, designed to photograph Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars.

Current intends call for it to hold steady to about a picometer, 100 to 1,000 times steadier than Webb.

Whether software can ease that requirement hasn’t been tested, and the authors pointed to the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope as the place to find out.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.
