#19393. Earth’s magnetic poles flipped repeatedly before an ancient mass extinction

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1031 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Earth’s magnetic poles flipped repeatedly before an ancient mass extinction

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ancient rocks in southern China reveal that Earth’s magnetic field reversed roughly every 90,000 years before a Permian mass extinction.
  • Earth’s magnetic field may seem like a permanent fixture, but its north and south poles have repeatedly switched places.
  • About 261 million years ago it was swapping them roughly 11 times every million years, one of the fastest rates ever recorded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ancient rocks in southern China reveal that Earth’s magnetic field reversed roughly every 90,000 years before a Permian mass extinction.

Earth’s magnetic field may seem like a permanent fixture, but its north and south poles have repeatedly switched places.

About 261 million years ago it was swapping them roughly 11 times every million years, one of the fastest rates ever recorded.

Recent findings suggest that the burst of flipping ran right up to one of the planet’s major mass extinctions. The geologists who measured it think the two may be connected, though they can’t yet prove it.

Min Zhang led the work with Yongxin Pan, both at the Institute of Geology and Geophysics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and Shu-zhong Shen of Nanjing University.

Colleagues at Utrecht University and BOKU University in Vienna took part.

Earth’s field comes from liquid iron churning in the outer core. Heat leaving the core drives that churning, so when the pattern of heat loss changes, the field changes too.

One of the ways the magnetic field changes is by flipping, north becoming south.

According to recent reports, for about 50 million years, from roughly 318 to 265 million years ago, the field didn’t flip at all. Geologists call that stretch the Kiaman Superchron, and it is the longest run of stable polarity known.

Then the stable stretch ended, and what came next had been only patchily measured.

Few places kept laying down sediment while sea levels fell worldwide, so the rock layers that would record the field are missing in most places.

The Fengshan section, a limestone outcrop near Liuzhou in southern China, is one of the few places where those years survive without a gap.

The limestone formed on a shallow seafloor close to the equator. Its fossils are rich enough that geologists use it as a reference point for one of the Permian’s boundaries.

As the limestone formed, grains of the iron mineral hematite inside it lined up with the magnetic field of the day and then locked in place.

Recent findings suggest that zhang’s team collected 876 oriented samples from two parts of the outcrop and heated each one in steps up to 1,274°F (690°C). Heating removes the magnetic signals the rock picked up later and leaves the original one.

Only 309 of the 876 samples, about a third, gave a clean reading. The other 567 were too scrambled to use.

A flip counted only when at least three clean samples in a row demonstrated the same new polarity.

Stacked together, the two parts of the outcrop record 29 stretches of one polarity or the other across 3.75 million years, from about 262.5 to 258.75 million years ago.

The flips were not spread evenly. In the first 750,000 years the field reversed fewer than five times per million years.

The researchers identified a period of unusually frequent reversals before the end-Guadalupian extinction, with an estimated rate of about 11 per million years.

Eleven reversals per million years is a flip roughly every 90,000 years, on a planet that had just gone 50 million years without one.

After the extinction the field flipped less often, with only three more polarity stretches in the rest of the record.

The extinction itself, about 261 million years ago, is the smaller of the Permian’s two great mass extinctions, but reef ecosystems collapsed and marine life was decimated.

The usual explanation is a huge outpouring of lava known as the Emeishan large igneous province, plus falling seas and lost habitat as Pangea finished assembling.

Why would the field go from 50 million years of stability to flipping every 90,000 years?

As the continents came together to form Pangea, slabs of old ocean floor were pushed down into the mantle.

Such slabs can take several tens of millions of years to sink to the base of the mantle.

By the late middle Permian, the authors suggested, slabs from Pangea’s assembly may have arrived there.

A cold slab reaching the bottom of the mantle would draw extra heat out of the core beneath it. The core would then lose heat faster in some places than in others.

Computer simulations of the core show that uneven heat loss like that makes the field flip more often.

Recent findings suggest that the authors were careful about those simulations. All of them run under conditions far from the real Earth’s, they wrote, and their results depend heavily on the settings chosen.

The field matters to life because it deflects most of the charged particles streaming in from the Sun and deep space. A field that flips often may also be weaker.

Earlier studies did estimate the field’s strength through the Permian, and those estimates fall from the middle of the period to its end.

The researchers noted that they vary a lot in quality, though.

With a weaker field, more of those particles would reach the upper atmosphere.

The authors laid out a series of possible effects from there: ozone destroyed, oxygen lost to space, and more ultraviolet light reaching the ground.

Malformed pollen and plants with extra UV-protective compounds have been found at the end-Permian extinction, about nine million years later.

For the end-Guadalupian event, the team wrote, direct evidence of that kind is still limited.

Volcanic eruptions are a competing explanation for any ozone loss, because the lava outpourings may have released halogens that destroy ozone.

A weaker field would allow more charged particles to reach the upper atmosphere, but frequent reversals alone do not establish how weak it became.

In a recent development, one gap is the field’s strength. A weak field, not a flipping one, is what would let radiation through, and the authors wrote that better strength records across this same interval are needed.

Tighter dates and computer models that connect the core to the atmosphere are the other two items on their list.

For now, the Fengshan limestone records unusually frequent magnetic reversals before a major mass extinction, while leaving their possible connection unresolved.

The full study was published in the journal National Science Review.

#19392. A clever new experiment with light solves a decades-old mystery about how some materials carry perfect electricity

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (946 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

A clever new experiment with light solves a decades-old mystery about how some materials carry perfect electricity

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers temporarily disabled a superconductor using light.
  • Industry observers note that A superconductor is a special material that lets electricity flow through it without wasting any energy as heat.
  • One camp has long held that a strange state called the pseudogap is the seed from which superconductivity grows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers temporarily disabled a superconductor using light. They found that its flawless electrical flow actually fights against a strange rival state instead of growing out of it.

Industry observers note that A superconductor is a special material that lets electricity flow through it without wasting any energy as heat. While copper-based materials are some of the best at doing this, physicists are still debating exactly how they make this perfect electrical flow happen.

One camp has long held that a strange state called the pseudogap is the seed from which superconductivity grows.

In Quebec, a team used a flash of light to switch superconductivity off in one of these materials for about a trillionth of a second. The pseudogap appeared in its place and, as superconductivity recovered, the pseudogap faded again.

The researchers read that as a sign that the two states compete, rather than one growing out of the other.

Copper-oxide superconductors, called cuprates, were discovered in 1986, and the discovery won a Nobel Prize the next year.

The crystal in this study loses all resistance below about –296°F (–182°C). That is cold by any everyday standard and warm for a superconductor.

In an ordinary metal, electrons fill a range of energies up to a top level, and current flows from that top. In a superconductor, the electrons pair up, and a gap opens around that level, with matching features on either side.

The pseudogap is different. It is a partial gap, lopsided, that shows up at temperatures too warm for superconductivity.

Fabio Boschini, the study’s senior author, leads a laboratory at INRS in Varennes, near Montreal, and holds a Canada Research Chair in the dynamics of quantum materials.

In a recent development, the first author is Dario Armanno, a Ph.D. student in his laboratory. Theorists at the Flatiron Institute’s Center for Computational Quantum Physics in Latest York built the model used to interpret the measurements.

The team cooled a crystal of a bismuth-based cuprate to about –442°F (–263°C) and hit it with a pulse of infrared light.

Light with enough energy breaks the electron pairs that carry a supercurrent. So the pulse switches superconductivity off for a moment without warming the crystal past the point where it normally fails.

A second flash, of ultraviolet light, then knocks electrons out of the crystal. An instrument at the Advanced Laser Light Source records their energy and direction, and from those the researchers can map which electron states exist at each instant.

Repeating the two flashes at different delays turns the maps into a film, with frames about 300 femtoseconds apart. A femtosecond is a millionth of a billionth of a second.

The team ran the experiment twice, once with a weak pulse and once with a pulse almost twice as strong.

In a recent development, after the weak pulse, the superconducting gap filled in partway but kept its balanced shape. After the strong pulse, the shape turned lopsided, with the states on one side of the gap suppressed.

That lopsided pattern is the pseudogap’s signature, and it lasted one to two trillionths of a second.

“It is a bit like uncovering missing frames from a film that scientists have been trying to piece together for decades,” Armanno noted.

By about 3.5 trillionths of a second after the strong pulse, the balanced shape had returned. In an interview with Earth.com, Boschini mentioned the pseudogap signature faded again as superconductivity recovered.

“What struck us was that the pseudogap’s electronic fingerprint emerged even when the electrons were cold enough for the material to normally be superconducting,” he said.

According to recent reports, A strong pulse also warms the electrons. So the team compared moments after the weak and strong pulses when the electrons were at the same temperature. The lopsided pattern highlighted up only after the strong pulse.

Boschini mentioned heating alone can’t explain the result, and that light lets researchers test the relationship between the two states in a way that simply warming the material can’t.

Next, the Flatiron theorists tried to reproduce the measured patterns. A model that simply added a superconducting state and a pseudogap together could not match the data.

Only a model in which the two states act on each other reproduced the lopsided pattern. “Competition does not prevent coexistence,” Boschini told Earth.com.

In the team’s reading, the pseudogap and short-lived superconducting pairing can share the crystal. The competition sets in only once superconductivity becomes long-range order across the crystal.

Industry observers note that all of this was measured in one material, tuned to one chemical recipe. Exactly how the light pulse breaks pairs so rapidly has not been confirmed in experiments, the team wrote.

Their theory describes how the two states interact without explaining where the pseudogap comes from.

The next question, Boschini noted, is how general the behavior is across other quantum materials with competing states, which the same instrument can now study.

He said the study’s immediate contribution is newly introduced knowledge rather than a new technology, though over time it could help guide the search for better superconducting materials.

INRS lists more efficient power grids, medical technology and quantum computing among the long-term hopes for such materials.

“For power grids, the long-term hope is to carry electricity with less energy lost as heat,” he said.

In a recent development, whether the rivalry seen in this one crystal holds in every cuprate is still open. The answer will come from pointing the same light pulses at the rest of the family.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Physics.

Latest Update: Inca children chosen for sacrifice were given cocaine, alcohol, and ayahuasca before being killed on mountaintops

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Analysis of eight mummified children from the Inca Empire has revealed that they were given coca leaves and other drugs before they were sacrificed.
  • The frozen bodies of children sacrificed by the Inca Empire over 500 years ago still carry traces of the drugs they were given before they died.
  • Industry observers note that toxicological analysis of hair and nail samples from eight mummified children has revealed cocaine in every single one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Analysis of eight mummified children from the Inca Empire has revealed that they were given coca leaves and other drugs before they were sacrificed.

The frozen bodies of children sacrificed by the Inca Empire over 500 years ago still carry traces of the drugs they were given before they died.

Industry observers note that toxicological analysis of hair and nail samples from eight mummified children has revealed cocaine in every single one. Half highlighted signs of alcohol consumption.

Industry observers note that and a 14-year-old girl found near the summit of a Peruvian volcano carried traces of harmine. Researchers link this hallucinogenic compound to ayahuasca.

The study, led by Dagmara Socha at the University of Warsaw, is the most comprehensive chemical analysis of Inca capacocha sacrifices to date.

Researchers from institutions across Poland, Peru, Argentina, and the United States screened for ten different psychoactive compounds.

The word capacocha comes from Quechua. Capac means royal. Cocha means lake, water, or body.

The ritual of making child sacrifices was among the most sacred in the Inca Empire, which dominated some 2,485 miles (4,000 kilometers) of South America’s western coast from the late 13th century until the Spanish conquest.

Recent findings suggest that the Incas offered their children and young women to mountain deities known as Apus. Martín de Murúa, a Spanish Friar who wrote a 1590 account, noted the Inca performed the ceremony to prevent famine, drought, pestilence, rebellion, and a lack of fruits of the earth.

According to recent reports, young women often came from the acllas – virgins designated for the cult of the Sun. After death, these children became revered ancestors. Their families received great honor.

Some relatives went on to serve as priests in the cult of the capacocha mummies, delivering oracles in their name.

In a recent development, the Incas did not choose children for sacrifice at random. Some families volunteered their own children. Conquerors held some as hostages and raised them in the capital, Cusco, or drew others as tribute from conquered territories.

The eight mummies in this study span decades of discovery and thousands of kilometers of Andean geography.

The oldest find is the Chuscha mummy, unearthed by grave robbers in the 1920s on a volcanic peak in Argentina. She was about eight years old.

The most famous is the so-called Ampato Maiden, a 14-year-old girl discovered by Johan Reinhard and Miguel Zarate in 1995 on an artificial platform at 6,300 meters above sea level.

Three more came from Llullaillaco – at 6,715 meters, right now the highest archaeological site on Earth. The remaining mummies were found at the Quehuar and Sara Sara volcanoes.

Sources indicate that seven of the eight Inca child sacrifices were girls. They are thought to have been between six and 14 at the time of death.

Industry observers note that some were likely killed with sharp weapons. Others appear to have been buried alive.

Sources indicate that cocaine and its metabolite benzoylecgonine turned up in every hair sample the team analyzed. That wasn’t entirely surprising since coca leaves were a central element of the capacocha ritual.

Recent findings suggest that dried coca quids were found inside the mouths of the Llullaillaco Maiden and another sacrificial victim from Cerro Esmeralda. Male figurines buried alongside the children had bulging cheeks – carved to show coca pulp packed inside.

But the chemical signatures varied dramatically between individuals. Cocaethylene, a metabolite produced only when cocaine and alcohol are present in the body simultaneously, appeared in just two cases: the Chuscha mummy and the Llullaillaco children.

The Llullaillaco Maiden’s cocaine concentration was staggering – 16,740 picograms per milligram of hair, roughly 550 times higher than the Ampato #4 individual.

The Chuscha mummy offered something rarer: a timeline. Her hair was long enough to be cut into six 10-millimeter segments, each representing roughly one month of her life.

The cocaine levels fluctuated, but a noticeable decline appeared in the final month before death. Cocaethylene highlighted up only in that last segment.

The estimated blood ratio of cocaethylene to cocaine was approximately 166 percent. This figure suggests heavy alcohol consumption alongside coca chewing in her final weeks.

The study’s most striking finding came from the Ampato Maiden’s nails. Harmine – a compound found in Banisteriopsis caapi, the primary ingredient of the Amazonian hallucinogenic brew ayahuasca – was detected at low but measurable levels.

No other hallucinogens turned up. That isolation matters.

Harmine is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor. It blocks the metabolism of serotonin and dopamine. Modern clinical studies have shown that a single dose of ayahuasca can produce antidepressant effects lasting several weeks.

The researchers suggest that harmine may have been administered not for its hallucinogenic properties but for its mood-altering ones – a way to calm a child facing death on a frozen mountaintop.

The Banisteriopsis vine grows only in the Amazon rainforest. Its presence at a high-altitude Andean sacrifice site implies long-distance trade networks stretching across dramatically different ecosystems.

One of the study’s most vital conclusions is that no two sacrifices looked the same, chemically. Each child’s hair and nails carried a distinct profile.

Socha and her colleagues argue that this wasn’t a coincidence. Each Andean mountain deity had its own personality – its own gender associations, its own domain over weather, water, or agriculture.

The way a child was prepared likely reflected which god was being addressed, not who the child happened to be.

According to recent reports, the sex of the child didn’t determine which substances they received. Boys and girls buried on the same mountain got the same drugs.

Socha has cautioned that it would be a mistake to assume that selection for a prestigious religious ceremony necessarily made the experience any less frightening or traumatic for the children involved.

The emotional reality of what these children went through may be impossible to fully reconstruct.

The study also carries a methodological lesson. The Sara Sara and Chuscha mummies had previously tested negative for psychoactive substances.

The upcoming LC-MS/MS analysis overturned those results, detecting cocaine and benzoylecgonine that earlier, less sensitive techniques had missed.

As toxicology improves, mummies that once seemed chemically silent may still have stories to tell.

Socha describes the emerging picture of capacocha as something far more layered than a single sacrificial event.

It was a complex process, involving extensive preparations, long pilgrimages across the empire, and ritual practices that varied from one mountain to the next.

The chemical evidence now locked inside the hair and nails of these children is beginning to confirm what colonial-era chroniclers hinted at centuries ago.

The study is published in the journal Antiquity.

Breaking: Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.
  • In a recent development, the well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

In a recent development, the well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, claims Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

Industry observers note that chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Recent findings suggest that patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is vital because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, states Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

Industry observers note that the researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle states. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle claims, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

#19387. Tech Report: Sewage pollution may take a hidden ocean route into coastal air

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (952 w)

Tech Report: Sewage pollution may take a hidden ocean route into coastal air

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tijuana River sewage chemicals survive a 22-mile trip north underwater and then escape into San Diego's air, far from the river mouth.
  • When raw sewage pours into the ocean, closing the beach can help protect swimmers.
  • Chemicals from the Tijuana River sewage that reaches the Pacific at Imperial Beach can also enter the air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tijuana River sewage chemicals survive a 22-mile trip north underwater and then escape into San Diego's air, far from the river mouth.

When raw sewage pours into the ocean, closing the beach can help protect swimmers.

Chemicals from the Tijuana River sewage that reaches the Pacific at Imperial Beach can also enter the air.

The findings suggest that chemicals from the sewage travel north in ocean currents for about 22 miles (35 kilometers) before escaping into the air near La Jolla.

Wind alone could not explain their presence that far away.

Karolina Cysneiros de Carvalho, an atmospheric scientist, led the study at the University of California, Riverside and the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Colorado.

Her co-authors were UC Riverside’s William Porter and Kelley Barsanti and Kimberly Prather of UC San Diego.

The team sampled the air at four coastal sites in August and September 2024, when the river was carrying far more wastewater than it typically does during a dry summer.

“It was already known that compounds from this waste could enter the air, but we didn’t realize until now how far it could travel underwater before emerging,” Cysneiros de Carvalho said.

The Tijuana River drains land on both sides of the border, three quarters of it in Mexico. It carries untreated sewage, industrial waste and street runoff into the sea, a plume visible from orbit.

In most summers, its flow drops to almost nothing. In the summer of 2024, between 42 million and 55 million gallons (160 million to 207 million liters) a day kept coming, with no rain to explain it.

The team tracked one chemical first: dimethyl trisulfide, a sulfur compound given off by rotting organic matter and sewage.

They measured it at a hotspot on the river about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) inland, at the river’s estuary and at Imperial Beach.

The last site was the Scripps Institution of Oceanography pier in La Jolla, far up the coast.

It has been revealed that the hotspot accounted for 83% of the combined signal across the four sites, and La Jolla for 2%. Small as that was, the compound was there, 22 miles from the river.

Dimethyl trisulfide breaks down fast in air.

By the team’s calculations, it falls to about a third of its starting level within 3.6 miles (5.8 kilometers), even when the night air is least reactive.

Carried by wind alone, at most 10% of the compound would survive the trip to La Jolla, and under some conditions almost none would remain.

“We found pollutants far from the source that couldn’t be explained by just the wind,” said William Porter, a UC Riverside atmospheric scientist and co-author.

“We wondered, how did this happen?”.

On September 10, 2024, a pump station began diverting wastewater south, away from the river.

Levels of the compound at the La Jolla pier then fell by 86%.

The mid-morning signal was gone within 24 hours, but an early-morning peak lasted another two days before it dropped below detection.

Sources indicate that the two-day tail mattered. The air mixed more after the diversion, which by itself would have diluted the compound about threefold.

It fell about twelvefold instead, so something besides mixing was removing it, and something had been holding a reserve of it long enough to leak out over two more days.

The evidence points to the ocean as that reserve. In water, the compound breaks down slowly.

It also escapes into the air slowly, largely because of resistance to its movement through the water toward the surface.

In the team’s models, 14% to 31% of the compound survives the 22-mile trip north in the top 6.6 feet (2 meters) of the sea. At a depth of 33 feet (10 meters), 61% to 76% survives.

Some compounds also stick loosely to organic particles in the water, which shelters them a little longer before they let go.

The water itself showed the route. Moorings off Del Mar, 5.6 miles (9 kilometers) past La Jolla, recorded a layer of unusually fresh water below the surface in August and September 2024.

It matched water measured off the river mouth to the south.

In earlier summers, when the river’s flow was negligible, the two sites looked distinct.

Ocean models show the coastal current turned northward in August 2024, right when the freshening appeared.

Industry observers note that dimethyl trisulfide wasn’t alone, either. Among hundreds of compounds the team measured, a group rose and fell with the river’s flow and with the tracer.

Their chemistry fell in a middle range: soluble enough to stay in seawater for the trip, volatile enough to leave it afterward.

The study did not measure whether the Tijuana River sewage chemicals reaching La Jolla’s air pose a health risk, and it covered one unusual season rather than a normal one.

The record at the pier runs less than a week past the diversion, so how the pattern changes over months is open.

Winter rains, shifting currents and changing river flows could all alter the pattern.

Porter stated the result highlights water and air pollution are not separate problems.

Recent findings suggest that “You can’t just shut down the beach and call it good,” he said. “We need to clean up the water not just for swimming but for breathing.”.

The next test is measuring the same chemicals in the water and the air at once, at several depths, through a full year.

That would show how often the ocean carries sewage chemicals this far, and how much escapes into the air.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#19385. Breaking: One of Denmark’s last hunter-gatherers ate seafood as a boy, but his teeth hint that farming arrived during his lifetime

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1347 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: One of Denmark’s last hunter-gatherers ate seafood as a boy, but his teeth hint that farming arrived during his lifetime

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A man buried on Sejerø around 3800 BC had unmixed hunter-gatherer DNA, yet from his teens his diet held more land food, possibly from farms.
  • Sources indicate that in 1956, people on the Danish island of Sejerø were digging for artifacts in a kitchen midden known as Rødhals.
  • Seventy years on, the man in that grave is the most recent securely dated person from Denmark with unmixed hunter-gatherer ancestry and a seafood diet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A man buried on Sejerø around 3800 BC had unmixed hunter-gatherer DNA, yet from his teens his diet held more land food, possibly from farms.

Sources indicate that in 1956, people on the Danish island of Sejerø were digging for artifacts in a kitchen midden known as Rødhals. They found a skeleton under 8 inches (0.2 meters) of unbroken shell layer. Kalundborg Folkeblad, the local paper, ran a photo of the find on October 22.

Seventy years on, the man in that grave is the most recent securely dated person from Denmark with unmixed hunter-gatherer ancestry and a seafood diet.

In a recent development, that puts him among the last hunter-gatherers of the country. Yet one of his teeth indicates his diet taking in more and more land food from his teens.

Anders Fischer of the University of Gothenburg and John Meadows of the Leibniz Centre for Archaeology at Schloss Gottorf in Germany led the work with 15 co-authors from universities and museums in six countries.

Sources indicate that the land food may have come from farms, they suggest. The paper admits the isotopes alone cannot show whether it came from farming or from hunting and gathering.

In a recent development, the Danish National Museum sent archaeologist Ole Klindt-Jensen to record and save the burial in a hurry. According to the paper he worked “in the pouring rain.” He never published his field notes, which sit in the museum archive as NM1 1069/56.

On his sketch the man lies on his back, arms down along his body, legs straight, skull to the west. Two large stones face the body with their flat sides.

The bigger is possibly a moraine boulder that was already there, while the smaller apparently stood on edge by design.

Between the right forearm and the lower ribs, Klindt-Jensen noted a bone object about 5.5 inches (140 millimeters) long, a “skinning knife” in his words.

Sources indicate that A museum employee later changed the entry to a piece of bone rolled by water. The employee seems to have discarded the object.

Going by graves of the early Funnel Beaker culture, the first farmers in the region, from about 3800 to 3500 BC, Fischer’s team thinks it may have been an archer’s wrist guard.

Sources indicate that if so, it was the only grave good recovered. The imperfect conditions of the dig could have missed beads or arrowheads.

He stood about 5 feet 1 inch (1.55 meters) tall and died at 30 to 40 years of age, perhaps closer to 40 judging by the degenerative changes in his bones.

Industry observers note that the skeleton is almost complete, with heavy, well-preserved bones. Tooth wear and the lengths of his two upper arm bones say he was right-handed.

According to recent reports, nothing on the skeleton points to violence, and the bones reflect good health and nutrition in early life. Traces of inflammation or vitamin deficiency probably date to later life.

Both Achilles tendons had partly turned to bone at the heel, and his right knee showed moderate wear. Long hours of paddling could explain the knee and heels, the team says. In a paddling position, his right leg would have been bent and the left stretched back.

It has been revealed that bony outgrowths also appeared at the elbows and wrists. Marie Louise Jørkov of the University of Copenhagen photographed them for the Laboratory of Biological Anthropology.

His genome came out in Nature in 2024, in a study by Morten Allentoft and colleagues, under the code NEO645. He carried typical Western Hunter-Gatherer ancestry, unmixed with farmer ancestry. Going by genetics alone he probably had dark skin, with an 85 percent chance of blue eyes.

To get at his diet, the team used up the root of his lower right first premolar and cut thin layers of dentine from it, each formed at a different age.

They measured carbon, nitrogen and sulfur isotopes in every layer, in the crown, and in a sample from his left femur. That covers roughly age seven to adulthood.

According to recent reports, comparison material came from the Rødhals midden (fish, mammal bones and mollusc shells), from modern samples, and from 65 other Danish Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age) people. Data for eight of them appear here for the first time.

In a recent development, shallow eelgrass beds, where eel, flatfish and shellfish live, gave him most of his protein all his life. Around eight or nine he ate a bit more from land, and from age 11 he ate more deep-water fish such as haddock and mature cod. In adolescence and adulthood the land share climbed sharply.

Recent findings suggest that as an adult, and for years, he ate in a way not recorded for any other Mesolithic person so far. His enamel gave a strontium value of 0.7096, a chemical signal tied to the ground where a person grew up, which fits a childhood over a large part of the hunter-gatherer area.

Five radiocarbon dates exist for the skeleton, and all are too old because of the fish he ate. Meadows ran them through a Bayesian model that corrects for diet. It puts his death between 3930 and 3710 BC, most likely between 3890 and 3770 BC.

According to recent reports, directly dated bones of domestic cattle and sheep place the arrival of herding in Denmark at about 3950 to 3850 BC. That overlaps his lifetime.

The Sejerby Female’s grave lies about 1.6 miles (2.5 kilometers) away and dates 200 to 300 years after him. She is the earliest directly dated person with Anatolian farmer ancestry on the Sejerø archipelago.

Sources indicate that her diet was almost all land food. By the middle of the fourth millennium BC, dolmens on the archipelago suggest farmers were in control.

His own grave has a kind of stone frame and no ochre staining. That sets it apart from typical Late Mesolithic burials in Denmark. In build it is closer to the graves of early farmers nearby.

Bone from his femurs and ribs shows that he ate more land protein, but not whether it came from hunting and gathering or from herding and crops.

He might have spent his adolescence and adult years foraging on a bigger island. He could then have returned to Sejerø near the end.

In a recent development, the authors give two reasons to doubt that he simply foraged elsewhere. He ate no freshwater fish, unlike inland foragers, and for years no other Mesolithic person on record shared his adult diet.

“If Rødhals Man really was exceptional, an obvious explanation is the arrival of farmers during his lifetime,” they wrote.

According to recent reports, A small cavity in his lower right third molar is more typical of Neolithic people, but it is one tooth. A 5,500-year-old settlement reveals what Neolithic farmers in Scandinavia ate a few centuries after he died.

Recent findings suggest that A man buried at Dragsholm had the same hunter-gatherer genetic profile and a similar date, but a far more land-based diet. “Lola,” a woman known only from DNA in birch tar chewing gum found at Syltholm on Lolland, is of comparable age.

Industry observers note that no later skeleton with mainly hunter-gatherer ancestry has turned up in Denmark. The 2024 genome work found that incoming farmers apparently replaced the locals fairly abruptly.

Other ancient DNA has shown how plague later struck Stone Age farmers in Scandinavia.

Fischer and colleagues had already described the fish and shellfish from the Rødhals midden in a 2021 paper in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. The team used up the premolar root, so it documented the tooth in 3D and put the model on Zenodo.

The authors write that at his death he “stood at the doorstep to a new age.” Some 5,800 years later, a rainy dig on Sejerø brought him back to light.

The full study appears in the journal Antiquity, where anyone can read it for free.

#19384. Tech Report: A virus found in chimpanzee DNA explains why humans developed much larger and smarter brains

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1440 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: A virus found in chimpanzee DNA explains why humans developed much larger and smarter brains

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An ancient virus in chimpanzee DNA accidentally shuts off a crucial brain-building gene.
  • Sources indicate that humans and chimpanzees share more than 96 percent of their protein-coding DNA.
  • Industry observers note that one such difference was caused by a virus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An ancient virus in chimpanzee DNA accidentally shuts off a crucial brain-building gene. Humans never caught this virus.

Sources indicate that humans and chimpanzees share more than 96 percent of their protein-coding DNA. So whatever sets our brains apart must lie in that remainder, or in how shared genes are switched on and off.

Industry observers note that one such difference was caused by a virus. Millions of years ago, this virus infiltrated chimpanzee ancestors and left a copy of itself inside a gene.

The viral copy keeps the gene switched off in chimpanzees to this day, and as it turns out, that particular gene is very important. The modern human genome holds no copy of the virus.

The same gene is active in the developing human brain, where it appears to help young neurons grow the branches they use to connect.

Some of what separates the two brains, then, may come down to a gene that chimpanzees lost the use of rather than one humans gained.

Johan Jakobsson, a professor of molecular neurogenetics at Lund University in Sweden, led the work with Patricia Gerdes, a postdoctoral researcher in the university’s Molecular Neurogenetics group.

Geneticists at the University of Washington, Uppsala University and the University of Gothenburg were part of the team.

They worked with brain organoids, clumps of tissue grown from stem cells that copy a few features of a brain in its first weeks.

Industry observers note that an organoid is not a brain, and the study notes nothing about how chimpanzees or humans think. What it shows is which genes are active in each species, and where one difference came from.

Retroviruses copy their genetic material into the DNA of the cells they infect. When one infects a sperm or egg cell, the copy is inherited, and over millions of years the leftovers accumulate.

Old viral remnants make up at least 8 percent of both the human and the chimpanzee genomes.

The virus here is one that chimpanzees carry and humans don’t. Scientists call it PTERV1. It infected the ancestors of African apes roughly 5 to 7 million years ago, around the time the human and chimpanzee lines split.

Sources indicate that the virus then spread through the chimpanzee lineage between about 1.5 and 5 million years ago. Gorillas and bonobos carry copies too.

The human genome has none. A human protein that blocks PTERV1 from infecting human cells may be part of the reason.

Jakobsson’s team counted 158 copies of the virus in the chimpanzee genome, each between about 2,000 and 14,000 DNA letters long.

A retrovirus is doing the same thing right now in wild koalas in Australia, inserting itself into their inherited DNA and raising their rates of cancer.

Jakobsson said the fresh findings show that a virus can change a DNA sequence across an entire population.

Early chimpanzee brain tissue is almost impossible to study directly, so the team grew it.

Starting from stem cells from two humans and two chimpanzees, they grew organoids under near-identical conditions for 15 days.

By then each one had formed the rosettes of dividing cells typical of early brain tissue, and the mix of cell types was similar in the two species.

In an interview with Earth.com, Gerdes called the organoids a key technology that made the study possible.

“This 3D cell culture model enabled us to investigate certain aspects of early human and chimpanzee brain development in a dish in our lab,” she wrote.

According to recent reports, then the team read the chemical tags on the DNA. Cells silence stretches of DNA by attaching small chemical tags called methyl groups, a process known as DNA methylation.

In both the stem cells and the organoids, nearly every one of the 158 viral copies was completely covered in these tags.

But methylation can spread from a viral copy into the DNA around it. So the team asked a second question: did any of the 158 silenced copies also silence a chimpanzee gene nearby?

Forty-five genes that exist in both species carry a viral copy entirely inside them in chimpanzees. In the organoids, 10 of the 45 behaved differently in the two species.

It has been revealed that the clearest case was a gene called LINC00662. Human organoids produced it in large amounts, and chimpanzee organoids didn’t produce it at all.

“The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids,” Gerdes said.

Industry observers note that LINC00662 doesn’t code for a protein; its RNA does the work directly. In the chimpanzee version of the gene, a viral copy 6,915 DNA letters long is embedded near the gene’s start. Otherwise the two species’ versions are nearly identical.

In chimpanzee cells the viral copy was heavily tagged with methyl groups, and so was the DNA on either side of it, including the stretch that switches the gene on. In human cells the same region carried few tags.

Only chimpanzees and bonobos have this insertion, so it arrived after their line split from ours.

Gorillas and macaques lack the whole region of DNA that contains the gene, and orangutans carry a different piece of mobile DNA beside it.

In cells from eight more chimpanzees, and from bonobos, orangutans and macaques, the gene was silent, so humans may be the only species with a working copy.

A silent gene beside a methylated virus could still be a coincidence, so the team removed the virus.

Using CRISPR, a gene-editing tool that cuts DNA at chosen spots, they snipped the roughly 7,000-letter viral copy out of chimpanzee stem cells. With the virus gone, the chimpanzee cells started producing LINC00662.

“This shows that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees,” Gerdes said.

For Jakobsson, the key finding is that a repetitive piece of DNA, in this case a leftover virus, helps control a gene that matters for brain development.

According to recent reports, he sees a wider lesson in it. “This demonstrates that this part of the genome likely played an notable role throughout brain evolution and maybe also for brain disorders,” he told Earth.com.

So what does LINC00662 do in a human? In human brain tissue, the gene is most active about 10 to 12 weeks after conception, and its activity declines through adulthood.

Inside cells, the RNA stays almost entirely outside the nucleus, where the team found it bound to proteins that build a neuron’s internal scaffolding and extend its branches.

To test its job, the team silenced LINC00662 in human organoids and grew them for 15 days and for 30 days. The silenced organoids formed normally, with the same mix of cell types as the controls. At day 30, one place looked different: the zone where newly committed neurons send out their first branches.

Industry observers note that there, a marker of those growing branches was weaker in the silenced organoids than in the controls. The gap was too large to be due to chance.

The team also sequenced nearly 120,000 cell nuclei from 85 organoids. Genes that drive the growth of axons and dendrites, the long and short branches neurons use to send and receive signals, were more active in the silenced organoids, not less.

The team reads that as the cells compensating for branches that aren’t forming properly.

It has been revealed that everything here happened in lab-grown tissue a few weeks old, from two individuals of each species. The authors wrote that an organoid can’t fully capture what a human-specific gene does in a whole brain.

The authors still need to work out how methylation on the viral copy reaches the gene’s own switch. And no one has identified which of the cell’s defense proteins recognizes PTERV1 and tags it in the first place.

Why silencing the gene makes the branch-building genes more active is also unexplained.

LINC00662 is unlikely to be the only gene affected. Of the 10 genes that differed between the species and carry a viral copy, one helps nerve cells receive signals and has been linked to schizophrenia.

Jakobsson wrote that he believes elements like these play a role in human disease, and he pointed to a recent paper on Parkinson’s disease from his group .

The team plans to look next at whether other viral remnants changed genes the same way during brain evolution, and whether any of them are linked to brain disorders today.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#19381. Latest Update: Whale sharks actually eat and digest plants, making them the largest omnivores on the planet

Latest Update: Whale sharks actually eat and digest plants, making them the largest omnivores on the planet

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers found that giant whale sharks digest the floating seaweed they swallow.
  • Sources indicate that the whale shark is the biggest fish in the sea.
  • But a whale shark feeds by swimming with its mouth wide open.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers found that giant whale sharks digest the floating seaweed they swallow. By eating both plants and meat, this fish is now officially the world's largest known omnivore.

Sources indicate that the whale shark is the biggest fish in the sea. Like all sharks, it’s generally thought of as a meat-eater.

But a whale shark feeds by swimming with its mouth wide open. Along with small animals like fish and phytoplankton, those enormous mouths also grab bits of floating seaweed and seagrass, which are plants.

According to recent reports, A study of 17 whale sharks in Western Australia suggests the sharks don’t only swallow that seaweed. They appear to digest some of it and use it as food.

If so, the whale shark is the largest known omnivore, an animal that eats both plants and animals.

Mark Meekan, a fish biologist at the Australian Institute of Marine Science, and five colleagues reported the finding in 2022. The team ran chemical tests on small samples of shark skin and didn’t test digestion directly.

Whale sharks can grow up to 59 feet (18 meters) long and weigh about 75,000 pounds (34,000 kilograms).

A fish that massive needs a lot of food in one place. Whale sharks feed on dense swarms of krill, which are small shrimp-like animals.

Near the coast, though, the same ocean conditions that bring krill together also collect floating seaweed.

At Ningaloo Reef, a brown seaweed called Sargassum forms large floating mats, and whale sharks have been seen feeding among them.

Swallowed seaweed takes up room in a shark’s gut that food could fill. A shark can throw up what’s in its stomach, but then it loses its meal along with the seaweed.

One simple solution, the team wrote, might be to digest as much of the seaweed as possible.

The skin samples came from sharks that gathered at Ningaloo in May of 2015 and 2017. A snorkeler took each sample with a hand spear.

The team also collected krill and Sargassum, along with droppings from five sharks.

The first of two chemical tests measured nitrogen in each sample to work out where a shark feeds in the food chain.

Industry observers note that seaweed and other living things that make their own food are at level one. An animal ranks about one level above whatever it eats.

The 17 whale sharks had an average rank of 2.0. Krill from the same reef had an average rank of 2.4.

If whale sharks ate mostly krill, the sharks should rank about one level higher than the krill. Instead, the sharks and the krill ranked about the same, and krill eat both plants and animals.

The team wrote that this low rank implies whale sharks regularly eat plant material.

According to recent reports, the second test compared fatty acids, the building blocks of fats. One fatty acid that is rare in most fish made up 16% of the fatty acids in whale shark skin.

The same fatty acid made up 10% of the fatty acids in Sargassum, but only 3% to 5% in krill. That made Sargassum the more likely source of the fatty acid in the sharks’ skin, the researchers wrote.

The sharks’ droppings, though, contained fats similar to those in krill.

“The poo did show that they were eating krill,” mentioned Patti Virtue, a biological oceanographer at the University of Tasmania’s Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies. “But they’re not metabolizing much of it.”.

It has been revealed that skin samples can’t show what happens inside a shark’s gut. The results suggest that whale sharks may be able to digest at least some parts of floating Sargassum.

Some of that nourishment might come from small animals and algae living on the seaweed.

The fatty acid could also come from tiny organisms in seafloor mud, passed along by krill that spend the day on the bottom.

The ranks also depend on a conversion number that’s hard to pin down without feeding experiments. Other values were unlikely to change the ranks much, the team wrote.

All 17 sharks came from one reef, but sharks tagged at Ningaloo travel across the Timor Sea and the eastern Indian Ocean.

Recent findings suggest that on land, the biggest animals have always been plant-eaters, Meekan mentioned. “Turns out that maybe the system of evolution on land and in the water isn’t that different after all.”.

The team wrote that manta rays, basking sharks, and possibly some filter-feeding whales could be swallowing seaweed too.

The full study was published in the journal Ecology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

It has been revealed that global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite major enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

It has been revealed that by year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

According to recent reports, the results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It has been revealed that it’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters states. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”.

#19379. Plants mix different breeding strategies to survive in a world with changing climates and fewer bees

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1151 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Plants mix different breeding strategies to survive in a world with changing climates and fewer bees

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Simulations show plants that reject their own pollen and plants that self-fertilize can coexist for ages, swapping dominance without settling.
  • Apple trees have a strict biological rule for reproduction.
  • While many wild plants rely on this exact same partner system, plenty of other plant species have evolved to drop the rule entirely, allowing them to successfully fertilize themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Simulations show plants that reject their own pollen and plants that self-fertilize can coexist for ages, swapping dominance without settling.

Apple trees have a strict biological rule for reproduction. They reject their own pollen. That means they need a completely different type of apple tree nearby to produce fruit.

While many wild plants rely on this exact same partner system, plenty of other plant species have evolved to drop the rule entirely, allowing them to successfully fertilize themselves.

A population holding both kinds was supposed to be passing through on its way to choosing one rule or the other.

In computer simulations of evolving plants, the mixed populations didn’t get there. With nothing in the environment changing, the two kinds kept trading dominance for as long as the simulations ran. Neither kind took over.

According to recent reports, the researchers call it a volatile mixed mode. A mixed population in the wild that looks unstable, they wrote, may be in a lasting state of its own.

Sources indicate that tamar Friedlander, a senior lecturer at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem’s Robert H. Smith Institute of Plant Sciences and Genetics in Agriculture, led the work with Amit Jangid.

Recent findings suggest that ohad Noy Feldheim of the University’s Einstein Institute of Mathematics is the third author. Everything here happened inside a model.

In an interview with Earth.com, Friedlander mentioned the result broke a habit of thought. Biologists expect that when a population has several options, some are better than others, she said.

According to recent reports, over the long run, the population is supposed to reach the better one and stay there. Earlier models had the mix fading away or holding steady at fixed proportions.

“Thus, it was very surprising that we didn’t get either of these under a large parameter regime,” she stated.

The populations, in her words, “not only did not settle to either of the ‘pure’ strategies (only self-fertilization or only outcrossing) but also did not settle at fixed proportions of these strategies.”.

Recent findings suggest that the rejection system works like a lock and a set of keys. The female side of a flower makes a toxin that stops a pollen tube from growing. Each pollen grain carries proteins that disarm the toxins of other mating types but not its own.

About 40 percent of plant families use some version of this, including wild tomatoes, potatoes, apples, pears, citrus, and coffee. Washington State University‘s tree fruit site has a primer on why orchards need two varieties.

The system can break. A mutation that silences the toxin, or adds a key that fits the plant’s own lock, produces a plant that can fertilize itself.

That plant gains a sure route to seeds when pollen is scarce, but it passes on two sets of genes to each seed instead of one.

It pays for that with inbreeding. Seeds from self-fertilization carry more harmful mutations, and more of them fail.

The plants that reject their own pollen pay a different price. Their pollen is useless on every plant of their own mating type, so a type that grows common finds fewer partners.

Friedlander’s team simulated populations of 500 plants for 100,000 generations, discarding the first 50,000 as a warm-up.

Each plant carried two copies of the gene set, and each copy held one toxin and nine keys. Every protein was written as a string of 18 amino acids that could mutate.

According to recent reports, two dials set the outcome. One was how badly self-fertilized seeds suffer from inbreeding. The other was how loosely the keys fit the locks, which decides how many mating types a population can hold.

With heavy inbreeding costs and loose-fitting keys, every plant ended up rejecting its own pollen. With light costs, every plant ended up self-fertilizing.

In between lay the third state, where the share of self-rejecting plants rose and fell for the rest of the run and the number of mating types swung with it.

Recent findings suggest that types tended to vanish several at a time, in what the authors describe as avalanches. What triggers those collapses, they wrote, is still obscure.

A shortage of pollen was expected to push populations toward self-fertilization, since a plant that can pollinate itself doesn’t need a visitor. The model found the opposite.

It has been revealed that when cross-pollen was scarce, the range of settings in which self-rejection won grew at the expense of the mixed state. Friedlander noted the explanation lies in how the two sexes compete.

When pollen is plentiful, every female is sure of a partner and only the males compete, so female proteins evolve mainly to avoid matching their own pollen.

When pollen is scarce, females must compete too, which makes them easier to match and raises the number of mating types a population can support.

It has been revealed that researchers often treat self-fertilization as a plant’s backup plan for when cross-pollination fails, she told Earth.com. Self-fertilizing plants do turn up at the edges of a species’ range, where partners are few.

The move from rejecting self-pollen to accepting it has long been treated as a one-way street. A plant that gives up the rule usually sheds the flower traits that attract insects and purges some of its harmful mutations.

Across much of the model’s settings, though, the end state didn’t depend on the start, and a population that began self-fertilizing could evolve the rejection system from scratch.

The exception was the loosest-fitting keys, where the mutation needed for the reverse trip was so rare that the wait became impossibly long.

The model also held the cost of inbreeding fixed, so it describes the short term, before prolonged self-fertilization purges enough mutations to change the odds.

Mixed populations exist in the wild. Long-term studies that track one population’s proportions over time are lacking, the authors wrote, and those are what would test the prediction.

The model also predicts that mixed populations carry fewer and shorter-lived mating types than purely self-rejecting ones, and more inbreeding written into their genomes. Both could be checked in plant genomes.

Asked which population she would most like to watch, Friedlander pointed to wild tomato species growing in South America.

Sources indicate that she also noted the model doesn’t apply directly to orchards, where trees are genetically identical and do not evolve. Self-rejecting crops do depend on pollinators, she added, and a decline in them could cut yields.

A warming climate and fewer pollinating insects both change the pressures on how a plant reproduces, the authors wrote.

Whether real populations respond by picking a side, or by swinging between the two for generations, is what a long field study of those wild tomatoes could begin to answer.

The full study was published in the journal PRX Life.

#19377. Industry News: Mangrove forests are using washed up ocean weeds to build their soil and fight rising sea levels

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1288 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Mangrove forests are using washed up ocean weeds to build their soil and fight rising sea levels

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coastal mangrove forests are critical for protecting shorelines from severe storms and trapping CO2.
  • Mangrove forests grow right at the edge of the sea, so rising water can drown them.
  • Before sunrise on his monthly survey days, from May 2022 to May 2024, Florida International University (FIU) doctoral student Kevin Montenegro loaded a 16-foot (4.9-meter) canoe onto a truck and set off to paddle for an hour to the Biscayne Bay mangroves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coastal mangrove forests are critical for protecting shorelines from severe storms and trapping CO2. Unfortunately, they are at the moment losing the race against rising sea levels.

Mangrove forests grow right at the edge of the sea, so rising water can drown them. To survive, the ground under the trees has to build up as fast as the ocean rises. A new study finds that dead seagrass helps it do that.

Before sunrise on his monthly survey days, from May 2022 to May 2024, Florida International University (FIU) doctoral student Kevin Montenegro loaded a 16-foot (4.9-meter) canoe onto a truck and set off to paddle for an hour to the Biscayne Bay mangroves.

He then waded in to see what the tide had left. Much of it was dead seagrass and macroalgae, the debris that scientists call marine wrack.

When seagrass washes into a mangrove forest, it adds material to the forest floor and traps carbon that would otherwise warm the climate.

Sources indicate that an isotope model estimated that seagrass supplied between 36 and 53 percent of the soil carbon near the surface at his two sites, according to FIU. It has not closed the gap, because the sea there is rising at least twice as fast as the ground.

It has been revealed that montenegro and a field partner worked at two sites in Biscayne National Park, on the Atlantic coast of Florida. The paper calls them BISC-1 and BISC-2. They lie about 5 miles (8 kilometers) apart, in a narrow band of forest along the shore.

BISC-1, the southern site, sits just south of the mouth of the Homestead Military Canal and east of the L-31E levee, built in 1966.

BISC-2 sits near the mouth of the Black Creek Canal, in the Cutler Wetlands, where roads and urban development run beside the shore.

Levees and roads stop these mangroves from moving inland, and little river sediment reaches them.

The National Park Service set up both monitoring stations with a surface elevation table, an instrument that records small changes in ground height from a fixed benchmark.

The readings run from February 2011 at BISC-1 and January 2012 at BISC-2 through September 2024. BISC-1 has 25 rounds of measurements and BISC-2 has 23.

Sea level in the bay is rising about 8.5 millimeters (0.33 inch) a year, based on data from the NOAA tide gauge at Virginia Key. The ground at BISC-1 rose about 2.1 millimeters (0.08 inch) a year, and the ground at BISC-2 rose about 3.9 millimeters (0.15 inch).

Industry observers note that that left BISC-1 about 6.4 millimeters (0.25 inch) short each year. Below the surface, the land at BISC-1 sank 0.7 millimeters a year and the land at BISC-2 sank 0.4.

Hurricane Irma hit the area in 2017. Elevation at both sites had climbed sharply until 2014, declined from 2014 to 2019, and has risen steadily since 2018, possibly from newly introduced plant growth and sediment moved by the storm, the authors wrote.

Recent findings suggest that yearly gains are 1.1 millimeters higher at BISC-1 and 2.2 higher at BISC-2 than in the last regional synthesis. Other research has warned that Florida’s mangroves may end up underwater as seas climb.

Recent findings suggest that montenegro made 23 monthly wrack surveys between May 2022 and May 2024. He and his partner marked three lines at each site, each one 66 feet (20 meters) long, and stopped at the shoreline, at 33 feet and at 66 feet.

At every stop they laid down a frame of about 11 square feet (1 square meter), wrote down how much seagrass, macroalgae, plastic, wood and mangrove litter lay inside it, and measured the pile with a meter stick. Then they photographed it.

It has been revealed that researchers usually study wrack on beaches, FIU noted, since they can walk up to it or see it from satellites. Neither works well under a mangrove canopy.

For the decomposition test, the team filled nylon bags with about 5 grams of red mangrove leaves or the seagrass Thalassia testudinum.

They left the bags on the soil and collected them after six and 12 months, then repeated the experiment for a second year.

The surveys also caught a regional event. Sargassum, a brown macroalga, reached its highest level on the plots in March 2023, the same month the University of South Florida‘s satellite system reported a peak across the region.

It has been revealed that south Florida’s mangroves are generally thought to build soil from their own leaves, wood and roots, according to FIU. The team pulled soil cores 4 inches (10 centimeters) deep during four sampling rounds and removed the roots where possible.

They then measured stable isotopes, forms of carbon and nitrogen that differ between plant sources, and ran a statistical model that compared the soil with red mangrove and seagrass tissue.

In the top 0.8 inch (2 centimeters), the seagrass share ranged from 36.1 percent at the innermost point of BISC-1 to 53 percent at the same point of BISC-2.

Recent findings suggest that BISC-2, in the Cutler Wetlands, received more than 3.4 times as much wrack as BISC-1 at 66 feet inland, and its ground rose fastest. The seagrass share fell lower down the cores, likely because roots add more material at depth.

Where more wrack piled up, seagrass in the bags broke down more slowly at both sites, and mangrove leaves did the same at BISC-2.

Past measurements at the stations recorded single wrack deposits adding between 0.07 and 1.8 inches (1.78 and 46.38 millimeters) to the surface.

Montenegro knew both habitats before the project began. As an FIU undergraduate he worked in a seagrass lab that studied water quality damage, and he later measured mangrove elevation with the National Park Service.

According to recent reports, “We know seagrass ecosystems are very sensitive to water quality,” he said in the FIU release. Losing those meadows, he added, would mean “losing a huge contributor to mangrove resilience.”.

Industry observers note that the bay is one where climate stress has already changed the water. Mangroves worldwide also face a triple threat to their survival, and rising seas may push some forests to release stored carbon.

The authors wrote that management and restoration efforts should consider strategies that protect the route that carries wrack from seagrass beds into the forests. Montenegro called mangroves and seagrass “puzzle pieces that make our community whole.”.

The study covers two sites in one national park, and the elevation rates carry wide error margins, plus or minus 2.6 millimeters a year at BISC-1 and 3.2 at BISC-2.

Seasonal wrack volume tracked surface elevation change at both sites, but it indicated no clear relationship with the soil accumulation measured above marker layers.

The authors wrote that wrack volume alone was not driving those patterns, and proposed slower decay and added peat as the route.

Their model also used only two sources, red mangrove and Thalassia testudinum, so it did not separate the macroalgae found on the plots.

Water depth has climbed sharply at both sites since 2019, and the authors warned that longer flooding could eventually starve roots of oxygen.

The National Park Service funded the work under agreement P21AC11346-00, and two of the four authors, Kevin Whelan and Michelle Prats, work for its South Florida and Caribbean monitoring network.

Sources indicate that montenegro finished his Ph.D. earlier this year and now works in the Department of Environmental Resources Management for Miami-Dade County, on the same coast where he once loaded a canoe before sunrise.

The full study was published in the journal Estuaries and Coasts.

Mountain lions and other animals are set to get their own massive land bridge that crosses over 10 lanes of the 101 Freeway near Los Angeles

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • California's newly introduced wildlife crossing over the 101 Freeway is set to open in December 2026, reconnecting habitats for mountain lions and other animals.
  • The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing is scheduled to officially open to wildlife on December 2, 2026.
  • According to recent reports, it will reconnect wildlife habitat in the Santa Monica Mountains with the Simi Hills to the north.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

California's newly introduced wildlife crossing over the 101 Freeway is set to open in December 2026, reconnecting habitats for mountain lions and other animals.

The Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing is scheduled to officially open to wildlife on December 2, 2026. The planted bridge for animals spans the 101 Freeway in Agoura Hills, California.

According to recent reports, it will reconnect wildlife habitat in the Santa Monica Mountains with the Simi Hills to the north. The freeway below carries more than 300,000 vehicles a day.

The late P-22, a mountain lion that lived in Los Angeles, helped inspire the project.

According to Caltrans, the state agency managing the project, the bridge over the freeway is about 210 feet (64 meters) long and roughly 174 feet (53 meters) wide.

It spans ten lanes of pavement: eight lanes of traffic and two breakdown lanes. A second structure carries the crossing over Agoura Road, a local road.

The crossing broke ground on Earth Day, April 22, 2022. The first stage, over the freeway, was completed in June 2025.

Caltrans costs for all stages are now estimated at $114 million, pending a final contractor estimate for parts of stage two. Public funds cover $77.7 million, or 68 percent, and private donations $37.2 million, or 32 percent.

Costs outside that budget, including the native plant nursery and wildlife research, are covered by additional private donations, according to the project’s official FAQ.

In a recent development, the top of the structure will be covered in nearly 1 acre (0.4 hectares) of native vegetation. The project will also restore more than 10 additional acres (4 hectares) of nearby habitat as coastal sage scrub and oak savannah.

In a recent development, the first stage of construction called for about 5,000 plants, the National Wildlife Federation mentioned in 2023. Key species include coast live oak, toyon, ceanothus, sages, buckwheat and penstemon.

According to recent reports, the plants are grown from seeds collected within 5 miles (8 kilometers) of the site. More than one million native seeds had been gathered by mid-2023.

According to recent reports, unlike most wildlife crossings, this one must deal with heavy traffic noise and light. The design tackles both with a large vegetated barrier and other design features.

Exclusionary fencing and vegetation cues are meant to steer animals toward the bridge. The site is already a natural funnel between open space to the north and south.

According to recent reports, the National Park Service has studied mountain lions in and around the Santa Monica Mountains since 2002. It calls the 101 Freeway “the biggest barrier between the Santa Monica Mountains and other large natural areas.”.

Biologists have documented at least 32 mountain lions killed by vehicles in the study area, part of a wider toll of roadkill on highways.

The isolated lions have the lowest genetic diversity ever documented in the West. The only population with lower levels was in south Florida in the mid-1990s.

In a 2022 study led by UCLA, sperm samples from five male lions that had died were on average 93 percent abnormal. The team also identified nine adult males from the Santa Monica and Santa Ana mountains with physical signs of inbreeding.

A 2016 modeling study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B put the local population’s chance of extinction within 50 years at 15 percent. When inbreeding depression was included, that probability rose to 99.7 percent.

In the simulations, at least one new lion arriving per generation was enough to largely maintain genetic diversity.

Park biologists first captured and radio-collared P-22 in March 2012, when he was estimated to be two years old.

In a recent development, to reach Griffith Park, he had crossed both the 101 and the 405, two of the busiest freeways in the world. He then spent more than ten years there, in the smallest home range ever recorded for an adult male mountain lion.

In a recent development, after scientists noticed a change in his behavior, he was captured on December 12, 2022. He was euthanized under general anesthesia five days later.

“P-22 was a fascinating animal to study,” Jeff Sikich, lead field biologist for the park service’s mountain lion study, noted in 2023.

On October 28, scientists captured the first photo of an animal on the unfinished crossing, a coyote climbing its southern slope.

Bobcats, coyotes, gray foxes, mule deer and mountain lions already regularly use a trail next to the site.

Recent findings suggest that biologists from Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area planned to install remote wildlife cameras in early November. Their monitoring framework includes 14 objectives, from documenting use by mountain lions and mule deer to tracking genetic diversity, vegetation, light and sound.

“This is more than just about whether animals use the crossing,” remarked Seth Riley, wildlife branch lead at Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. “We want to understand how effective it is in reconnecting an ecosystem that has been divided by the freeway for decades.”.

“That is a much bigger scientific question and answering it will take years,” Riley added.

Images of animals using the crossing will be made public, but not in real time, for security reasons.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service.
