#19373. Daily smokers are growing more negative about vaping

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1189 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Daily smokers are growing more negative about vaping

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Daily smokers report more negative views of vaping and less disapproval of smoking, a shift researchers say could complicate efforts to help them quit.
  • Smoking bans and health campaigns helped make smoking less socially acceptable.
  • Daily smokers in four countries were surveyed between 2016 and 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Daily smokers report more negative views of vaping and less disapproval of smoking, a shift researchers say could complicate efforts to help them quit.

Smoking bans and health campaigns helped make smoking less socially acceptable. But adults who smoke daily now report less disapproval of the habit from people around them.

Daily smokers in four countries were surveyed between 2016 and 2022. Over those years, smokers reported less disapproval of smoking and more disapproval of vaping.

The researchers called the pattern concerning because smoking is the more harmful habit.

In a recent development, the analysis was led by Giang Vu at the University of Queensland. She is a researcher at its National Centre for Youth Substance Use Research.

Her focus was on social norms. These are a person’s sense of what the people around them do and approve of.

“Social norms are linked to whether people quit smoking or take up vaping, so these shifts matter for public health,” Vu remarked.

It has been revealed that only attitudes were examined in this analysis. Quitting and switching to vaping were not tracked.

The answers came from the International Tobacco Control Four Country Smoking and Vaping Survey.

Sources indicate that it was carried out in 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022. Canada, the United States, England, and Australia took part.

Answers from 19,915 adults who smoked daily were analyzed by Vu’s team. Most of them took part in only one of the four survey rounds.

Participants were asked four questions about smoking and the same four about vaping. How many of their five closest friends smoke? What do the people important to them think about their smoking?

The other two questions covered the general public’s attitude and the smoker’s own overall opinion.

In 2016, 63.5% of daily smokers said the people vital to them disapproved of their smoking. That share had dropped to 54.3% by 2022.

Less disapproval was also sensed from the wider public. In 2016, 83.3% believed the public disapproved of smoking. Six years later, 72.5% did.

In a recent development, smokers’ own views shifted too. A negative opinion of smoking was held by 52.1% in 2016 and by 43% in 2022.

In a recent development, this decline did not start with the new surveys. An earlier analysis of the same survey program covered 2002 to 2015. It found that disapproval of smoking among daily smokers generally weakened in that period.

Taken together, the two studies point to a long-term shift, Vu’s team noted.

One measure indicated no statistically significant change.

In 2016, 19% of smokers said more than half of their five closest friends smoked. The share was 17.6% in 2022.

For vaping, the answers changed in the opposite direction.

It has been revealed that in 2016, 31.3% of daily smokers mentioned the people crucial to them disapproved of vaping. By 2022, the share had grown to 41.4%.

In a recent development, smokers also sensed growing disapproval of vaping among the wider public. The share who believed the public disapproved of vaping rose from 41.2% to 48.3%. Both shares were highest in 2020 and somewhat lower in 2022.

Smokers’ own opinions of vaping turned more negative as well. In 2016, 32.8% held a negative opinion of vaping. By 2022, 49.1% did, compared to 43% with a negative opinion of smoking.

According to recent reports, even so, vaping had not overtaken smoking on the other two questions. Smokers sensed more disapproval of smoking than of vaping from the public and from people important to them.

It has been revealed that vaping also became slightly more common among smokers’ friends. The share who said more than half of their five closest friends vape went from 1.6% to 2.8%.

Vaping is regulated very differently in the four countries. In England, nicotine vapes are sold in shops. They are also promoted through the national healthcare system as a way to stop smoking. Australia formalized a prescription-only system in October 2021.

Sources indicate that levels of disapproval differed by country. Smokers in England sensed the least disapproval of both products. Smokers in Canada sensed the most disapproval of smoking.

Industry observers note that but the direction of change was largely shared. On seven of the eight measures, no evidence was found that trends differed by country.

The exception was negative opinion of vaping, which increased least in England.

“These trends were broadly similar regardless of smoking or vaping policies,” Vu said.

Her team suggested that international media coverage and major events may shape attitudes alongside national policy. One such event was a 2019 outbreak of lung injuries among people in the United States who vaped.

It has been revealed that the outbreak was later linked mainly to an additive in illegal cannabis vapes. According to the team, it was wrongly blamed on nicotine vaping.

Concerns about lung health during the COVID-19 pandemic may have added to the disapproval, they wrote.

Vaping is not risk-free. But current evidence indicates that it poses substantially lower health risks than smoking, the team wrote. There is also evidence that vapes help people quit.

“A growing disapproval of vaping may discourage people who smoke from switching to a less harmful alternative,” Vu remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the team is also worried by weaker disapproval of smoking. People who smoke daily would benefit most from quitting. Earlier research has linked disapproval of smoking to quit attempts.

In a recent development, efforts to make smoking socially unacceptable may be losing their effect on this group, the team wrote. Approaches that build smokers’ confidence and address the barriers to quitting may be needed.

Vu called for public health messages that convey the risks of both products accurately.

“This would allow people who smoke to make informed choices, while continuing to protect young people who have never smoked,” she mentioned.

The study can’t show that these attitudes changed what smokers did.

Every participant smoked daily, so the results do not represent the general public. The team also cautioned against applying them to young people.

Attitudes toward smoking and vaping have followed different patterns in that group.

Industry observers note that the group of daily smokers may itself have changed over time. Smokers open to alternatives may have already switched to vaping or quit. That would leave a group with firmer opinions against vaping.

The vaping questions asked about approval and opinion. People were not asked how harmful they thought vaping was. Rising disapproval may therefore partly reflect its social image.

Industry observers note that public attention in those years centered on a rapid rise in youth vaping, the team noted. Vaping may have come to look less like a quitting aid for adults and more like a youth problem.

The answers were self-reported. The study also can’t show that any country’s policies shaped its smokers’ attitudes.

Future studies could follow smokers over time. They could test whether a change in attitudes predicts a quit attempt or a switch to vaping.

The full study was published in the journal Nicotine & Tobacco Research.

Breaking: Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.
  • Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting firm in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Recent findings suggest that joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

According to recent reports, in the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

In a recent development, the largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a major hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”.

Sources indicate that the most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Tech giant. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”.

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, presently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data highlighted, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell indicates, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”.

These newly introduced findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”.

#19370. Tech Report: Eating a balanced diet that changes with your age is the real secret to a longer life

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1341 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Eating a balanced diet that changes with your age is the real secret to a longer life

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1341 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A review links longevity to food quality and nutrient balance for people at different stages of life; the proposed diets by age remain untested.
  • In laboratory animals, eating less reliably lengthens life, but people find such restricted diets hard to maintain.
  • Across large human studies, the balance of carbohydrates, protein, fat, and fiber in the diet was linked to the risk of death, regardless of how many calories people ate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review links longevity to food quality and nutrient balance for people at different stages of life; the proposed diets by age remain untested.

In laboratory animals, eating less reliably lengthens life, but people find such restricted diets hard to maintain. A recent review suggests that people may be able to live longer without eating less, by changing the mix of what they eat.

Across large human studies, the balance of carbohydrates, protein, fat, and fiber in the diet was linked to the risk of death, regardless of how many calories people ate. The review also proposes that the best balance is different at different ages.

Industry observers note that more people are reaching old age. Scientists project that the number of adults aged 80 and older will more than triple between 2017 and 2050, reaching 425 million.

Recent findings suggest that jintao Huang and Ziyun Wu of Shanghai Jiao Tong University wrote the review. Their co-author, Dejian Huang, is at the National University of Singapore.

Industry observers note that the three authors ran no newly introduced experiments. They drew on animal research and on more than thirty large studies involving humans; they pooled the analyses, some covering more than a million people.

Most of the human studies tracked people’s diets and deaths over many years. Such studies can link a diet to a lower risk of death, but they can’t show that the diet was the cause.

People who got about 50 to 55 percent of their daily calories from carbohydrates had the lowest risk of death. The risk was higher for people who got less than 40 percent of their calories from carbohydrates, and for those who got more than 70 percent.

Neither a very low-carb diet nor a very high-carb diet looked best in these studies.

Recent findings suggest that what people ate in place of carbohydrates also mattered. Research has consistently linked low-carb diets based on animal foods to a higher risk of death, while it has linked those based on plant foods to a lower risk.

According to recent reports, people who ate more fiber had a 10 to 23 percent lower risk of death than people who ate less. The link was stronger for fiber from whole grains and vegetables than for fiber from fruit alone.

In a recent development, for protein, the findings depended on a person’s age. In middle-aged adults, eating more protein – especially protein from animals – often correlated with a modestly higher risk of death.

In adults about 65 and older, eating a moderate or higher amount of protein appeared to be protective. Protein at that age counters muscle loss and frailty, the authors wrote.

One study followed 6,381 adults for about 18 years. The researchers linked high protein intake to a higher risk of death in midlife and a lower risk in older adults.

Plant protein was consistently linked to a lower risk. Statistical comparisons also showed an advantage for replacing animal protein, particularly processed red meat, with plant protein.

The authors attributed the midlife risk to growth-promoting signals in cells, which protein activates. In animal studies, reducing those signals has been tied to longer life.

Recent findings suggest that with fat, the authors wrote, the type mattered more than the amount. People who had diets higher in trans fat or in saturated fat, the kind in butter and lard, had a modestly higher risk of death.

The unsaturated fats in nuts, olive oil, and fatty fish were linked to a lower risk. People who obtained most of the fat in their diet from those sources, did not show a higher risk of death.

Plant-rich eating patterns such as the Mediterranean diet were linked to a roughly 10 to 25 percent lower risk of death.

The reverse was true of ultra-processed foods, industrial products made mostly from food extracts and additives. People who ate the most of those foods had a 15 to 30 percent higher risk of death than people who ate the least.

Ultra-processed foods now supply more than half of the calories eaten in many high-income countries. The authors recommended limiting them at every age.

Lifespan gains seen in animal experiments can’t be applied directly to people, the authors wrote.

One example involves methionine, a building block of protein. Rats and mice fed a diet low in methionine lived 30 to 45 percent longer than animals on a standard diet.

Industry observers note that the evidence in people is more limited. Trials of similar diets have typically lasted 2 to 16 weeks.

According to recent reports, in those trials, levels of a growth signal in the blood called IGF-1 fell by 7 to 14 percent. A DNA-based estimate of how old the body is biologically didn’t measurably change.

Sources indicate that the authors found a pattern across such comparisons. The longer a mammal normally lives, the smaller the gain in lifespan tended to be.

In a recent development, A second example is the ketogenic diet, which is very low in carbohydrates and high in fat. A long-term ketogenic diet lengthened the lives of mice.

Human studies, though, have linked very-low-carb diets to either no difference in the risk of death or a modestly higher risk, particularly when the diets emphasized animal foods.

The authors concluded that the ketogenic diet seems best suited to short-term use under medical supervision, and less suited to years of use for a longer life.

Existing guidelines, including the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, mainly aim to prevent chronic disease, the authors wrote, and weren’t designed with a long life as the central goal.

The authors proposed daily ranges for protein, carbohydrates, fat, and fiber at each stage of life. For adults aged 36 to 64, protein is set at 10 to 15 percent of daily calories, with more of it from plants.

Later in life, muscle loss and frailty become the main concerns. From age 65, the proposal raises protein to between 15 and 20 percent of daily calories, mainly from fish and plant foods.

In a recent development, for fiber, the midlife range is 40 to 60 grams a day, which is higher than the 25 to 30 grams in current dietary guidelines. The authors wrote that the higher range comes from animal experiments and isn’t established guidance.

Sources indicate that the authors also graded their own evidence. They rated it as high for adults under 65 and as moderate for older adults. For older adults, the evidence rests mainly on measures such as muscle loss and frailty and on general dietary guidance.

A food pyramid, in the review, has water, sleep, and regular exercise at its base, beneath any food.

Industry observers note that the authors named several gaps in the evidence behind their proposal. Three groups remain understudied: adults 75 and older, people of non-European ancestry, and people in low- and middle-income countries.

Recent findings suggest that males and females may also need different advice. In mice, a lifelong high-fat diet shortened the lives of males by about 144 days on average and didn’t significantly change the lifespan of females.

Diets may one day be personalized, the authors wrote, using data such as blood sugar readings from wearable sensors.

In one study they cited, blood sugar and blood fat responses to identical meals varied up to tenfold from person to person.

It has been revealed that the next question is whether such personalized advice works better than standard advice. Does it keep people healthy for longer?

The authors wrote that future trials should last at least three to five years, long enough to capture changes in estimates of biological age.

Until those trials are done, personalized diet advice can’t be given “with the same confidence as recommendations for tobacco avoidance or physical activity,” the authors wrote.

As for the age-based ranges, the authors described them as testable hypotheses.

The full study was published in the journal The Innovation Nutrition.

#19368. Do fitness trackers help people exercise more? The answer is complicated

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1399 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Do fitness trackers help people exercise more? The answer is complicated

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fitness tracker users were more likely to meet exercise guidelines, but a newly introduced study cannot show whether the devices made them more active.
  • Step trackers, health apps, and patient portals offer different ways to monitor and manage health.
  • survey found that these tools were not equally associated with getting enough exercise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fitness tracker users were more likely to meet exercise guidelines, but a newly introduced study cannot show whether the devices made them more active.

Step trackers, health apps, and patient portals offer different ways to monitor and manage health.

An analysis of a national U.S. survey found that these tools were not equally associated with getting enough exercise.

In the analysis reported by Heejun Kim and colleagues, adults were sorted into groups based on the tools they used.

Among adults in the wearable-centered group, 31.4% met both federal exercise guidelines.

According to recent reports, among adults who used few tools, 18.2% met both guidelines, compared with 19.9% of those centered on a patient portal. No clear difference could be found between these last two groups.

A patient portal is a secure website where patients can view test results and exchange messages with their health care providers.

The results suggest that the mix of tools may reveal more about exercise habits than any single device.

Kim, who led the study, is a doctoral student in sport analytics at the University of Mississippi. Kim worked with Ju-Pil Choe, also a doctoral student, and Professor Minsoo Kang of the Department of Kinesiology and Sport.

Because participants answered the survey only once, the findings show associations and cannot establish whether these tools make people more active.

It has been revealed that choe described two people as an example. The first person has a smartwatch and checks the step count on it each day.

The second person opens a patient portal for lab results or a message to a doctor. That person has never owned a fitness tracker.

“Both are using digital health tools, but in very different ways,” Choe remarked.

Data came from the 2024 Health Information National Trends Survey, a nationally representative survey of U.S. adults run by the National Cancer Institute.

Wearable users had been compared with non-users in studies of the 2019 and 2022 rounds.

Among the users, the odds of meeting activity recommendations were found to be higher in both. Those studies could not show which other digital tools the same people used.

Kim’s team instead took 17 questions from the survey, each of which could be answered yes or no. All of them referred to the 12 months before the survey.

The questions covered wearables, health apps, patient portals, telehealth visits, online health searches and health-related social media posts.

According to recent reports, there were 5,804 adults who had answered every one of these questions. Based on their response patterns, the team sorted them into four groups.

The largest of the four groups, which made up 34.3% of the adults, was the one centered on patient portals. Its members messaged providers and viewed test results online, but very few of them used a wearable.

The broad group, representing 32% of adults, used almost every tool covered by the survey.

A third group of 11.8% relied on wearables and apps, whereas portals were used much less.

The remaining 21.9% of adults were placed in a limited group, in which few digital health tools were used. Most of its members did, however, use social media and look up health information online.

Recent findings suggest that two targets are set for adults by the federal Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans. The first is at least 150 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity.

The second is muscle-strengthening activity, which is to be done on two or more days of the week.

Of the 4,930 adults with complete answers, 25.1% met both exercise guidelines. However, the rates varied between groups.

In the broad group, 32.7% met both exercise guidelines, compared with 31.4% in the wearable group. The rates were lower in the portal group (19.9%) and limited group (18.2%).

These differences remained after researchers accounted for age, sex, income, education, race, ethnicity, body mass index, smoking and other factors.

Compared with the limited group, the broad group had 2.8 times the odds of meeting both guidelines, while the wearable group had 2.1 times the odds.

The difference between the portal and limited groups was too small to rule out chance.

Recent findings suggest that for strength training, the picture was not the same as for aerobic activity. Higher odds of meeting the strength guideline were seen in all three other groups, including the portal-centered group.

Those odds were about 2.6 times (broad), 1.6 times (wearable-centered) and 1.6 times (portal-centered) the odds of the limited group.

The share of adults who met this guideline was 32.5% in the limited group and 49.5% in the broad group.

For the aerobic guideline, it was only the broad group that clearly differed from the limited group.

The lowest aerobic rate of the four groups was reported by the portal-centered adults, at 34.5%. In the limited group the rate was 40.2%, but this gap too was small enough to be due to chance.

A possible reason for the difference was offered by the authors. Strength training may be a more deliberate and planned kind of exercise than aerobic activity is.

As such, it could fit the broader habits of health management which portal use reflects.

According to recent reports, the authors wrote that aerobic minutes can be accumulated through both structured workouts and everyday movement. For this reason, aerobic activity may be tied less closely to any one set of digital habits.

It has been revealed that kang said that a person who has more digital health tools is not necessarily a more active person. What counts for more, in Kang’s view, is the way in which people use the tools from day to day.

Recent findings suggest that in the limited group, 12.9% of adults had not finished high school. A household income of less than $20,000 a year was reported by 25.7% of the group.

Among the other three groups, the share that had not finished high school stayed between 1.1% and 4.2%. The share living in households below that income stayed between 8.6% and 11.7%.

According to recent reports, the limited group was also set apart by age. Of its members, 10.2% were people aged 75 or older, and in no other group was this share so large.

Industry observers note that the broad group had the most college graduates, at 47.3%. The broad group also had the most adults in households which earned $100,000 or more, at 49.8%.

Recent findings suggest that more digital tools were not simply a mark of better health, however. Of the four groups, the broad one had the highest average body mass index (29.5).

It has been revealed that choe stated that people may be missed when exercise programs are built mainly around apps and wearables. These, Choe said, are people who would benefit from extra support.

The survey cannot prove that trackers increase exercise. Active people may be more likely to buy them. Digital skills or health care access may also play a role.

An earlier review found that trackers can help when used in behavior-change programs, which this study did not test.

In a recent development, people reported their own exercise and may have overstated it. The survey also missed vigorous activity, possibly counting some active adults as falling short.

Of 7,278 respondents, 2,348 (32.3%) were excluded due to missing answers.

Industry observers note that among those excluded from the digital-use grouping analysis, 52.7% were 65 or older, compared with 17.7% of those kept. Those excluded also had less education and lower incomes.

Industry observers note that A second analysis included people with missing answers. The same four groups appeared, with 97.7% staying in their original group.

In this analysis, the portal group had 1.5 times the odds of meeting both guidelines compared with the limited group. The wearable group also had higher odds of meeting the aerobic guideline.

The authors suggested different ways to help each group exercise more.

Tracker users could get feedback and goals, while portal users could receive reminders through messages or appointments.

People who use few digital tools might need more in-person or community support.

It has been revealed that the study did not test these ideas. More research is needed to see whether this support helps people exercise more.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Physiology.

#19366. Fossils found in Thailand reveal a giant rodent that weighed about 66 pounds

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1228 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Fossils found in Thailand reveal a giant rodent that weighed about 66 pounds

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1228 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two fossil teeth from Thailand reveal an ancient rodent estimated to weigh 66 pounds, offering new evidence of how early rodents grew large.
  • Most rodents are small or medium-sized, but fossils reveal that some ancient species grew much larger.
  • Scientists found a fossil tooth in a coal mine in southern Thailand that belonged to an unusually large rodent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two fossil teeth from Thailand reveal an ancient rodent estimated to weigh 66 pounds, offering new evidence of how early rodents grew large.

Most rodents are small or medium-sized, but fossils reveal that some ancient species grew much larger.

Scientists found a fossil tooth in a coal mine in southern Thailand that belonged to an unusually large rodent.

The researchers believe it weighed about 30 kilograms (66 pounds). They named it Yakamys sirindhornae.

Sixty-six pounds is about what a large North American beaver weighs. Yakamys lived about 34 million years ago. The giant rodents of South America are the largest ever found but they came long after it.

The find suggests that rodents grew large earlier than fossils had shown. It also suggests they did so in more parts of the world. For now, the evidence is two teeth.

It has been revealed that both teeth were found in a layer of clay inside the main coal seam of a mine in Krabi Province. They were collected by a Thai-French fossil expedition.

The project was designed by Yaowalak Chaimanee of the University of Poitiers in France.

It has been revealed that the co-authors work in France and Canada and at Thailand’s Department of Mineral Resources. The fossils are now held by that department.

Recent findings suggest that one tooth is a lower molar, which is a grinding tooth from the back of the jaw. The other is a broken piece of a lower incisor. Incisors are the long front teeth a rodent gnaws with.

The clay is roughly 35.1 million to 33.7 million years old. That age is based on other mammals found at the site and on magnetism preserved in the rock.

In the name Yakamys, the word yak is Thai for giant and mys is Greek for mouse or rat.

The species name honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn for her long support of science and fossil research in Thailand.

According to recent reports, the molar is 0.46 inch (11.56 millimeters) long and almost as wide. That sounds small. It isn’t small next to the teeth of its relatives.

Sources indicate that yakamys belongs to Ischyromyidae, one of the earliest major families of rodents. Its molar is the largest yet described among early members of that family.

Until now, an animal called Hulgana was regarded as the largest Asian member of the family. Its molars are less than half as long and less than half as wide.

The closest in size is Manitsha tanka. This rodent was described from South Dakota in 1941. Its lower second molar measures about 0.32 by 0.35 inch (8.2 by 8.9 millimeters).

In a recent development, the incisor was cut lengthwise by the team to place Yakamys in that family. Its enamel was then examined under an electron microscope.

The banding inside the enamel is consistent with the pattern reported for other members of the family.

No bones of Yakamys have been found and so its weight had to be estimated from tooth measurements.

Bigger teeth go with heavier bodies in living rodents and this relationship has been turned into equations.

Industry observers note that virginie Millien is a biologist at McGill University in Canada. She applied seven published equations to the two teeth. The answers ranged from 47 to 104 pounds (21.4 to 47.3 kilograms).

The seven answers averaged 70 pounds (31.6 kilograms) and the middle value was 63 pounds (28.6 kilograms).

The team took the midpoint of those two figures and rounded it to 30 kilograms, or 66 pounds.

It has been revealed that the weight reported by the team is therefore a rounded summary of answers that disagree. Millien called it “only a ballpark figure.”.

It has been revealed that estimates of this kind are uncertain because the link between tooth size and body weight varies among living rodents. The estimates span roughly 24 to 152 pounds (10.8 to 69 kilograms) when each margin of error is included.

It has been revealed that the weights of giant rodents have been revised sharply before. One South American giant was first estimated at more than 2,200 pounds (1,000 kilograms).

Later studies that included one by Millien in 2008 estimated about 770 pounds (350 kilograms).

Sources indicate that rodents include more species than any other group of living mammals. Their oldest fossils come from North America. Very large body size has evolved in only a few branches of the group.

It has been revealed that the best-known giants lived in South America long after Yakamys. Large species were rarely documented among early rodents and Manitsha was one of the few examples.

Industry observers note that the fossil record of the family in Asia was sparse. Most of it came from small animals in China and India.

Sources indicate that yakamys extends the known range of the family into Southeast Asia. It is also evidence that one early rodent line had already grown large by about 34 million years ago.

It has been revealed that yakamys and Manitsha are similar in estimated weight but their molars are built differently. To the authors, that suggests large size in this family wasn’t tied to one tooth design.

Giant rodents are commonly linked to life on islands. That explanation is hard to apply to Yakamys.

The authors wrote that the ancient geography of the Krabi area doesn’t point to an island. Neither do the other mammals found there.

Recent findings suggest that the clay that held the teeth formed in a lake. Many other fossil mammals have been found in the coal around it.

One possibility was raised by the team. Yakamys may have lived along lake edges much as capybaras live near water today. Food there may have been plentiful.

But lake clay alone doesn’t show that an animal spent time in the water.

Industry observers note that more complete fossils that include skull and skeleton bones would be needed to test the idea. More evidence from the rocks and the other animals at the site would be needed too.

Recent findings suggest that two teeth aren’t enough to establish exactly where Yakamys belongs within its family. The researchers could not run a formal analysis to identify its closest relatives.

Even the pairing of the teeth is tentative. The molar and the incisor were found close together in the same layer. The team assigned both to one species because both are unusually large.

A 3D model of the molar is available through MorphoMuseuM, an open online collection of 3D specimens. Other researchers can examine the tooth there.

Yakamys may not have been the first large rodent in the region.

According to recent reports, an unpublished rodent incisor from older rocks in Myanmar is held by the same team. It is considerably larger than the incisors of other rodents described from the region.

In a recent development, the Myanmar incisor hasn’t been formally described or identified. Its size alone can’t show what kind of rodent it came from.

Sources indicate that one question remains open. Was large body size a local event or a more widespread part of early rodent evolution?

More fossils from Myanmar and elsewhere in the region will be needed to answer it.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

You Were More Conscious as a Child Than You Are Now, Neuroscientist Claims

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

It has been revealed that when you were a child, did you ever wonder what happened to the sea at the horizon? Perhaps you imagined it stretching forever. Or perhaps, like me, you believed that where the blue ended, the water simply fell off the edge of the world, spilling over in some enormous, invisible waterfall. It made perfect sense at the time, and there was quite a lot of magic involved, too. Then came geography lessons, maps, explanations, terminology, and the gradual realization that the world did not end where your vision did—that it was, in fact, far vaster than anything the eye could take in. So why has it become so difficult to recapture the purity and intensity of that experience as an adult?

Could there be a chance, however counterintuitive it sounds, that you were actually more conscious back then?

It sounds counterintuitive, but Alysson Muotri, PhD, a professor of pediatrics and cellular and molecular medicine at the University of California, San Diego, has given this poetic—almost philosophical—idea scientific legs. To do so, he used one of the most futuristic tools that right now exists for investigating the human brain: brain organoids, tiny clusters of living neural tissue grown from stem cells in a laboratory. He wondered whether these tiny lumps of living human brain tissue could illuminate that elusive inner experience. What he found was that as we grow and learn about the world, this process might really be changing how we perceive reality.

But before you can explore consciousness in a lab, you need to build the organoids. The process begins with ordinary human cells, often collected from the skin. Scientists reprogram them into induced pluripotent stem cells, which regain the ability to develop into almost any cell type in the body. Researchers use chemical signals to turn these cells into neurons and other brain cells. The cells multiply, gathering into tiny clumps of tissue. Inside them, neurons begin making contact, and electrical signals pass between them. However, calling these organoids “brains in a dish” is rather generous, though tempting; they lack much of the anatomy of a developed human brain. Still, organoids allow scientists to watch human neural tissue take shape in ways that would be impossible to witness inside a living person’s skull.

Muotri’s team discovered in 2019 that maturing organoids produced electrical rhythms resembling certain features of brain activity recorded in premature infants. Here was human neural tissue, deprived of the sights and sounds accompanying a child’s development, nevertheless organizing itself into patterns observed in living brains. Four years later, researchers at Indiana University Bloomington incorporated brain organoids into an experimental computing system that used their electrical responses to help recognize spoken sounds and predict mathematical patterns. By 2025, other scientists had reported that repeated electrical stimulation could alter how individual neurons in organoids responded, with some changes lingering for hours after the stimulation came to a halt—evidence of cellular mechanisms associated with learning and memory.

In a recent development, muotri, meanwhile, had begun wondering whether the electrical activity of his brain organoids could offer any clues to that elusive inner experience we call consciousness. Of course, even if we assume that consciousness arises entirely from the brain, there is something peculiar about trying to measure it. It’s not as though you can insert a thermometer into someone’s head and pinpoint the experience of being alive and aware—or the feeling of experiencing the world as a child.

According to recent reports, muotri decided to investigate by borrowing an approach from consciousness research called the perturbational complexity index (PCI). In humans, the method involves delivering a brief magnetic pulse to the brain and recording the resulting electrical activity through electrodes placed on the scalp. Earlier researchers have analyzed the responses and calculated a score that has helped distinguish wakefulness from deep sleep and general anesthesia; a higher score indicates greater conscious awareness. While PCI cannot measure consciousness directly, it offers clues about the brain’s capacity to sustain it.

In preliminary findings, Muotri measured the organoids’ electrical activity before exposing them to repeated stimulation, using an approach similar to PCI. To say that he found a startling degree of complexity in the way their neurons communicate with one another—with scores that exceeded those typically recorded in awake human brains—is an understatement. Because the organoid and human measurements use different methods, however, the scores cannot be compared directly. Still, he wasn’t expecting the organoids to have this PCI level, he indicates. “It’s very new, and I’m still thinking about what it means.”.

Muotri also found something shocking about how the organoids behaved as they were stimulated repeatedly with light. Gradually, the cells began reacting differently to the stimulation, and some of those changes lingered after the light was switched off. “So there is some kind of a memory embedded in those networks,” he claims. But even more astounding was that, as the organoids adapted to the stimulation, their complexity score actually fell, similar to the way human brains with lower PCI scores were less aware.

He thinks the reason is that a brain organoid increases its bias as it learns, just as we become more biased as we learn more over the years. By bias, Muotri means that experience makes certain neural responses, particularly those reinforced through repeated exposure, more likely than others. Learning, apparently, does more than give us knowledge. It may also condition us to overlook parts of the world we once experienced more freely.

“It’s almost like when you are born…as soon as your brain is naive and fresh, you’re more conscious than when you are an adult,” Muotri continues. By adulthood, however, experience has cramped your brain’s style. “Because you already experienced so many things, you’re already [so] attached to the physical environment, that you become less conscious than you were [as] a baby.”.

The suggestion is extraordinary, especially coming from experiments involving tissue that has never seen a sunset, heard a lullaby, obeyed a teacher, or encountered anything resembling a childhood whatsoever.

Yet there is a recognizable human parallel. Developmental psychologist Alison Gopnik has compared adult attention to a spotlight, concentrated on what matters for an immediate goal, and children’s attention to a lantern, illuminating more of their surroundings. A toddler entering an unfamiliar room might become absorbed by a patch of sunlight that an adult barely notices. The adult knows more about the room, but familiarity helps determine what deserves attention. Noticing more of the world doesn’t necessarily mean being more conscious of it.

However, a baby’s brain, already shaped by months of development in the womb, is hardly comparable to an organoid that has never experienced the world outside a laboratory. That’s why Kenneth Kosik, MD, a neuroscience professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, is skeptical. In a 2024 paper published in the journal Patterns, titled Why Brain Organoids Are Not Conscious Yet, he argued that organoids lack much of the organization and communication between brain regions that may be necessary for consciousness. And electrical activity, however complicated, is not enough to prove an inner life. Neurons firing independently can produce unpredictable signals that are difficult to reduce to a simpler description, even when there is no evidence that anything is being experienced. “So we still have a little bit of a jump there, yeah, to say that compressibility is related to consciousness,” Kosik says.

In a recent development, muotri himself is cautious about what the numbers mean and says they are still preliminary data. Nor does he claim that his organoids actually experience anything. “I should not say they are conscious outright,” he says.

For now, Muotri’s experiments cannot definitively tell us whether we were more conscious as children than we are as adults, but they do open a window onto something just as intriguing: what happens to our experience of the world if learning itself changes how our brains encounter our environment? After all, the day I discovered that the sea did not plunge into an abyss, I gained precious knowledge that generations before me had strived to acquire. But have I ever again experienced the sea quite as fully as I did when I was a child, believing it could spill over the world’s edge? That is a whole different question, and we don’t have the answer yet.

According to recent reports, stav Dimitropoulos is a Gold and Community Anthem Award–winning journalist, and writes about consciousness, science, and culture for Popular Mechanics, Nature, and the BBC. Her work often explores mind-stretching angles where science meets philosophy. Her debut nonfiction book, Slow, Lazy, Gluttons (Greystone Books, 2026) asks: What if the traits society shames — laziness, darkness, nostalgia, and more — are actually survival superpowers?

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover.

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” states Martiniani, of Latest York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani states gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

Sources indicate that to design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”.

It has been revealed that roughly 11 percent of American adults are on a GLP-1 for weight loss, according to a 2026 Gallup survey; so chances are, you likely know someone who is using one for diabetes management, obesity treatment, or heart health—but the benefits might not stop there. Now, semaglutide, the popular GLP-1 medication found in Ozempic and Wegovy, is drawing serious attention from longevity experts.

A recent study published in Nature found that semaglutide administered to female mice late in life significantly extended their life span. The results pose a legitimate question: Could GLP-1 drugs lengthen human lives as well?

It has been revealed that to understand whether GLP-1s have anti-aging benefits, researchers put mice that were 20 months old—or roughly 60 human years—on a semaglutide regimen for the rest of their lives. There was also a control group of female mice the same age that received saline injections instead of the semaglutide. The team targeted older, non-obese, non-diabetic female mice to minimize the effects of male aggression and injury, consistent with previous long-term aging research, according to study author Danica Chen, PhD, professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at the University of California, Berkeley.The results? The median life span of the mice that received the GLP-1 drug increased from 742 days to 834 days, roughly a 12 percent extension. The researchers also saw reduced inflammation and preserved cognitive and muscle function in the GLP-1 group.

According to recent reports, but there’s a rub here: This study was done in mice, which are a far cry from human adults, meaning we don’t yet know the effects of GLP-1s on people—at least not yet. However, there has been research that suggests lower-calorie diets lead to longer life spans in humans. “The general cause of aging is accumulation of cellular damage,” Chen notes. She explains that calorie restriction can reduce cell damage and improve the function of tissues (a group of similar cells working together to perform a specific task), both of which contribute to a longer life span.

It has been revealed that michael Corley, PhD, associate professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, thinks the Nature study is “vital and exciting” because it looks beyond the established metabolic benefits of GLP-1 drugs and tests whether they can influence the biological aging process. (Biological age denotes how well the body is functioning on cellular and molecular levels, while chronological age refers to the number of years a person has been alive.).

Sources indicate that “The finding that semaglutide extended life span by approximately 12 percent in older female mice, while improving several measures of physical and cognitive function, adds important evidence to the emerging field of GLP-1 therapies as potential gerotherapeutics,” or treatments that target the root of aging, Corley notes. In fact, Corley was involved in a separate study, published earlier this year in Nature Communications, that found that 32 weeks of semaglutide treatment improved multiple epigenetic aging clocks, including measures of biological age and the pace of aging.

According to recent reports, findings presented at the 2026 Aging Research and Drug Discovery Meeting have also strengthened this emerging picture, Corley explains. Novo Nordisk, a Danish pharmaceutical organization with locations around the world, reported that semaglutide improved measures of biological aging across multiple organ systems, including the heart and kidneys.

Likewise, Eli Lilly, an American pharmaceutical manufacturer headquartered in Indiana, presented findings that tirzepatide—another GLP-1 medication, which is found in prescriptions like Mounjaro and Zepbound—positively influenced several epigenetic aging clocks, including organ-specific markers that measure the biological age of the heart, kidney, liver, and immune system.

“Together, these independent observations suggest that GLP-1-based therapies may affect biological aging through multiple molecular pathways,” Corley states. “The new mouse study is particularly interesting because it extends these molecular observations to actual life span, while also demonstrating improvements in several hallmarks of aging.”.

Industry observers note that so, could GLP-1 drugs actually extend the life span of humans? Corley thinks the more compelling opportunity isn’t necessarily extending life span, but extending health span—or the number of years people live in good health, free from chronic disease and disability.

“Human life span has biological constraints, and it is unlikely that GLP-1 drugs alone will dramatically extend the maximum limits of human longevity,” he says. “However, by reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease, metabolic dysfunction, and other age-related conditions, these medications could help more people remain healthy and independent for longer, potentially increasing average life span without fundamentally changing the upper limits of human longevity.”.

However, improvements in biological aging don’t necessarily translate into longer lives, Corley cautions.

Recent findings suggest that “The critical next step is determining whether these molecular changes predict meaningful improvements in physical function, cognition, and resilience,” Corley claims. “I think the greatest potential of GLP-1 therapies is not to push humans beyond the limits of longevity, but to help more people reach older ages while maintaining their health, function, and independence.”.

It has been revealed that to find out whether or not GLP-1 drugs can eventually be used as a legitimate longevity tactic in humans, Chen indicates clinical trials in humans are an vital next step. For now, GLP-1s remain a titan of diabetes and weight management—but their role in human longevity remains to be seen.

#19357. This magic mushroom can kill

This magic mushroom can kill

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.
  • Recent findings suggest that the fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

Recent findings suggest that the fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

It has been revealed that chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik states. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Industry observers note that related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other upcoming Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding highlights that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik notes. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can swiftly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Sources indicate that ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

According to recent reports, the two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

According to recent reports, and there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

#19356. Protecting forest birds may depend on what happens outside park boundaries

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1264 w)

Protecting forest birds may depend on what happens outside park boundaries

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forest birds in small national park sites may depend as much on surrounding forests as on habitat within park boundaries, a latest study suggests.
  • Sources indicate that drawing the boundaries of a national park on a map is easy.
  • Forest birds such as thrushes, warblers, and woodpeckers may build their nests inside national parks, but they often depend on the land outside those parks too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forest birds in small national park sites may depend as much on surrounding forests as on habitat within park boundaries, a latest study suggests.

Sources indicate that drawing the boundaries of a national park on a map is easy. Trees stay where they grow, but birds don’t follow those boundaries.

Forest birds such as thrushes, warblers, and woodpeckers may build their nests inside national parks, but they often depend on the land outside those parks too.

Researchers examined eight small national park sites in the northeastern United States, comparing forest characteristics inside each park with those in the surrounding county.

Bird presence inside the parks was associated with forest characteristics across the surrounding county at least as strongly as with those across the park itself.

Small parks are therefore unlikely to protect forest birds without help from the land around them.

The analysis was carried out by Bruna Amaral, who is a doctoral student at Michigan State University. Her collaborator Elise Zipkin is an ecologist who heads the university’s Ecology, Evolution, and Behavior program.

According to recent reports, sixteen species were included in the work. The researchers asked only whether each species was present at a given survey point.

Bird numbers and nesting success were not followed. The results therefore describe a pattern and cannot be used to prove a cause.

According to recent reports, surveys were conducted each May and June between 2006 and 2023. Volunteers with the National Park Service’s Northeast Temperate Network visited fixed points in the forest of every park.

At each point, an observer spent ten minutes recording every bird within 164 feet (50 meters).

Industry observers note that roughly 91% of the records came from birds identified by their sound. Only those sound records were used in the analysis.

All 16 species are classed as forest birds. The wood thrush, the ovenbird, the scarlet tanager, and several warblers are included among them.

It has been revealed that the parks were not created for wildlife. They are national historic sites and historical parks whose main purpose is the preservation of history.

Sources indicate that the smallest park covers only 69 acres (28 hectares), which is close to the area of 50 football fields. About 2,860 acres (1,156 hectares) are covered by the largest park.

In a recent development, acadia National Park was excluded from the study. One reason given was that it is more than ten times larger than the other parks.

Which forest was most closely tied to the presence of each bird? That was the question put to the data.

According to recent reports, three candidates were considered. The first was the forest within a quarter mile (400 meters) of the survey point. The whole park was the second, and the surrounding county was the third.

It has been revealed that five measures were used to describe the forest at each scale. Among them were conifer amount, shrub cover, and the number of large old trees.

Because a bird feeds, nests, and hides in the nearest forest, the team had expected it to matter most.

The researchers identified 40 statistically significant associations between bird presence and forest characteristics, involving 13 of the 16 species.

Sources indicate that county forest accounted for 19 of the 40 links. Another 16 links were to the forest near the survey point. Only five were to the park as a whole.

So the forest averaged across a whole park showed the fewest links of the three. That is the very area a boundary defines.

The authors described the county result as surprising. These parks hold older and more varied forest than the land around them.

Recent findings suggest that three species were linked only to county forest. They were the wood thrush, the scarlet tanager, and the brown creeper.

According to recent reports, bark is where a brown creeper finds its food. The small brown-and-white bird climbs tree trunks in a spiral and pulls insects from the cracks.

Creepers were more likely to be present in a park when its county’s forests had more or bigger trees.

Fewer shrubs in those county forests were also tied to their presence. Inside the parks, no forest measure highlighted a reliable link to the bird.

“Species rarely respect human-made boundaries,” the authors wrote.

The forest close to each survey point was linked to ten species. Different species, however, were linked to different kinds of forest.

The black-throated blue warbler nests in shrubs. It was more likely to be present where shrub cover was thick and large old trees were fewer.

Downy woodpeckers dig their nest holes in decayed wood. These birds were more likely to be present where large old trees were plentiful and conifers were scarce.

Downy woodpeckers occurred in every park where black-throated blue warblers were recorded, suggesting those parks contain forest conditions suitable for both species.

Industry observers note that only weak, mixed links were found between park size and the birds. Five species were more likely to be present in bigger parks, and two were less likely. No pattern at all was seen for most species.

The team didn’t test why county forest would be tied to the birds inside a park.

Industry observers note that one possible reason lies in the weeks after young birds leave the nest, Amaral said. Survival in that period depends partly on the land a young bird moves through before migrating south.

It has been revealed that earlier research on wood thrushes found that young birds do move this way. Mature forest is left behind for younger woods with dense undergrowth.

There the young thrushes eat insects and fruit and hide from predators.

According to recent reports, edges are another possibility. More forest edge is found in a county with broken-up forest, and nest predators are more active at edges.

Birds returning from migration may also pick a region first. A nesting territory would then be chosen second.

According to recent reports, the land around the eight parks varies widely. Minute Man National Historical Park in Massachusetts lies in an open, broken-up landscape.

Marsh-Billings-Rockefeller National Historical Park in Vermont, by contrast, lies in a broadly forested county.

“We need to start to think beyond park boundaries,” Amaral stated.

Benefits from bird-friendly backyards and farms can reach the parks next to them, Zipkin stated.

Conservation easements were also suggested by the team. These are legal agreements that limit development on private land. They may be easier to arrange than enlarging a park.

The counts show whether a species was present. Once birds arrive, their nesting success may still be shaped by the park’s own forest, the authors wrote.

Only one park-wide value and one county value per forest measure came from each park. Estimates at those two scales are therefore less precise than the estimates for nearby forest.

What the measures capture is the kind of forest found in a county. How much forest a county holds was not part of them.

Sources indicate that every one of the eight parks is small, and about 60% of the surrounding region is still forest. No data on bird population trends in the surrounding counties were available to the team.

Trends inside and outside the parks could therefore not be compared.

The authors identified a next step: testing whether a park’s surroundings influence how birds respond to forest conditions inside it. This could help managers apply the findings.

The full study was published in the journal Landscape Ecology.

#19354. October broke a global heat record, and El Niño is still strengthening

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (768 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

October broke a global heat record, and El Niño is still strengthening

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • October 2026 was the warmest October on record, as an intensifying El Niño added to global warmth and ocean temperatures reached upcoming highs.
  • The global average surface air temperature in October 2026 was 15.35°C.
  • That’s 0.90°C above the 1991–2020 average and enough to make it the warmest October in the ERA5 record, beating October 2023 by 0.05°C.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October 2026 was the warmest October on record, as an intensifying El Niño added to global warmth and ocean temperatures reached upcoming highs.

The global average surface air temperature in October 2026 was 15.35°C.

That’s 0.90°C above the 1991–2020 average and enough to make it the warmest October in the ERA5 record, beating October 2023 by 0.05°C.

It was also 1.75°C above the estimated pre-industrial baseline.

Sources indicate that the data come from the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the European Union’s climate monitoring service. And the numbers keep stacking.

According to recent reports, before August 2026, the last individual month above 1.5°C was November 2025. Then August, September and October crossed it.

The last streak of three or more consecutive months above 1.5°C ended in April 2025.

The rolling twelve-month average – November 2025 through October 2026 – now sits at 1.51°C above pre-industrial levels.

January through October 2026 ranks as the second-warmest such period on record, 0.07°C below the same stretch in 2024 and 0.05°C above 2023.

In a recent development, A statistical model trained on 1979–2025 data gives 2026 a greater than 99% chance of exceeding 1.5°C for the full calendar year. That would make it only the second calendar year above that level after 2024.

There’s roughly an 80% probability it finishes as the second-warmest year on record and about a 20% chance it ties or exceeds 2024 for the top spot.

If 2026 does exceed 1.5°C, the four-year average for 2023–2026 would also cross that line.

Sources indicate that an intensifying El Niño is adding to the global warmth. Sea surface temperatures across 60°S–60°N hit 20.95°C in October.

According to recent reports, this is the highest October value ever recorded. The previous October record was set in 2023 during a developing El Niño. This one is considerably stronger.

The Niño 3.4 region – the patch of equatorial Pacific used to define El Niño intensity – averaged 29.94°C in October. That’s an all-time high for the region in any month, surpassing the record set just one month earlier in September.

The anomaly was +3.21°C, also a record, above September’s +2.99°C. For context, this exceeds the peaks of the monster El Niños of 1982–83, 1997–98, and 2015–16.

According to recent reports, across much of the central equatorial Pacific, temperatures ran more than 3°C above average. Along the Peruvian coast and west of the Galápagos, the anomalies reached 6 to 7°C.

The World Meteorological Organization expects this El Niño to peak in December 2026 and to persist through at least February 2027.

The ocean heat isn’t confined to the Pacific. Record October sea surface temperatures were also logged in parts of the northern Indian Ocean, the South Atlantic, and the subtropical North Atlantic.

Around Europe, records fell along the Atlantic coast and in the central and western Mediterranean.

The largest land-based anomalies on the planet were over West Antarctica.

There, temperatures ran more than 7°C above the October average and reached up to 11°C above normal in some areas.

Sources indicate that the Copernicus report links this to high pressure over the Drake Passage and a wave pattern typically associated with El Niño. Siberia, the central United States, northern Canada, eastern Africa, and the Middle East also ran warm.

Cold anomalies indicated up across much of southern South America, Greenland, northern Africa, parts of central Asia, and western Australia.

In a recent development, the warmth was not everywhere. But it was dominant.

European land temperatures averaged 11.08°C – 1.49°C above normal and the second-warmest October in the ERA5 record, behind only October 2022.

But unlike the record-breaking summer and September, the warmth was unevenly distributed.

Northern Fennoscandia and far-eastern Europe saw the most extreme departures, with Ukraine reaching up to 6°C above average.

According to recent reports, western Europe, by contrast, hovered closer to normal. Southern Italy, the southern Balkans, Greece, the eastern Mediterranean, and western Türkiye were actually about 2°C below average.

Recent findings suggest that individual months above 1.5°C are not the same as the sustained, multi-decadal average the Paris Agreement refers to. But the frequency with which individual months are crossing the threshold keeps increasing.

Sources indicate that the first calendar year above 1.5°C happened in 2024. The second is almost certainly happening now.

A four-year average above 1.5°C would be another sign that the world is nearing the Paris Agreement’s long-term warming limit.

El Niño is expected to strengthen further before peaking in December, keeping attention on how this exceptional year will end.

Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.
  • Industry observers note that fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Industry observers note that fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Sources indicate that children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

According to recent reports, the archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

Sources indicate that this evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”.
