General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.
  • It has been revealed that on November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

It has been revealed that on November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

In a recent development, didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

In a recent development, the cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”.

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.).

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

It has been revealed that didymos spins so promptly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

In a recent development, scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” indicates planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” indicates planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer fresh avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

According to recent reports, for example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always highlighted the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” indicates planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

According to recent reports, similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

Nov. 15, 1988: The Buran orbiter introduces

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1976, the Soviet Union began development of the Buran orbiter.
  • According to recent reports, the Buran program marked several achievements – the development of 230 new technologies, a fully recoverable rocket capable of lifting 220,000 pounds (100,000 kilograms) to orbit, a shuttle that could carry up to 10 cosmonauts.
  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

In 1976, the Soviet Union began development of the Buran orbiter. Concerned that the American space shuttle program might be used for military purposes, the Soviets responded with Buran and its Energia booster rocket, which were capable of carrying antisatellite and antimissile weapons and targeting locations on Earth’s surface. Though the nonmilitary objectives for Buran included ferrying crew and supplies to the Mir Space Station, Buran was also capable of flying unmanned and fully automated.

According to recent reports, the Buran program marked several achievements – the development of 230 new technologies, a fully recoverable rocket capable of lifting 220,000 pounds (100,000 kilograms) to orbit, a shuttle that could carry up to 10 cosmonauts. However, it only made a single flight: On Nov. 15, 1988, Buran released from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, performed two orbits, and returned to Earth. The 206-minute flight was seamless, and was performed fully under remote control, with no crew members aboard. Despite this success, the colossal expense of the program and the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union meant the end of Buran. In 2002, the roof of a hangar at Baikonur collapsed, killing eight people and destroying the orbiter and its rocket.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.
  • According to recent reports, neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

According to recent reports, neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

In a recent development, although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

It has been revealed that “You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman notes. The upcoming study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

It has been revealed that the amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

In a recent development, patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao indicates.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao indicates, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao states.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 15: Mars and Jupiter in conjunction.

It’s a great night to catch Saturn’s largest and brightest moon, Titan, as it skims south of the planet. Two hours after sunset, Saturn is roughly 40° high in the southeast, outshining all the other stars in this region of the sky. It lies to the lower left of the Circlet of Pisces and to the upper left of the bright star Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus.

Zoom in on Saturn with a telescope to first catch sight of its ring system, stretching 43” from end to end and tilted 8° to our line of sight. Presently we are seeing Saturn’s southern side, including the entirety of the planet’s southern hemisphere. The gas giant’s disk now measures 19” across.

Titan is difficult to miss, shining at mid-8th magnitude just south of the ringed planet. Don’t be fooled by a fainter 10th-magnitude field star, which lies just to Titan’s west. The three next-brightest moons, also 10th magnitude, are Tethys, Dione, and Rhea. They lie closer to the planet. Tethys sits about 40” west of Saturn’s center shortly before 8 P.M. EST, while Dione is just west of the limb and Rhea just east of the planet. Dione and Rhea are moving westward, and Rhea will skim just north of Saturn’s pole along the way, standing due north of the planet around 10:40 P.M. EST. Tethys is moving east, and will disappear behind the planet’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 2:35 A.M. EST on the 16th (still late on the 15th along the Pacific Coast).

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Astronomy ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical shapes, such as ovals or pears, depending on composition?
  • Bodies large enough to be considered planets have enough mass that gravity molds them into a roughly spherical shape.
  • In a recent development, the key word here is roughly — other factors also come into play, such as a planet’s composition (rocky or gassy) and its rate of spin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could planets that orbit other stars be nonspherical shapes, such as ovals or pears, depending on composition?

Rich LivitskiSeal Beach, California.

Bodies large enough to be considered planets have enough mass that gravity molds them into a roughly spherical shape.

In a recent development, the key word here is roughly — other factors also come into play, such as a planet’s composition (rocky or gassy) and its rate of spin. The faster a planet spins, the more its rotation causes it to bulge outward at the equator. That’s because as a planet rotates, there’s a tug-of-war between the way material wants to fly off the planet due to rotation and the way gravity wants to pull all that planet’s material inward. The battle between these forces is most intense at the equator.

In our solar system, Mercury and Venus are slowly spinning rocky planets; therefore, they are the most spherical of the Sun’s worlds.

In a recent development, earth and Mars spin a little faster, so they are about 0.3% and 0.6% thicker at the equator than the poles, respectively. This shape is called an oblate spheroid. However, because these planets have a solid surface that is higher in some places than others, they are not perfect oblate spheroids — they are minutely lumpy and bumpy, as data from orbiting satellites have detailed. In fact, the surface area of Earth’s Southern Hemisphere is very slightly larger than its Northern Hemisphere, making Earth marginally pear-shaped. It’s important to note, however, that despite these deviations, Earth is still almost spherical — if you used a basketball to represent the shape of our planet, its deviation from a perfect sphere would be only about 0.03 inch (0.08 centimeter) at the middle.

It has been revealed that the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn bulge outward the most — Jupiter is nearly 7% thicker at its equator than its poles, and Saturn is 10.7% thicker around the middle. Ice giants Uranus and Neptune have smaller central bulges, only 2.3% and 1.7% thicker at the equator, respectively.

It has been revealed that what about exoplanets, though? Some planetary systems we’ve found experience much more extreme conditions, with large, gassy planets orbiting very close to their stars (called hot Jupiters). One of these hot Jupiters is WASP-121 b, which orbits a blazingly hot star. In fact, this planet orbits so closely to its star that gravitational forces have stretched it out into a football shape. Astronomers believe that if the planet were much closer to its star, it would be ripped apart entirely.

In addition to its stretched-out shape, WASP-121 b and other planets, including WASP-69 b and KELT-9 b, appear to have puffed-up atmospheres and cometlike tails. These tails form as their host stars blast the planets with high-energy radiation, knocking gas particles into space.

Sources indicate that as for pear-shaped exoplanets, astronomers haven’t found anything to suggest they exist to the extent you’re likely picturing. Other terrestrial planets likely have deformations similar to Earth’s — or perhaps slightly more extreme — but even “extreme” in this case probably translates to a planet appearing essentially spherical from a great distance.

This question and answer were originally published online October 24, 2020.

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In a recent development, in 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

It has been revealed that this chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

According to recent reports, these fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”.

Industry observers note that angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”.

Nov. 16, 1974: Arecibo sends a message

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the communication was aimed at M13, a globular cluster about 25,000 light-years away in Hercules.
  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

On Nov. 16, 1974, a group gathered at Arecibo Observatory in the rainforest interior of Puerto Rico, there for a reopening celebration after upgrades to the facility. After the requisite speeches, scientists used the radio telescope to send what would be known as the Arecibo message: 1,679 bits of data in 73 lines, each 23 characters long. To the assembled crowd, the dispatch sounded like nearly three minutes of two tones. But encoded in those tones was message crafted by a team of scientists led by Frank Drake and including Carl Sagan: a rough illustration of a human, the structure of a DNA double helix, and a map of the Earth’s position in the solar system.

Sources indicate that the communication was aimed at M13, a globular cluster about 25,000 light-years away in Hercules. Since it would take thousands of years for the signal to arrive there – not to mention time for a signal to be sent back by any extraterrestrial civilization that intercepted it – the Arecibo message wasn’t so much an actual attempt at communication as it was a demonstration of how we might do so.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#19317. Ancient Egyptians Revered Cats as Sacred. Then 131 Skulls Revealed What Really Happened to Them.

Ancient Egyptians Revered Cats as Sacred. Then 131 Skulls Revealed What Really Happened to Them.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Not every Egyptian necropolis was meant for humans.
  • Early archaeologists usually ignored animal mummies in favor of human mummies, which were often showcased at theatrical unwrapping parties.
  • It has been revealed that “Attention was also paid to the presence of pathologies and marks on the skulls, which could provide information about the conditions in which the cats were kept and their cause of death,” Van Neer and his colleagues wrote in their study, recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not every Egyptian necropolis was meant for humans. Across Egypt, the cemeteries of Bubastis in the eastern Nile Delta, the Bubasteion in northern Saqqara, and Speos Artemidos near Beni Hassan, along with others in Giza and the Dakhla Oasis, were meant for animals, especially cats. Cats were seen as the earthly embodiment of the feline goddess Bastet. Yet although they were often mummified as votive offerings, their treatment did not always match their status.

Early archaeologists usually ignored animal mummies in favor of human mummies, which were often showcased at theatrical unwrapping parties. Some animal mummies were used as ship ballast for the journey home after an expedition, while others were powdered for questionable medicine, burned for fuel, or ground into fertilizer. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, however, some animal mummies were unwrapped (without a party) so that their skeletal remains could inform studies of Egyptian fauna. Many of these skulls remain in museum collections in Egypt and abroad. Zooarchaeologist Wim Van Neer of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences and his research team studied one such collection: 131 exceptionally well-preserved skulls of small cats from Beni Hassan, now housed at the Natural History Museum in Vienna. Their goal was to find out how the cats lived before they died.

It has been revealed that “Attention was also paid to the presence of pathologies and marks on the skulls, which could provide information about the conditions in which the cats were kept and their cause of death,” Van Neer and his colleagues wrote in their study, recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science. In addition to carbon and nitrogen isotope analysis to determine diet, “characteristics such as dental abnormalities, infectious or metabolic disorders and trauma were recorded.”.

Most of the skulls turned out to be from domestic cats (Felis catus), with several jungle cats (Felis chaus) among them. Many of the animals apparently suffered from conditions such as gum disease and infections, and some skulls had puncture marks and fractures that could indicate fights between cats. How the cats met their end, however, was more disturbing. Evidence suggests that cats were deliberately killed so they could be turned into offerings to Bastet. Fourteen of the skulls show traumatic injuries, including blunt-force and sharp-force trauma. Sharp-force trauma is thought to have possibly killed the humans who were sacrificed to join First Dynasty pharaohs in the afterlife. Beyond fight wounds, some injuries were inflicted long enough before death to show signs of healing, which suggests that the animals may have endured physical violence from humans while still alive.

When Van Neer and his team took a closer look at one skull, they found marks consistent with blows from a sharp metal weapon. Wounds on some of the other skulls were thought to have been made by strikes from a heavy wooden implement. The cats’ treatment before death also seems to have been deplorable. Although no ancient records describe how the cats were kept, the researchers inferred that they were probably held in crowded enclosures. This could explain the fights, as well as the attacks on domestic cats by jungle cats, which were caught in marshlands or along the banks of the Nile when Egypt was lusher than it is today. Isotope analysis highlighted that the jungle cats’ diet clearly differed from that of the domestic cats, further suggesting that this species was unlikely to have been bred in captivity.

Even among the wild-caught jungle cats, six of the seven skulls came from animals with conditions similar to those of their domestic relatives. This was probably a sign that all of the cats, the overwhelming majority of which were adults, were kept in conditions that caused illness and injury before death. Radiocarbon dating revealed when they died.

In a recent development, cats are generally thought to have first been domesticated in the Fertile Crescent of the Near East roughly 10,000 years ago, although some recent genetic studies suggest it happened later, in Egypt or elsewhere in North Africa. In Egypt, the earliest clear evidence of domestic cats dates to the Middle Kingdom (c. 2000–1700 B.C.E.). However, demand for mummified cat offerings was greatest much later, in the Late and Ptolemaic Periods. Older feline mummies do exist, and one of the nine dated skulls goes back to the Third Intermediate Period. The other eight, however, date to between 380 and 40 B.C.E., from the end of the Late Period into the Ptolemaic era.

Industry observers note that as for how the cats were killed, blunt- or sharp-force trauma appears to have been the main cause of death. Some cats were strangled, but a blow to the head was apparently the more common method. “Skull fractures were the most common cause of death, whereas evidence of strangulation occurred less frequently,” the researchers mentioned. “Our observations of traumatic lesions on the skulls provide evidence of fatal injuries, as well as cases of animals that survived violent interactions with humans.”.

#19314. Why Do Helmets Still Fail to Stop Concussions? Scientists May Have Been Fighting the Wrong Force All Along.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (754 w)

Why Do Helmets Still Fail to Stop Concussions? Scientists May Have Been Fighting the Wrong Force All Along.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An estimated 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur in the U.S.
  • In a recent development, although helmets have grown safer over the years in certain sports, concussions are still commonplace.
  • Industry observers note that during World War II, Scottish physicist A.H.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An estimated 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur in the U.S. each year. They’re so common that you might assume they’re not as serious as other injuries—but in fact, these mild traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) can often be more dangerous. While tendons, muscle, and bone heal good as new, repeated and sustained concussions—a typical occurrence in many athletic endeavors—can lead to dementia and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), an aggressive degenerative brain disease.

In a recent development, although helmets have grown safer over the years in certain sports, concussions are still commonplace. That’s especially true in football, even after the high-profile introduction of the Guardian Cap for NFL preseason practices in 2022 and then in regular-season games in 2024. This suggests that there’s something about concussions, specifically the relationship of linear and rotational acceleration and the brain, that scientists still don’t understand.

Industry observers note that during World War II, Scottish physicist A.H.S. Holbourn argued that rotational acceleration (think of an uppercut to the jaw) was more dangerous than linear acceleration (a straight-on, direct hit whose force goes through the center of the head). His theory was that rotation was worse because it stretches and strains brain tissue by moving different parts at different speeds. Scientists have focused on protecting against rotation ever since.

It has been revealed that however, a latest Stanford Medicine-led study suggests that linear acceleration, not rotation, may be the better predictor of concussion. The research comes from the lab of bioengineer David Camarillo, who’s spent more than a decade studying concussions and helmet safety. By analyzing unprecedentedly accurate impact data from motion-sensing mouthguards worn by 203 athletes across seven different sports, Camarillo and his team discovered that Holbourn’s initial assumptions weren’t correct. The results of their study were published in the journal Annals of Biomedical Engineering.

“Holbourn’s reasoning was based just on mechanics; it wasn’t biology,” David Camarillo, senior author of the study, mentioned in a press statement. “The question we started out with many years ago was, ‘What are the forces required to cause concussion?’ If we understand the nature of those forces and the limits of the human brain, then it might be possible to prevent concussions.”.

Previous studies relied on helmet-mounted sensors, but the authors note that those sensors are often inaccurate because helmets tend to move around a lot. Across the mouthguard-enabled data set, the researchers analyzed 3,851 impacts, of which 47 were verified as concussions. In their mathematical models comparing the data, peak linear acceleration was the single most predictive factor in whether a hit eventually produced a concussion. Camarillo and his team haven’t pinned down a mechanism for this result, but they suspect one of two culprits: the brain striking the inside of the skull, or cavitation, in which sudden pressure changes form tiny bubbles that then collapse.

According to recent reports, if these results hold up in future studies, they could have profound implications for helmet safety and design. The mouthguard data highlighted that a hit producing 100 g of linear acceleration (100 times the acceleration of gravity) carries a 50 percent risk of concussion. That’s far lower than the often-cited 192 g threshold from earlier helmet-sensor studies. At 150 g, a hit that older data would have considered below the danger line, concussion risk tops 99 percent.

Sources indicate that “Why are there so many concussions even when people are wearing helmets?” Camarillo asked. “Part of the answer could be in this paper, which is that the linear accelerations that we previously thought were safe, we now see are much more dangerous.”.

According to recent reports, in a way, the newly introduced results offer a bit of hope that helmets do have room for improvement, and with a greater focus on addressing linear acceleration, concussions could significantly drop in the coming years and decades. One Stanford-developed technology is a helmet with liquid-filled pads that reduces peak linear acceleration and knocks nearly 20 percentage points off the chances of concussion on high-impact hits versus standard football helmets.

Sources indicate that “If linear acceleration is its own distinct mechanism of concussion and it’s very common, then we’ve been missing a lot,” Camarillo said. “We haven’t tried as hard to optimize for this variable. It gives me some hope that there’s a new opportunity for preventing concussions.”.

  • As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.
  • The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, states at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

According to recent reports, despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover fresh life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Luján Agusti/National Geographic.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Sources indicate that throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

In a recent development, then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber states. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

It has been revealed that from the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

In a recent development, “The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy claims. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”.

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

Industry observers note that but it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”.

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” states Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

According to recent reports, as a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Recent findings suggest that expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

November 16: Titan south, Rhea north.

Sources indicate that early this evening brighter targets are best, as the Moon doesn’t set until late. Ready for viewing as the winter constellations start to dominate earlier each day is the Pleiades, an open cluster cataloged as M45.

Known since antiquity and readily visible to the naked eye, the Pleiades contains several bright stars arranged in a tiny dipperlike shape. Located in northwestern Taurus, the cluster is sometimes mistaken for the Little Dipper, although that asterism is much larger and lies in the northern sky, anchored at the end of its handle by Polaris, the North Star. The Pleiades shines with a collective magnitude of 1.6 and spans roughly 110’ — a huge swath of sky. It lies above the sideways V-shape of Taurus’ face as the Bull rises in the east this evening, and is already 30° high by 7:30 P.M. local time. How many stars can you make out with the naked eye? Most observers see six or seven.

Once you’ve taken in the cluster without any optical aid, zoom in with binoculars or a finder scope. (Any higher magnification and you won’t see most of the cluster at once, but instead be limited to a smaller portion.) Many more stars will now pop into your field of view. If you do opt for high magnification, look for a faint grayish haze around the stars — this is nearby dust reflecting the stars’ light, and requires clear, dark conditions to make out.

It has been revealed that the Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight, with the best meteor viewing overnight into the early-morning hours of November 18, as the Moon sets around midnight and the radiant rises higher. Keep reading for more detail below on how to observe the shower.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:47 A.M.Sunset: 4:42 P.M.Moonrise: 12:56 P.M.Moonset: —Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (57%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early on the morning of the 18th, after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.

Recent findings suggest that two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.

It has been revealed that to catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per hour.

Archaeologists Found a Castaway Camp on an Island at the End of the World. Did a Legendary Sailor Build It?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that while hunting penguins for oil (yes, people really do that) in 1873, famed Argentine sailor Luis Piedra Buena wrecked his schooner brig Espora off the southern tip of South America. He and his crew regrouped on a deserted beach, spent about two months building a new cutter, the Luisito, and sailed safely to Chile to tell their tale. Now, researchers believe they may have found pieces of a shipwreck and the remains of a “castaway camp” possibly tied to Piedra Buena on Isla de los Estados, an island “at the end of the world.”.

In a new study published in the journal Antiquity, lead author Nicolás Ciarlo of Spain’s University of Cádiz and his colleagues describe how their research into the maritime history of the island, which lies across the Strait of Le Maire from the tip of Tierra del Fuego, led them to a castaway camp. They believe the camp may link the island’s Lacroix Inlet in Franklin Bay to the more than 150-year-old survival story.

Isla de los Estados is probably best known for a lighthouse that inspired Jules Verne’s novel The Lighthouse at the End of the World. The island forms the easternmost point of Argentina’s Tierra del Fuego Province, and from the 17th century onward it lay along a key sailing route.

In a recent development, by 1870, the Argentine government had granted the island to Piedra Buena. Although he never established a settlement there, he sailed past it countless times while pursuing his interests throughout Patagonia. Then disaster struck. “During a campaign for exploiting penguins for oil, he and his crew lost the schooner brig Espora,” according to the study.

The crew survived, built a cutter, and sailed to Punta Arenas, Chile. There, Piedra Buena described the time they had spent at Lacroix Inlet, although experts have long doubted that he identified the location correctly.

In a recent development, to test his account, the research team visited Lacroix Inlet in January 2026 with help from the Argentine Navy. There, they found the “remains of a shipwreck and a temporary camp” on a wind-battered stretch of coast at the base of a cliff, exposed to strong southwesterly storms. The “possible castaway camp” sat near a stream.

In a recent development, “Although there is still no common agreement, Piedra Buena’s account and other documentary evidence suggest that this bay is likely the place where the Espora sank,” the authors wrote. “The location and material culture of the temporary occupation at Lacroix Inlet point to a connection between this site and the nearby shipwreck remains and thus, possibly with the Espora and her crew.”.

At the camp, which the team described as a “short-term occupation,” they found glass beads, buttons, and a bottle, along with nautical items such as a deck prism and a rudder hinge. Elsewhere in the inlet lay the remains of three wooden hulls, including timber that may have been used to build a structure. All the wood likely came from ships’ hulls, but it’s unclear whether it all came from the same vessel.

It has been revealed that the team called the finds “novel data” on the history of seafaring around the island. Their preliminary assessment points to at least one shipwreck that led to a temporary settlement. “The identity of the vessel/s and the castaways’ trajectories are the subject of ongoing inquiry,” they wrote, adding that a thorough study of the timbers may provide definitive answers.

Some artifacts are especially telling. “The deck glass located on the surface is one of the most revealing artifacts,” Ciarlo told Discover Magazine. “To assess the identity of the Espora—as it happens with other shipwreck sites—is like putting together a puzzle. It does not rely on a unique proof, but on a critical analysis and merging of multiple lines of evidence.”.

According to recent reports, still, questions remain. In the study, the authors acknowledged that they found no trace of the site where the Luisito was built, and it’s unclear whether the Espora was ever completely taken apart. They wrote that more work is needed at the camp and on the shipwrecks in the weather-beaten inlet.

“As archaeologists,” Ciarlo noted, according to Phys.org, “being in this isolated and wild place allowed us to taste what a small group of castaways saw and felt about 150 years ago.”.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

An overwhelming percentage of transgender and gender diverse young people in the United States express satisfaction with gender-affirming hormone therapy.

Industry observers note that almost 400 transgender and gender diverse young people reflected on their decision to take hormone therapy in the largest such survey to date. Nearly 97 percent affirmed it was the right decision, researchers report November 9 in JAMA Pediatrics. Only about 3 percent, or 10 individuals, remarked they regretted the step, and of those, seven felt the experience was harmful.

With concerns around youth well-being fueling limits on gender-affirming hormone therapy, the researchers write, “the results provide further support for the existing standards of care [and] do not support efforts to categorically restrict or ban access.”.

Gender-affirming hormone therapy — with the masculinizing hormone testosterone or the feminizing hormone estrogen — allows a person’s body to better match their gender identity. Around 3 percent of 13- to 17-year-olds in the United States identify as transgender.

Among the study’s 376 young people, who were former patients of a clinic for transgender and gender diverse youth, nearly 92 percent began hormones at 17 or younger. Thirty percent took estrogen and 70 percent took testosterone, with the amount of time since starting the hormones averaging five years.

As per clinical guidelines for transgender health care, young people interested in medical treatment, joined by parents or guardians, began with an assessment visit with a mental health professional. For the study, participants took a yearly survey, filled out anytime from one month prior to six months following the anniversary of this initial visit. The research team analyzed surveys submitted from 2023 to 2025.

In a recent development, the latest research adds to growing evidence on the benefits of gender-affirming hormone therapy for transgender young people. Gender-affirming hormones improve the alignment these young people experience between their appearance and their gender, increase their satisfaction with life and reduce depression and anxiety.

But state bans have curtailed young people’s access to gender-affirming care, which can include hormone therapy and puberty blockers. As of November 2026 in the United States, 28 states have laws or policies that limit this care, according to the health policy organization KFF. More than half of transgender young people age 13 to 17 reside in states that restrict gender-affirming care. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Endocrine Society support gender-affirming health care for young people and provide evidence-backed guidelines for treatment.

Industry observers note that the phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

According to recent reports, the phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

RELATED: 20 things to see on the Moon.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

According to recent reports, blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Industry observers note that black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four Newly introduced Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Sources indicate that harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

Sources indicate that what is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

Recent findings suggest that how does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and Upcoming Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

Breaking: NASA's Voyager 1 mission forever changed our view of Jupiter

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a fresh milestone.
  • While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune.
  • In a recent development, one of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Wednesday (Nov. 18), humanity's most distant spacecraft will hit a fresh milestone. NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been exploring our solar system at increasingly remote depths since 1977, will reach 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth — a distance so vast, it takes light 24 hours to traverse the space between Voyager and our planet.

While we celebrate this achievement on Earth, Voyager 1 will observe its "light-day" in darkness; mission scientists turned off the probe's camera in 1990, immediately after it snapped its iconic "Pale Blue Dot" and "Solar System Family Portrait" images from beyond the orbit of Neptune. But before that, Voyager 1 had already taken tens of thousands of images of our cosmic neighborhood, and some of them totally transformed our understanding of the outer planets.

In a recent development, one of the most significant pieces of Voyager 1's legacy is its trip to Jupiter. From January to April 1979, the probe observed the solar system's largest planet and several of its giant moons up close, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As it approached, Voyager snapped a photo of the gas giant every 96 seconds to create this incredible time-lapse movie of Jupiter's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of a month in 1979.

Voyager observed discrete bands of Jupiter's atmosphere spinning at various speeds and in different directions, like a cosmic Rubik's Cube being twisted by an invisible hand. Clouds speed by as if on conveyor belts as giant, planet-size storms swirl.

It has been revealed that voyager's time-lapse film captures about 60 full days on Jupiter — the equivalent of about a month on Earth, since each Jupiter day is roughly 10 Earth hours —- providing the most comprehensive and high-resolution look at the planet yet. The observations significantly built on the data captured by NASA's Pioneer 10 and 11 Jupiter probes, which introduced half a decade prior, showing the planet's atmosphere to be much more dynamic than astronomers realized.

According to recent reports, just before making its closest approach to the planet, Voyager spotted something remarkable: Jupiter had a thin, faint ring system. Made primarily of dust, the rings appeared only when Voyager saw Jupiter backlit by the sun. No telescope had ever seen this before, but ground-based observatories soon confirmed the rings' existence, and Voyager 2 took even clearer pictures of the rings when it reached Jupiter in July 1979.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring of dust around Jupiter when it was backlit by the sun.

We now know that all four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — have rings. Today, scientists suspect Jupiter's dusty rings are replenished partially by volcanic eruptions on the planet's volatile moon Io.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This discovery, too, can be linked to Voyager. While making a close approach to Io, the spacecraft witnessed the first-ever volcanic eruption on a world beyond Earth. This observation highlighted that moons, not just planets, can be geologically active. In this image, a giant volcano called Loki Patera (the largest volcano on Io, measuring an estimated 125 miles, or 200 km, wide) spews its guts into space.

Voyager 1 witnessed a volcanic eruption (blue) on Io — the first volcaic eruption seen beyond Earth.

It has been revealed that taken together, these observations of Jupiter and its moons revealed the largest planet and its moons to be a far more dynamic, complicated and chaotic system than anyone had realized. Moreover, the close-up views of these distant worlds made them more than just dots in the sky. It made them fully realized worlds — places to explore, map and eventually visit. Just this week, China's space agency unveiled its intention to send a lander to Jupiter's moon Callisto in the first-ever landing mission to the Jovian system.

Voyager 1's work continues in interstellar space, which it officially reached in 2012. With its camera off, it studies the radiation environment of space using magnetic field and plasma detectors — the last two of its 10 science instruments still receiving power. Scientists suspect the legendary probe will fully run out of power in the 2030s.

#19298. We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1644 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

We know how to stop computer worms. But what if AI helps them persist?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AI is already powering latest, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar.
  • Sources indicate that recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen.
  • In a recent development, the results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, AI is already powering latest, more adaptable forms of cyberattack, but hackers typically wield the technology from afar. What if they set the AI models themselves loose to self-replicate and spread in a malicious manner?

Sources indicate that recent experiments have demonstrated two different ways this could happen. Two independent teams highlighted how a cyberattacker could turn an AI model into a “worm,” a type of malware that, unlike a computer virus, spreads on its own. And AI unlocked a latest worm power: adapting attacks to different devices.

In a recent development, the results hint at a new way AI could be used to ramp up cybersecurity threats — not just to computer systems but to smart devices such as security cameras or refrigerators. The good news is that the world still has time to build up defenses as several obstacles remain before this type of malware would work in the real world, claims AI researcher Jonas Guan.

AI could indeed make a worm “much harder to stop,” he says, but “there are a lot of kinks to iron out before something like this really works at scale.”.

Sources indicate that here is how a worm cyberattack works. A malware worm squirms through the internet, copying itself onto whatever systems it can hijack. Hackers can then mine hijacked systems directly for their data or link them together into a botnet and use its computing power, often to send spam email or overwhelm websites with traffic, knocking them offline.

In a recent development, historically, computer worms have been small, simple programs preprogrammed to take advantage of specific security weaknesses. So they could only get into devices that had that weakness. When defenders patched a worm’s target, it could no longer spread. With an AI model directing its actions, however, a worm can adapt and learn on the fly, choosing its line of attack depending on the device, notes Guan, of the University of Toronto.

That adaptability enables the worm to burrow into many different types of devices, both experiments revealed. When hackers unleash AI from afar, they orchestrate what the model does. An AI worm that copies itself widely could hypothetically escape anyone’s control.

Industry observers note that still, there’s a caveat to the experiments’ results, says Michael Alexander Riegler, a cybersecurity researcher at Simula Metropolitan Center for Digital Engineering in Oslo, Norway. Both teams’ test environments made it easier for the AI worm to spread than it would be in the real world, says Riegler, who was not involved in either study.

In a recent development, and there’s another practical obstacle to the unleashing of AI worms. They use more computing power and take up more space than a conventional worm. The Mirai worm, which took down a slew of websites including Reddit and Spotify in 2016, was a few kilobytes in size, while the medium-sized AI models in the experiments were tens of gigabytes. That’s still way smaller than the massive, top-of-the-line models behind the “rogue AI” incidents that made headlines earlier in 2026. (And those weren’t worms, because they didn’t copy themselves and spread.).

Most devices — including typical laptop computers — don’t have enough space or the right kind of chips to run worm-capable AI models, Guan claims. But new versions of devices, such as security cameras, are coming out with advanced hardware for running AI, researchers at the AI company Anthropic write. And at the same time, even smaller AI models are becoming more capable of sophisticated cyberattacks. These developments could expand the pool of devices an AI worm could exploit.

Recent findings suggest that “The ingredients are converging” to make AI worms more realistic, Riegler notes. How quickly they will converge is up for debate. Anthropic puts the timeline at months into the future, but both Riegler and Guan say it will probably take longer.

According to recent reports, the Mirai worm spread itself through smart devices including home routers, security cameras and even baby monitors. It broke into these devices by trying a small set of common default usernames and passwords. “Just using this very simple technique, this Mirai botnet was able to infect hundreds of thousands of devices,” says cybersecurity expert Zane Ma of Oregon State University in Corvallis, who presented an analysis of the attack at a 2017 security symposium. High-profile downed sites such as Reddit were actually collateral damage: A small group of young hackers had created the worm to mess with gaming servers.

Recent findings suggest that rebooting an infected device cleared Mirai. Changing its default login credentials prevented reinfection through the same route. But an AI-powered worm might make cleaning up this type of cybersecurity breach much more difficult. Why? Because the AI worm acts more like an octopus, Guan claims.

Guan and colleagues tested this octopus-worm in a virtual network. Anchored by several powerful computers that each had a chip called a graphics processing unit, or GPU, the faux networks also contained simulations of smart devices, including office printers and security cameras.

Industry observers note that the octopus’s AI model head started on a single machine with a GPU. From there it sent out tentacles to take control of smaller devices. Upon encountering a fresh device, the head would use AI to blueprint how its tentacle could hack in. Often, a hack wouldn’t work, but the octopus wouldn’t give up. It would use info about how it failed to come up with a new hack to try. That ability is “a new, hypercharged way of attacking systems,” Riegler notes. Whenever it found a computer with a large enough GPU, it would copy its head onto that new machine.

An attacker would probably launch an octopus-style AI worm from the cloud. Click through this slideshow to see how it might spread autonomously. First, it takes over and copies itself onto a device with the right kind of hardware (chip icon) to house an AI model (first image). From there, it sends out tentacles (red arrows) to hack into any connected devices, like 3-D printers and security cameras (second image). Devices that don’t have enough space for the AI model become jumping-off points for the octopus-worm to discover newly introduced places to copy itself (third image).

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

According to recent reports, J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

J. Hirshfeld; adapted from J. Guan et al/arXiv.org, 2026.

Industry observers note that the head could also search a simulated internet for information about newly discovered vulnerabilities. (The team didn’t connect it to the real internet for obvious reasons — protection against an AI octopus invasion — and spent considerable effort making sure their creation couldn’t escape the lab, Guan indicates.).

The octopus-worm even came up with a way to survive a reboot, something Guan notes they hadn’t asked it to do. The team posted a preprint of their findings at arXiv.org on June 2, and the paper is now going through peer review.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, at Anthropic, researchers indicated another way an AI worm might work by building on Guan and his colleagues’ research. If an octopus-worm wasn’t weird enough, Anthropic dubbed its creation a “digital slime mold”, a name that captures the model’s slow, oozing behavior. Anthropic declined to comment for this story, but Guan says the company’s work indicates that “unlike human reasoning, AI reasoning can be distributed.” That means an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily need to hijack a powerful computer to copy and run itself — it could spread its “thinking” out among smaller devices.

And that’s exactly what the slime mold version of an AI worm does. It breaks itself up and runs pieces of the model on multiple smaller devices. In their report posted online October 12, the Anthropic researchers used 15 Android smart TVs that they had networked together.

In a recent development, anthropic’s chopped-up model processes data thousands of times more slowly than what’s possible with GPUs similar to the ones Guan and colleagues relied on. That’s because the model’s data has to travel over internet connections that could take it all around the world during processing, rather than remaining in one place, within chips optimized for AI processing. That pace was too slow to demonstrate an ability to spread like a computer worm, Guan notes. So the Anthropic team ran a separate experiment with an AI worm running on GPUs that showed it could spread and adapt its attacks to different kinds of devices.

Sources indicate that whether AI worms are coming in months or whether we have longer to prepare, defenders should get ready now, Guan notes. And AI worms do have weaknesses.

For one thing, the large size of an AI worm could be its downfall. Even if smaller AI models become more capable, these are still big programs that guzzle computing power. You might not notice if your fridge or microwave suddenly started sending lots of traffic onto the network, but your internet service provider would. They’d realize “there’s something weird going on on these devices,” Ma says. From there, they could quarantine affected devices, disconnecting them from the internet to prevent further spread.

Ma also points out that most smart devices in a person’s home aren’t directly connected to the public internet. Most home networks use a router as a central hub, and that provides a layer of protection against a worm attack.

Strong passwords, regular updates and other normal security measures would also protect against the attacks demonstrated in both experiments, Riegler claims.

Sources indicate that guan and some colleagues are now testing specific defenses to stop AI worms, including devising an AI-driven defender. Trying to anticipate emerging threats and protect systems ahead of time is “what I’m passionate about,” Guan states. “We are working on the problem day and night.”.
